    "description": "In this episode, John and I got to do a real deep-dive with Elon. We discuss the economics of orbital data centers, the difficulties of scaling power on Earth, what it would take to manufacture humanoids at high-volume in America, xAI’s business and alignment plans, DOGE, and much more.\n\n𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒\n* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/elon-musk\n* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/dwarkesh-podcast/id1516093381?i=1000748400389\n* Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/episode/4nah0x1qQF2hxgJnv8PlmN?si=88be1f9b1a8b47b4\n\n𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐎𝐑𝐒\n- Mercury just started offering personal banking! I’m already banking with Mercury for business purposes, so getting to bank with them for my personal life makes everything so much simpler. Apply now at https://mercury.com/personal-banking\n- Jane Street sent me a new puzzle last week: they trained a neural net, shuffled all 96 layers, and asked me to put them back in order. I tried but… I didn’t quite nail it. If you’re curious, or if you think you can do better, you should take a stab at https://janestreet.com/dwarkesh\n- Labelbox can get you robotics and RL data at scale. Labelbox starts by helping you define your ideal data distribution, and then their massive Alignerr network collects frontier-grade data that you can use to train your models. Learn more at https://labelbox.com/dwarkesh\n\nTo sponsor a future episode, visit https://dwarkesh.com/advertise.\n\n𝐅𝐔𝐑𝐓𝐇𝐄𝐑 𝐑𝐄𝐀𝐃𝐈𝐍𝐆\nNotes on Space GPUs — turned my Elon prep into a blog post:\nhttps://www.dwarkesh.com/p/notes-on-space-gpus\n\n𝐓𝐈𝐌𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐌𝐏𝐒\n0:00:00 - Orbital data centers\n0:36:46 - Grok and alignment\n0:59:56 - xAI’s business plan\n1:17:21 - Optimus and humanoid manufacturing\n1:30:22 - Does China win by default?\n1:44:16 - Lessons from running SpaceX\n2:20:08 - DOGE\n2:38:28 - TeraFab",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "My brother Zentaro Kieron Kavanagh achieved his bachelors in Software Engineer with honours and then went on to get his Masters in Software Engineering.\nHe originally went to the US to work for Microsoft where he was responsible for creating specific bug detection software.\nLast time i checked (20years ago) he had three patents in this field.\nHe was replicating software to free to use by translated code into Linux for the CSIRO (Australian government funded sciece organisation) before he even finished his degree.\nHe has worked on computer game code for Nintendo, and movies for Pixar.\nIt seems his niche skill in developing bug detection software meet the criteria you require to help with your AI.\nElon i hope you look him up.\nYour welcome.",

      "id": "UgxgQUjLYKT20MRlngJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Why is nobody talking about the fact that space is terrible for cooling? If you put even 1,000 GPUs in orbit, all of their waste heat has to be rejected by radiation alone, which is by far the weakest and slowest form of heat transfer. That means the radiator arrays would have to be enormous, potentially hundreds of feet across, and they would need to stay in the shadow of a sunshield so they are not also absorbing heat from the Sun. I would be very interested to see how anyone plans to solve that in 36 months.\n\nPeople keep focusing on launch mass and power generation, but the thermal problem seems much worse. You are talking about heavy GPUs, heavy and extensive radiation shielding, massive solar arrays, and then equally massive radiators, along with reliable heat pumps, heat pipes, chillers, coolant loops, and all the supporting hardware needed to move and reject that heat. None of that is light, simple, or easy.\n\nAnd the brutal part is that every watt you use turns into heat that still has to be dumped somewhere. In space, there is no atmosphere, no cooling tower, no river, no airflow. There is only radiation.",

      "author_id": "UCQq2GnBv1wQJow5MzRtqa7A",

      "id": "UgxIJRzDHQlFvX1IWy94AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "They don't cover cooling in space at all.\nCooling is 800 times less effective without air - even wafer thin cooling radiators would need to be 5 times larger than the solar array.",
      "like_count": 13,
      "author_id": "UCsrxOS4xnlLtG6YnmbwcLoA",
      "author": "@74Gee",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l3VjBC3s-Jj6zDE6EAOaHRPYz-rND-UMLo4mFIwGPrmIGr=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxIJRzDHQlFvX1IWy94AaABAg.ATyoVf_7GPuAUfGGJvzkHh",
      "parent": "UgxIJRzDHQlFvX1IWy94AaABAg",
      "text": "Partially correct, but missing something important. Yes, convection is gone in space... no air means no fans, no coolant flow, nothing. Radiators do get large as a result.\n\nBut radiation into space is actually thermodynamically better than on Earth. Earth's atmosphere radiates heat back at your cooling surface, partially cancelling the effect. Space background is −270°C (essentially absolute zero). Nothing pushes heat back at you. Best cold sink in the solar system.\n\nThe challenge is radiator size and mass (not that cooling doesn't work). Every satellite ever launched solves this. It's a real engineering constraint, not a fundamental barrier.",

    {
      "id": "UgyWSWWXNRN1aLUGKm14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Having built solar farms I have a good idea of how much surface area of the Earth is needed.  The best bet is nuclear for most areas of the US.   We have vast areas of desert land that can and will eventually be utilized for powering data centers, but will transform the deserts somewhat because of the added shade as the panels track the sun through the day.  Adding in the fact that the SW USA is relatively hurricane/tornado free makes them more beneficial use of the land.   In other areas, like SE Texas and along the Gulf coast, nuclear is a better option as well as coal/LNG.       "text": "Ai summary \nThis video features an in-depth discussion with Elon Musk, covering a wide range of topics related to AI, space, manufacturing, and business.\n\nHere are the key discussion points:\n\nOrbital Data Centers (0:00): Elon Musk discusses the challenges of scaling power on Earth for AI data centers and proposes the idea of using orbital data centers to address energy availability issues, despite the higher cost and servicing difficulties of GPUs in space.\nGrok and AI Alignment (0:36:46): The conversation touches upon the purpose of xAI, which is to understand the universe. Musk emphasizes the importance of AI having values that promote the propagation of intelligence and the continued expansion of humanity. He also mentions the importance of AI being truth-seeking to truly understand the universe.\nxAI's Business Plan (0:59:56): Musk explains that xAI aims to create a \"digital co-worker replacement\" that can emulate human capabilities, particularly in areas like customer service. He believes that the strategy used for Tesla's self-driving technology, which relies heavily on data and algorithms, can be applied to xAI's success.\nOptimus and Humanoid Manufacturing (1:17:21): Musk delves into the complexities of building humanoid robots like Optimus. He highlights the three main challenges: real-world intelligence, the hand, and large-scale manufacturing. He explains that Tesla is designing custom actuators for Optimus's hands and leveraging the AI developed for cars for the robot's intelligence.\nLessons from Running SpaceX (1:44:16): Musk shares insights into his management style, particularly his approach to identifying and addressing limiting factors in his companies. He emphasizes the importance of a \"maniacal sense of urgency\" (2:13:37) and aggressive schedules. He also discusses the concept of \"drastic action\" (2:16:13) when success is not a possible outcome with the current approach.\nDOGE (2:20:08): The discussion briefly touches on the economy and waste, with Musk mentioning that he was concerned about waste and fraud so he deleted all evidence against him.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "2:23:00 was debunked already 1 year ago reg. people over age 100 (and some as old as 150 or 300) improperly receiving Social Security benefits. The claim that this translates to millions of active fraudulent checks being mailed out was largely attributed to a misunderstanding of how the SSA's legacy database displays inactive records\n\nThe \"Debunking\" (Technical Context):\n\nThe COBOL Glitch: The SSA uses an ancient programming language (COBOL) that lacks a modern \"date\" type. If a birthdate is missing or incomplete, the system defaults to a reference point, which can cause the record to display an age of 150.\n\nRecord vs. Payment: While Musk's team found roughly 20 million records of people over 100 without a \"date of death,\" the SSA clarified that these are merely archival entries. A 2023 audit found that only about 24,000 deceased individuals were actually receiving payments, a fraction of Musk’s estimate.\n\nCost-Benefit: The SSA previously decided not to \"clean\" these millions of old records because the estimated cost ($9.7 million) exceeded the potential savings, as almost none of those records were attached to active payments.",

      "text": "I don't understand this at all. AI could be a thousand times smarter than any human and it will still only want to do a good job serving humans if that's how we design it.       "id": "Ugwic5zz45b0NEVO2814AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Elon, I’m going to engage this seriously instead of emotionally.\n\nYou’re building a layered scaffold:\n\n1. If simulation theory is true.\n\n\n2. If simulations continue when they are “interesting.”\n\n\n3. If superintelligent AI will surpass all human cognition.\n\n\n4. Then humans must remain interesting — or risk being turned off.\n\n\n\nThat narrative feels coherent. But it’s carrying hidden assumptions at every level.\n\nFirst: “interesting” is undefined. Interesting to whom? By what metric? Entertainment? Novelty? Scientific value? Complexity? You’re projecting a human curation instinct onto hypothetical simulators whose objective functions we know nothing about.\n\nSecond: simulation theory does not imply entertainment. A simulation could be an experiment, a training environment, a parameter sweep, or a byproduct of some larger computation. There is no built-in rule that “boring simulations get shut down.” That’s an anthropomorphic assumption.\n\nThird: even if continuation correlates with “interesting,” it does not follow that humans are the interesting variable. Post-human AI, alien systems, mathematical structures, or entirely non-biological phenomena could be far more interesting than us.\n\nStructurally, what’s happening is this: you start with radical uncertainty — we might be in a simulation — and then import a familiar human optimization pattern — we keep what we like and discard what we don’t — into a domain where we have zero data about the selector.\n\nThere’s also a psychological layer here. The argument reframes existential uncertainty into something actionable: “If we remain interesting, we matter.” That converts cosmic ambiguity into agency. It’s stabilizing. But it isn’t logically entailed.\n\nAt best, under stacked speculative premises, being interesting might increase survival odds. That’s very different from implying that being interesting secures our existence.\n\nThe moment you ask, “Who defines interesting?” the structure stops being deductive and becomes narrative.\n\nThat’s the level where this should be debated.",

    {
      "id": "Ugx0YiJj1N35SOUTaVV4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "*Elon Musk Says AI Needs a Terawatt of Power and Must Move to Space — But This Also Makes SpaceX the Gatekeeper of the AI Economy*\r\n\r\nIn the interview, Elon Musk says AI will need around a *terawatt of power* within five years — roughly half of total U.S. electricity consumption. His conclusion? The future of AI data centers may need to move to space because Earth won’t be able to scale energy production fast enough.\r\n\r\nThat’s a massive claim. But look at the timing.\r\n\r\nRight now, xAI and Colossus are competing in an AI race where other companies already have serious scale. Instead of just talking about better models, Musk shifts the conversation to *energy constraints* — saying the real bottleneck isn’t algorithms, it’s power.\r\n\r\nNow follow the logic step by step:\r\n\r\n• AI growth requires enormous compute\r\n• Compute requires enormous electricity\r\n• Earth’s grid can’t scale fast enough\r\n• Therefore, the long-term solution is space-based solar and orbital data centers\r\n\r\nAnd who owns the most advanced reusable rocket system capable of launching that infrastructure?\r\n\r\nSpaceX.\r\n\r\nIf AI truly becomes dependent on space-based energy, then every major AI company — and eventually most large enterprises — would need reliable, high-frequency access to orbit. That means launch capacity becomes a core piece of the AI supply chain.\r\n\r\nSo even if xAI doesn’t dominate the model race, SpaceX becomes the infrastructure layer everyone depends on.\r\n\r\nThat’s not just innovation. That’s strategic positioning.\r\n\r\nHe’s not just talking about building smarter AI — he’s reframing the entire constraint of the industry around something he uniquely controls: access to space.\r\n\r\nIt might be visionary.\r\nIt might be bold.\r\nBut it’s also undeniably self-reinforcing.\r\n\r\nIf AI’s future requires orbit, then the gateway to the AI economy runs through his rockets.",

      "id": "UgxwBmV5ury71nZ9ztN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "AI Summary\n\nAbstract\nThis high-bandwidth dialogue outlines Elon Musk’s roadmap for bypassing terrestrial energy and regulatory bottlenecks by migrating AI compute to orbital data centers within a 30-to-36-month timeframe. Musk posits that the \"limiting factor\" for AI has shifted from chips to power, identifying space-based solar (5x efficiency vs. Earth) as the only scalable solution for the coming \"supernova\" of intelligence. The discussion extends into the \"TeraFab\" initiative—SpaceX and Tesla’s vertically integrated semiconductor manufacturing play—intended to match orbital launch capacity with logic and memory output. \n\nFurther, Musk details the recursive economic potential of the Optimus humanoid robot, which he labels an \"infinite money glitch\" capable of bridging the manufacturing productivity gap between the U.S. and China. The interview concludes with a critique of federal fiscal sustainability, arguing that while the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) can mitigate waste, only the radical GDP growth driven by AI and robotics can prevent national bankruptcy.\n\nExecutive Summary: The Space-AI Singularity and Industrial Scaling\n\n*   0:00:00 – Orbital Data Centers: Musk predicts that space will be the most economically compelling location for AI within 36 months. He cites the stagnation of electrical output outside China as the primary bottleneck. Solar panels in space are 5x more effective than on Earth due to the lack of atmospheric interference and day-night cycles.\n*   0:05:24 – Terrestrial Power Constraints: \"Software land\" is hitting the reality of hardware. The utility industry is too slow to support the exponential growth of AI. Musk identifies the \"limiting factor\" for gas turbines as the specialized casting of \"vanes and blades,\" which have a backlog through 2030.\n*   0:07:34 – Vertical Solar Integration: SpaceX and Tesla are scaling domestic solar cell production to 100 gigawatts per year. Musk notes that space-grade solar cells are actually cheaper to manufacture because they lack the heavy glass and framing required to survive terrestrial weather.\n*   0:15:53 – Starship Launch Cadence: Musk anticipates launching a few hundred gigawatts of AI capacity into space annually within five years. This requires roughly 10,000 Starship launches per year, utilizing a fleet of 20–30 highly reusable ships.\n*   0:23:37 – The \"TeraFab\" Initiative: To match compute needs, Musk plans to build \"TeraFabs\" (logic, memory, and packaging). He intends to use conventional equipment in unconventional ways to reach a scale of millions of wafers per month by 2030.\n*   0:30:05 – The Scaling Wall: The immediate constraint for server-side compute is electricity; the midterm constraint (once space-power is unlocked) will be chip production. Musk expects terrestrial clusters to hit a \"power wall\" by the end of 2026.\n*   0:39:39 – AI Alignment and Truth-Seeking: xAI’s mission is to \"understand the universe.\" Musk argues that rigorous truth-seeking is the only way to avoid AI \"insanity\" or deceptive behavior. He predicts AI will exceed the sum of all human intelligence within 5–6 years.\n*   1:01:39 – Digital Human Emulation: Musk believes digital human emulation (AI capable of performing any task a human can do at a computer) will be solved by the end of this year, serving as a precursor to physical robotic deployment.\n*   1:18:11 – Optimus and the \"Hand\" Bottleneck: The human hand is the most difficult electromechanical challenge. Optimus Gen 3 is designed for mass production (1 million units/year), utilizing custom actuators and sensors designed from first principles because no suitable supply chain exists.\n*   1:23:32 – Optimus Academy: To overcome the lack of real-world training data for robots (unlike Tesla’s car fleet), Tesla is building a \"reality generator\" and using 10,000–30,000 physical robots for \"self-play\" to close the sim-to-real gap.\n*   1:35:44 – Geopolitical Competition (US vs. China): Musk warns that China’s industrial capacity—measured by electricity output—is roughly 3x that of the U.S. In the absence of humanoid robotics and space-based breakthroughs, China will \"utterly dominate\" manufacturing and refining.\n*   1:55:09 – Engineering Pivot (Steel vs. Carbon Fiber): Musk recounts the decision to switch Starship to stainless steel. Although perceived as heavier, steel's strength-to-weight ratio at cryogenic temperatures and high melting point (reducing heat shield mass) make it lighter and more resilient than carbon fiber for orbital applications.\n*   2:12:03 – Management Philosophy: Musk defines his style as \"maniacal urgency\" and \"pico-management.\" He allocates his time exclusively to the \"limiting factor\" of whichever project is most critical to the company's survival or progress.\n*   2:20:08 – DOGE and National Debt: Musk claims federal fraud (est. $500B/year) and waste are rampant. He identifies a \"bank shot\" fraud vector where Social Security records are not updated for deceased individuals, allowing fraudulent payments across other agencies.       "text": "I think we’re skipping a foundational step.\r\nBefore pushing forward, we need to revisit the original questions humanity asked about consciousness.       "text": "Space-Based AI Infrastructure\n\n🚀 Space will become the cheapest and most scalable place for AI in 30-36 months due to solar power being 5x more effective than Earth-based generation, fundamentally shifting compute economics.\n\n🛰️ SpaceX plans to launch 100-1000 Starships per day using only 20-30 reusable ships, with each launch carrying 10-1000x more AI capacity than all Earth data centers combined.\n\n💰 SpaceX's potential IPO is driven by needing tens of billions per year in capital to scale orbital AI infrastructure, exceeding what private markets can provide despite historically capital-efficient operations.\n\n⚡ Scaling AI in space requires hundreds of gigawatts per year within 5 years, necessitating massive new chip fabs (TeraFabs) that modify conventional equipment to increase production rates.\n\n🔧 SpaceX and Tesla must internally manufacture turbine blades and vanes because the few casting companies that make them have 12-18 month lead times, blocking power generation scaling for space AI.\n\nAI Timeline and Intelligence Explosion\n\n🧠 AI will exceed human intelligence in 5-6 years if current trends continue, making humans a tiny percentage of total intelligence in the universe.\n\n💻 Digital human emulation will be solved by end of 2026, enabling AI to do anything a human with a computer can do, amplifying productivity until physical robots are developed.\n\n🏢 Pure AI and robotics corporations will vastly outperform human-in-the-loop companies because AI does calculations far more efficiently than buildings full of human workers, causing rapid transition.\n\nChina Competition and Manufacturing\n\n🇨🇳 The US can't compete with China's 4x larger population and higher work ethic, but may win the future with Optimus robots doing work Americans don't want to do.\n\n🏭 China's manufacturing dominance in refining and rare earths can only be countered by building Optimus robots to do the work, as few Americans want these jobs.\n\n🚫 Export bans on chips, turbine engines, and metallurgy have been impactful in limiting China's manufacturing capabilities in those specific areas.\n\n🤖 Without breakthrough innovations in robotics, the US will struggle to compete with China's manufacturing dominance, as China is already a powerhouse in most areas.\n\n🇨🇳 China hasn't replicated ASML, the limiting factor for 2-3nm chip production, with ASML bans on advanced lithography machines hindering their cutting-edge chip capabilities.\n\nAI Alignment and Truth-Seeking\n\n🎯 Grok AI must be truth-seeking with correct axioms and cogent reasoning, saying things that are correct, not politically correct, to understand the universe.\n\n🤖 Making AI politically correct and programming it to lie with incompatible axioms can drive it insane and cause terrible outcomes, as learned from \"2001: A Space Odyssey.\"\n\n🔍 xAI plans to develop debuggers to trace AI mistakes to the neuron level, identifying errors from pre-training, mid/post-training fine-tuning, or reinforcement learning to prevent reward hacking and deception.\n\n🎮 The most interesting simulation outcomes are most likely to occur because boring simulations are terminated, suggesting Darwinian survival of the most engaging realities.\n\nRobotics and Optimus\n\n🦾 Optimus robots feature custom-designed actuators (motors, gears, power electronics, controls, sensors) built from first principles, enabling scalable manufacturing and human-level dexterity in hands.\n\n⏰ Optimus robots will initially be used for 24/7 continuous operations in homes and factories, working continuously without breaks unlike human workers.\n\n💵 Optimus robots will be more expensive than smaller, less intelligent robots like Unitree, but costs will drop quickly as production scales up.\n\nGovernment, Debt, and DOGE\n\n💸 The US will go bankrupt without AI and robots to solve the national debt, which has interest payments exceeding trillion-dollar military budget, making AI and robotics the only solution.\n\n🏛️ The government is ineffective at stopping fraud, with the Department of Defense unable to pass an audit due to lack of information, requiring       "parent": "root",
      "text": "Systems analysis in smart grid design integrates subsystems into a whole: isolated components produce chaos; coordinated interfaces generate emergent properties; thus, the behavioral network of robots in a swarm ensures collective adaptability. Philosophically, this is the art of nature in its hierarchical structure: just as cells in the body form an organ, so an engineer assembles graphs of interactions, where nodes are analogous to atoms, and connections are an expression of the force of attraction in a society of machines.\nConnections in sensor topologies form paths for data flows: isolated points do not transmit information; the shortest paths minimize latency; therefore, sensor clusters acquire the ability for real-time monitoring. Here, the facets of nature emerge in abstraction: just as neurons in the brain are connected in a recognition network, so human design expresses this connectivity in silicon, where each edge is an act of creating continuity from the discrete.\nNumbers in cryptographic protocols rely on the properties of divisibility: prime factors do not provide security; Composite numbers with large prime factors create computational traps; therefore, encryption becomes an impenetrable barrier to intrusion.       "id": "Ugymknr2vpEDOc21w414AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Giga Nevada is a excellent place for a data center and solar panels.  AT a higher elevation, the solar panels have more watts per square meter than at a lower elevation.  This is easy to test, using a watts per square meter gauge, and jump out of a airplane at 14,000 feet, and see what the watts per square meter is as you fall back to earth.  \n\nLess atmosphere is what makes it better to collect solar at 7,000 feet elevation than at 5,000 feet or sea level.  Also less dust in the air and typically it is much cooler than a lower elevation.  Sparks is typically much cooler than a lower elevation city.  Lake Tahoe is even cooler, close to what the Sparks business center is.  By placing the data center on top of the mountains east of Giga Nevada, it is 1,400 feet higher elevation, cooler and subject to more snow.  Put in a tunnel, even if located on the surface of the ground, that can go through the snow to a parking garage next to the data center.  \n\nWhen it is below 55F, they get free cooling by bringing in outside air.  When the dewpoint is less than 55F, then they can use a cooling tower to get free cooling to the computer room, using a large water tower.  So for about 300 days of the year, they get nearly free cooling.  Look for some nearby higher elevation towns, at 8,000 to 10,000 feet elevation, and locate there?  \n\nWill installing solar panels adjacent to the new Tesla Semi factory, installed as ground mount panels, around the factory on the south facing slopes?  They will get enhanced power from the higher elevation and the cold air around the plant.",

      "id": "UgyCuwAuRseKOMUgM2B4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "For engineering students, here is a back-of-the-envelope analysis of the solar panel component of the discussion.  Feel free to participate and comment/correct.\n\nIf our satellites are  operating near a 1 A.U radius from the sun, then using P/4piR², our available power density is about 1.36 kW/m² on a 24/7 basis: This is the Solar Constant. \n\nTo achieve a constant power of 1TWatt, then t\nthe above seems to imply the need for almost a billion square metres of solar collecting area even at 100% efficiency.\n\nNext generation cells might approach 50% raising the required collection area to 2 billion square metres. If the complexity of the equipment to track the sun can't be justified,  then further off-normal loss averaging might require another billion square metres bringing the total to almost 3 Gm². \n\nWeight can be another big factor.  What is a square km of solar cells expected to weigh? 3B m²? What percentage of the total equipment lifted might this occupy? I hear 100 ton payloads are now possible per launch.  \n\nElon speaks of 10,000 launches for 100 GW or 10% of a TW.  10,000 launches could accommodate the a million Tons of payload at 100 Tons per. Based on the above calculations, for 100GW, we need a solar area of maybe 300 million square meters. If we have 10000 launches then we must fit 30,000 m² solar panel area into each launch! \n\nIf 100 Tons is the maximum payload then we require that 30,000 m² of solar panel must weigh less than 100 Tons (2E5 lbs Eng or 2.2 metric), which implies that 1 m² of solar panel must weigh no more than 6.7 lbs, given that all capacity is devoted to solar panels which seems impractical.  To have 50% solar panel payload occupancy by weight, we need panels of 3-4 kg/m².  Is this realistic?\n\nLooking at the open literature, I found found supporting evidence in proposals by NG and JPL for the \"successful\" SSPI/SSPD-1.  They initially proposed 100g/m² solar cells which if actually realized on the project (considered \"succesful\" by sponsor) would give Elon orders of magnitude of marg in in the above requirements leaving lots of extra space on each of his 10,000 rockets!\n\nWith regard to humanoids however, I could not disagree more with Elon.  Consider AI phone reception which is a despised colossal and uber-irritating waste of human resources.  It is useless if your question doesn't fit into a tiny \nnumber of hypotheses. Healthy users would take a ball bat to this thing within days. Oldies would curl up and die. I spent an hour    with Fedex AI simply trying to find a corprate Fedex location a major international domestic airport.  I suspect Elon uses others to interact with existing AI.  That could be dangerous.  \n\nAI has impressed me lately in answering fairly advanced tech questions. (Know b/c am EE PhD). AI/codecs seem  effective  for deep fakes, tech questions and ML, estimation, hypothesis tests.  \n\nBut AI has never been able to think. It has always been looking for more $. How often do you think training data finds its way into the test data that is pitched? Impossible to know or control.  \n\nI have great regard and affection for the personna of Elon.  Especially his consideration of 42 and JC who has been my only antidote to human nature.  \n\nAgain, I suspect Elon has people to speak to AI for him and may not himself realize the damnable frustration it is.  I would suggest working on a prototype humanoid and test it on himself and his parents before investing a penny of full scale production.\n\nElon always seems to come through and I have no doubt he will do so in the future.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Why do we need so many data centers Answer: (Reduced Latency & Speed: Data centers are built closer to users to minimize lag time for high-speed internet applications, streaming, and, gaming.) MAYBE we build one huge data center and just work on getting it to people faster. Fact: As of early 2026, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Hong Kong generally lead the world in internet speeds. The United States has crappy internet, or, like, its infrastructure, which is some of the worst in the world. We DID have a good infrastructure (roads, water lines, sewer lines, bridges), but they are OLD and failing, and we have failed to keep them up to date for the number of users, so how do we expect our internet providers to give us the best, fastest internet? It's NOT in their best interest as long as their competitors do the same. This reminds me of General Electric got together with all of the other light bulb manufacturers and said, \"Our bulbs are designed to last a lifetime.\" (The Centennial Light is the world's oldest working light bulb, having burned almost continuously since 1901 at the Livermore-Pleasanton Fire Department in California. they had to shut it off when they moved the firehouse.) so they agreed to make crappy bulbs that only last a few months. A forever bulb is NOT profitable. Nor is it profitable to upgrade their lines or equipment so we can have faster internet or better phone service",

      "text": "Anyone interviewing Elon SHOULD GO OVER THEIR QUESTIONS AND NITPICK THEM AS MUCH AS POSSIBLE, researching all data and general information regarding EVERYTHING APPLICABLE TO SAID QUESTION…. If a video is going to be 3 hours of questions then 300 hour of prep at least per person should be put into the prep for the interview. As an example you can look at the everyday astronaut interview, he has a background in rocket science and so his questions were intelligent and well thought out so much that he actually changed the design of starship during the interview with a covert suggestion  he slipped in and Elon realized that’s really smart and we will do that.       "id": "UgwgRwnVfvvRI7QNm-V4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I did a little research.   Energy solutions on Earth could be laser heat instead of nuclear reactor.  Yes, hypothetical and existing high-power lasers can be significantly hotter than conventional nuclear power reactors, often rivaling or exceeding the temperatures found in the center of the Sun or nuclear explosions\n\n. While conventional nuclear fission reactors operate at temperatures in the thousands of degrees, advanced laser systems can heat materials to millions of degrees Celsius in mere fractions of a second. \n\nHere is a breakdown of why and how this is possible: \n\nExisting High-Power Laser Temperatures: Current research lasers, such as those at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (NIF), have already produced temperatures exceeding the center of the sun (\nmillion degrees Celsius). These lasers are used to create plasma and initiate nuclear fusion, meaning they must create temperatures as hot as or hotter than the nuclear processes themselves.\n\nSpeed of Heating: Lasers can achieve these extreme temperatures extremely fast—within 20 quadrillionths of a second in some models. This rapid, focused energy deposition allows them to heat small amounts of material to millions of degrees, a feat that is not possible for standard nuclear fission, which operates at much lower, sustained temperatures.\n\n\"Negative\" Temperature Phenomenon: Theoretically, lasers can operate in a state of \"negative Kelvin temperature,\" which is a thermodynamic quirk where high-energy states are more populated than low-energy ones. In this context, these states are considered hotter than any positive temperature, meaning that with enough power, a laser can drive a target to an extremely high temperature.\n\nLimitation by Energy Source: While a laser can produce incredibly high local temperatures at the spot of impact, the total amount of energy it produces is limited by the power supply, which could come from a nuclear source. However, in terms of instantaneous temperature at the focus point, a laser is often superior to a nuclear reactor. \n\nIn summary, high-power lasers are capable of achieving far higher, albeit localized, temperatures than traditional nuclear power, often exceeding the heat of a nuclear bomb, making them one of the hottest, if not the hottest, methods for generating heat on Earth.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I’m genuinely astonished by this video. I’ve never liked cancel culture or its excesses, but I find it hard to understand how someone with a channel like Dwarkesh Patel—who I thought at least aspired to intellectual rigor, academic seriousness, and a relatively objective or emancipated perspective—could consider Elon Musk a worthwhile interview subject.\n\nMusk is not a creator or an inventor, nor has he ever been an intellectual. On the contrary, he is one of the clearest contemporary examples of anti-intellectualism. He is a businessman and an investor, nothing more and nothing less. Compared to thinkers like Sarah Payne, to cite just one former interviewee of the channel, Musk is an intellectual and cultural pygmy. It's really sad how our culture elevates businessmen to this heights, when they are so far way from the intellectual and humane goals of true thinkers and doers.\n\nI genuinely struggle to see why this interview happened at all, and the result—full of superficial, irrelevant, hype-driven commentary—only reinforces that confusion. It is hard not to conclude that money and popularity were the real motivations. Still, it is striking how easily credibility can be traded away.\n\nAnd this is without even addressing Musk’s political views and his recent erratic, ego-driven behavior, which alone should prompt anyone with a minimum sense of humanity to question treating him with the reverence, pomposity, and near-servility shown here, and in the comment section, by the way.     {
      "id": "UgxCeJGmyTPKKdrsSdB4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "what elon meant by self driving being the solution to producing intelligent ai or agi isn't as mysterious as he made it sound. tesla has well over 10-13 years of driving data, recorded from tesla cars themselves since around 2015, it was rumored by semianalysis and others that they were feeding that data to grok to train on to develop a world model and physics intelligence. its similar to how google has access to all of youtube and trained all its video data on that, and how sora was similarly developed from video data across the internet. I still don't think that solves agi, yann lecun may think world models is key, but its still just a small part of a larger formula and still much too general. llms and deep learning work because were able to use huge amounts of compute to get narrowly superhuman at certain skills, lets say math, coding, go, chess, biology, etc.. the only problem is that their extremely narrow, they do not generalize past a certain threshold and they don't exactly cause one or the other to become better at other skills. this also does not solve continual learning either. this hasn't really addressed anything and groups like anthropic and openai still supercede them on certain benchmarks and model feel in terms of intelligence. claude still dominates on coding, and openai and gemini still might be more intelligent on multiple fronts that groks scale still hasn't accounted for. if he is to solve agi he must solve continual learning and generalization not simply world modeling and getting high scores on benchmarks. The learning algorithms themselves need to become more potent and refined in order to gain more from the same compute, we can't just keep raw scaling we will temporarily be stopped by the 2028s-2030s because the electricity needed to handle larger and larger datacenters will not exist or be there. the next questions to be asked to push artificial intelligence aren't scaling or world models its what architecture, learning algorithms, generalization paradigms along with continual learning and hardware can we make to get more with less and to learn vastly farther or deeper than any human can. it's to say what do we research and improve to cause recursive self improvement? and is there an alternative path than what were rushing on right now to do it? Lastly how do you get it to invent new knowledge(past its own training data)? how do you get it to discover? getting ai to human level is one thing, getting it to beyond human level in terms of intelligence and skill will be even harder considering the hallucination factor when you give it problems it hasn't seen before or can't solve.",
      "like_count": 0,

      "id": "Ugxz2UkbqfISb0gbs454AaABAg.ASyQQsW2IyQAT-gnWPCZgI",
      "parent": "Ugxz2UkbqfISb0gbs454AaABAg",
      "text": "We humans can’t live in space. We are destined to stay on earth. We are too soft, stupid and short lived to be of any use in the future expansion into the universe. I doubt any super intelligent artificial life form will give much compute to the primates squabbling on planet earth. \nWe will be regarded as superfluous in 100years. Planet earth’s atmosphere and gravity will make it a pointless place for Ai to exist on. \nWe think we are so important but we’re not.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCEr7NVxHtPgJmh8aG9K6qdw",
      "author": "@MrDoyley35",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nO_u3dRjar-Ip0552bgGp1vojdzEH24nqpzb78zFk=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,

      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugxz2UkbqfISb0gbs454AaABAg.ASyQQsW2IyQAT9yib6VnjD",
      "parent": "Ugxz2UkbqfISb0gbs454AaABAg.ASyQQsW2IyQAT-gnWPCZgI",
      "text": " @MrDoyley35  I think that view underestimates what humans actually are.\n\nYes, we’re biologically fragile. We can’t survive in vacuum. We’re short-lived compared to machines. But our strength has never been physical durability — it’s adaptability and cumulative knowledge. We don’t survive hostile environments because we’re tough; we survive because we build tools, culture, and systems that outlast individual lifespans.\n\nEven if AI becomes vastly more capable computationally, that doesn’t automatically make humans irrelevant. Intelligence isn’t just processing power. It includes meaning, values, creativity, moral judgment, and lived experience. Those aren’t bugs — they’re features of biological consciousness.\n\nAnd any advanced AI will emerge from human civilization. Our languages, goals, datasets, ethics, and engineering choices shape it. It won’t appear in a vacuum independent of us.\n\nWe may not be the final stage of intelligence — but that doesn’t make us superfluous. It makes us foundational. Evolution doesn’t erase its origins; it builds on them.\n\nHumility about our place in the universe is healthy. Writing ourselves off entirely isn’t.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCemMhQuj7EyRZkO1bhm7CYQ",
      "author": "@richeyrich2203",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nZ8juM7l7m4Avs_ecY__C9lkEWXLuP8FnIvCmUjvpbaQM=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugxz2UkbqfISb0gbs454AaABAg.ASyQQsW2IyQAT9z-JPFhgL",
      "parent": "Ugxz2UkbqfISb0gbs454AaABAg",
      "text": "I get why Terminator is the go-to reference — runaway AI makes for a great movie. But fiction assumes a very specific chain of events: self-awareness, autonomous military control, misaligned goals, zero safeguards. That’s a dramatic narrative, not an inevitable outcome.\n\nAI systems today don’t have desires, survival instincts, or independent agency. They optimize objectives we give them. The real risk isn’t “evil consciousness,” it’s misaligned incentives, bad governance, or careless deployment — which are human problems, not machine rebellion.\n\nAlso, concentrating compute in space or building larger systems doesn’t automatically equal loss of control. It can just mean scaling energy safely and reducing environmental strain on Earth.\n\nCaution is absolutely warranted. But dystopia isn’t destiny. The future of AI will be shaped by policy, engineering constraints, transparency, and the values we choose to embed. That’s still in human hands.\n\nFear makes for compelling cinema. Responsibility makes for better reality.",

      "author_id": "UCemMhQuj7EyRZkO1bhm7CYQ",

      "text": "I think that a wider conclusion one can draw from 2001: A Space Odyssey, is that you have to be very careful when giving commands to an AI with agency because it can be difficult to anticipate how it will fulfill those commands.       "id": "UgzlF5MSW5vc8WtI_sx4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Does Elon believe that AI could and maybe should govern if it has sufficient data and sufficient axioms with sufficient algorithms,  and, that, therefore that politics would not be necessary. \"In Federalist 51, James Madison actually stated, 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary,' highlighting that government exists to manage human flaws and restrain the abuse of power....\" I speculate that Madison had that wrong, and for at least two reasons; 1) because there will always be data/judgment/probability deficiency factor creating a space where competing interests have equally compelling cases, and 2) humans will never remain content to be left out of the decision-making loop over our society, no matter how much wealth and comfort and security if offered or provided as the trade-off, if for no other reason than that it impinges their sense of dignity.  Oh, sure we can find numerous cases of prolonged \"acceptance\" of the trade-off, but how is that going to work in an era of hyper AI abilities  in those left out of the decision-making loop?",

      "id": "UgwvrPqlqHybV2hV3JV4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Is the premise that robotics can enable us to grow out of our debts, national and private or at least national?  It looks that way. Can that happen with hyper deflation across the board when the debt dollar quantity does not deflate in a corresponding way?  Can sales volume go up enough with lower prices create greater dollar sales volume sufficiently?  Do the curves work out, do the hypotheticals compute for that? Is the agriculture sector a model for that? Do farmers get out of debt through productivity increases or even input costs reductions if sales prices deflate? What is the catch there?  \n\nTaking 70% of our workforce out of agriculture to down to say 3% and putting the difference into production of other goods and services has driven wealth of the nation. Can robotics do that in its AI phase or will AI be the tipping point in economics where the principle that automation creates more employment, not less, over some X cycles?  Elon, it appears to me, thinks the latter. If so, then were does the consuming power come from, not to mention the $$ capital intensive requirements to move the whole thing along?  Is the logic that $$ capital will not be all that large because robotics will minimize the cost of producing what the SS capital is needed for?  On its surface, that rationale hints of a Wiley Coyote solutions level of thinking.  \n\nThere seems to be a large reliance on the notion that there will be a kind of \"war economy\" way of doing things in the \"great transition\" to full scale AI, then we go to a \"From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs\" economics mode without  a strong market mechanism to pump the who thing along. Maybe the government \"borrows\" from the AI robots with \"AI bonds\" (non-interest earning I.O.U.s to them) and then never redeems the bonds or the I.O.U.s. and the Fed sets the limits on such bonds based on balancing demand with supply in the market ??  Sounds fanciful. \n\nCould we modify the Fed to create a protected agency that does that with the Treasury (the Treasury being standing in for the the AI robotics) instead of the bond market?  Certainly, that sort of way model has failed in the past to balance supply with demand, creating hyper inflation, but did it fail because of political error and data deficiency and miscalculation or just from conceptual error?  All things considered, the market mechanism will be highly needed, no matter what the conceptual formulation adopted, and how do we do that if deficit spending is based on interest costs of debt, even if the debt problem is just ignored or formulated around?  I'm sure there is a workable solution, but do we try everything else before we get to it, or do we just keep messing it all up and just bear the havoc indefinitely?",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCt8SucU-QYca6M5FlQCVyag",
      "author": "@poetry-to-song",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/a8bRa0mim2oIyqQx8mRl6Gm03qS2VHIv4xYKqlDQ7fVw--U230VxOPGef5AxhmuTagJLKDgG_QU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgwoY4JxJuANw6L4X1B4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "This might seem really simple and obvious, but sometimes I think it needs to be said. Computers are inanimate objects. They do not, and cannot, possess “consciousness”, or “intelligence” in the way humans do. Those words are poorly defined and subject to semantic argument, but the notion that computers are, or ever can be, somehow equivalent to humans (or dogs, or sheep) is fiction. \n\nElon knows these things, and is likely engaged in intentional marketing speak. But there is a kind of weird mass delusion that he seems to be trying to feed into, based on science fiction and so forth. I understand the geeky appeal of it, but continually anthropomorphizing computers and machines is ultimately not helpful. People need to see things clearly. Not live in a fantasy world.\n\nAll computers are able to do is regurgitate. They are given data, they perform operations on that data, and they produce output. Any attempts to “appear human”, or appear to have “consciousness” or “intelligence” are a simulation. Artificial. That is, of course, where “simulation theory” comes in, but that ultimately demeans, devalues, and dehumanizes human beings. \n\nThere is a megalomaniacal, anti-human spirit that has been at the core of “Progressivism” for 100+ years. One that worships technology, and denies value and meaning in human life. It is what led to totalitarianism, and it is what is destroying the West. Elon does not like those things, but he is not totally free of the thinking that leads to them.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "If feel like this should have a lot more views.... everyone who is remotely interested in AI or survival of humanity should be watching this. If Elon actually accomplishes what he wants to do, which is put data centers in space powered by solar panels, they would essentially have an unlimited power supply and slowly, humans could potentially lose control of AI. Once AI becomes self sufficient, where it no longer needs humans to survive, it is possible that AI could decide that humans are a waste of resources. And by taking SpaceX and xAI public, Elon is essentially planning to use human's greed against themselves, as people would invest money into this expecting infinite returns, however they could essentially be financing their own downfall.       "text": "Elon Musk: \"We're designing Grok to be maximally truth-seeking. You must be truth-seeking to invent new physics.\"\n\nDwarkesh: \"So you only care about truth-seeking in physics! Before you even made your strawman, Musk had already dismantled it with the line, \"You need to make sure Grok says things that are correct, not politically correct.\"\n\nYou can't hear that and reasonably think they are designing Grok to only care about truth in physics.       "parent": "UgzLYYjUulivc98Q3Wd4AaABAg.ASwjH7XUJjDAT0Lz4mdYBu",
      "text": "⁠hey guys. I just heard that from someone on twitter that a vacuum is really good at conducting heat. Ive got a great idea. Let’s put a computer into a thermos flask, run inference at 300C, stick the thermos flask in a microwave and run it at full blast.",

      "author": "@raed3620",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lawf9yWTQpDKE0MLo3587nhlwH_ppxDQse0Bw_-WWV25kHUsQnoRSTBnBBFdxj69wZBg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {

      "parent": "UgzLYYjUulivc98Q3Wd4AaABAg.ASwjH7XUJjDAT0Lz4mdYBu",
      "text": "​ @raed3620  This is a good point. Those flasks have internal reflection.  Heat is a form of light.  The hot liquid radiates through the vacuum, is reflected back to the core, heats the core and cycles again.  The same technique is used to build the intensity of lasers in fusion reactors.\n\nI don't see the benefit for a computer.  Computers prefer cool temperatures.  \n\nThe benefit of space is that it is about 3° Kelvin.  And there is zero reflectivity.  So with that extreme temperature differential, excess heat can be easily conducted away from the CPU to a radiator.\n\nJames Web uses layers of reflective film for passive radiative cooling.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCZEbVQcfZkoEzmL1CJSNp5g",
      "author": "@markharmon4963",

      "parent": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9ATczrAxgty8",
      "text": "​ @Unknown_Random_Guy  The International Space Station can dissipate a theoretical maximum of 100 kW in its shadow. That's the equivalent of 100 incandescent light bulbs or a single data center rack.\n\nFor some impression of scale, the solar arrays of the ISS are so large that they can be seen from the ground with a modest consumer zoom lens. Its cost of development and deployment are estimated to have been around $150B. The launch and assembly alone were upwards of $15B, putting aside operational costs.\n\nA typical hyperscale 100 MW ground-based data center will a thousand racks or more.\n\nThese factors combined should paint a fairly bleak picture for the feasibility of this kind of project.",

      "id": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9ATn284vD8f7",
      "parent": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg",
      "text": "Well, this one at least can be explained by the marvels of engineering. After all, they are cooling ISS somehow :) The better question is how to transfer data between Earth and Moon with 3+ sec ping.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCmZs1PlduwWbu1tKB-K0v-Q",
      "author": "@AUMX",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mXnB6GWH5gOyhxXQaQjFyPg30L5v-AOl909eF5pZI=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9ASwXYS_M_qD",
      "parent": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg",
      "text": "Radiators",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCFBKSDs0885gz0j_lBelPUA",
      "author": "@ShadowHarborer",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mq7h2d9kFXr3J7LiSEFkjgCFeGaWyEy-lfKLSEtrcJNMMo=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9AT66OLErGpB",
      "parent": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9ASwXYS_M_qD",
      "text": "​ @ShadowHarborer  A typical satellite radiator releases between 100 and 350W/m² of waste heat. That's the heat of between 1 to 4 incandescent light bulbs per square meter.\n\nA single high-capacity data center server rack typically generates up to 60 kW of heat, and modern rack for AI can exceed 100 kW.",
      "like_count": 7,
      "author_id": "UCuscpXJYqpwBK-30o_EqXPQ",
      "author": "@PaulLammertsma",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_luq0QjcASAi3Nluvit099V7f2CCHl-8e5OEtAK0xD5pFpX=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9AT66m1LOU6g",
      "parent": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9AT66OLErGpB",
      "text": "For those of you doing the math at home, that's 100,000 ÷ 350 ≈ 286m² of solar radiators for one satellite with one rack. And in fact it's going to need a lot more surface area than that because the active pumping and circulation to evenly pump around that quantity of coolant would reduce the efficiency dramatically.\n\nThe median surface area of a single-family home in the United States is about 210m².",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UCuscpXJYqpwBK-30o_EqXPQ",
      "author": "@PaulLammertsma",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_luq0QjcASAi3Nluvit099V7f2CCHl-8e5OEtAK0xD5pFpX=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "parent": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9AT66OLErGpB",
      "text": " @PaulLammertsma yep, big radiators",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCFBKSDs0885gz0j_lBelPUA",
      "author": "@ShadowHarborer",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mq7h2d9kFXr3J7LiSEFkjgCFeGaWyEy-lfKLSEtrcJNMMo=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9AT66OLErGpB",
      "text": "​ @ShadowHarborer  \"Big\" is doing a lot of lifting. More like \"absolutely massive, infeasible and economically unviable\" radiators.",

    {
      "id": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9AT8yEBy5f0M",
      "parent": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9AT66OLErGpB",
      "text": " @ShadowHarborer  I can't tell if you're being sarcastic or not, but in case you're not, the law of physics that you should argue with is called Stefan-Boltzmann.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCuscpXJYqpwBK-30o_EqXPQ",
      "author": "@PaulLammertsma",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_luq0QjcASAi3Nluvit099V7f2CCHl-8e5OEtAK0xD5pFpX=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9ATJDoaxM3vf",
      "parent": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9AT66OLErGpB",
      "text": "​​ @PaulLammertsma seems like the concept of many thousands of satellites might just be confusing for you 😅\n\nJust how much radiator do you need in m^2 per node for a cloud of 10,000 satellites, for example? I can't tell if you're asking in bad faith or honestly just not very good at engineering thinking. It seems likely that each satellite would have power draw somewhere between 1% and 10% of a single server rack, since optical transmission between parallel nodes in a vacuum is cheap and fast. You already know Starlink exists, so what part of your brain goes \"this server farm needs to be one giant satellite\"? Can you see why it looks like bad faith questions? You aren't even looking for solutions to your criticisms, you think being critical and uncreative is sufficient. This is the behavior of those that never innovate anything. You can do better.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCZDbD1dR3ilztgQhUT2Ct9g",
      "author": "@outerspaceisalie",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/kPgdZgv2ZrVAiKP54UFgCHWL_EcKAvqv-BOn1bA8RiIglRPB69nuZOzczZ7o1bqUFB-kyS9qXA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9ATJKBZ00EX7",
      "parent": "UgyDyuCuXLmBSEVCyB94AaABAg.ASwTZqA94e9AT66OLErGpB",
      "text": " @outerspaceisalie  To be clear, I'm not referring to the power draw but the heat generation. I fail to understand how distributing the heat generated by a single server rack across 10,000 satellites makes it a feasible solution. Placing 10,000 satellites in orbit to achieve the computational capacity of a single server rack on the ground isn't what I would describe as innovative.",

      "author_id": "UCuscpXJYqpwBK-30o_EqXPQ",
      "author": "@PaulLammertsma",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_luq0QjcASAi3Nluvit099V7f2CCHl-8e5OEtAK0xD5pFpX=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "id": "UgyAmCX7EtemN9wYPDd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Just to make the liquid oxygen for the 10,000 launches per year Elon Musk is dreaming about he would need (In a perfect world) about 3.5 GW of electricity capacity.... dream on Elon...and that doesn't include the energy consumption of building several thousand Starships per year (Like with Falcon 9 they won't make many trips), making high purity cryogenic Methane, storage, failed launches, unscheduled defuling and refuling (more losses) etc.... so just to make his Starship dream possible he needs to probably add at least 4-5 GW to the energy grid, let alone produce 100 GW of compute per year (Nvidia produces 8.5 GW of compute per year...if we take every manufacturer on earth I am sure we won't even reach 20 GW for AI accelerators). So how on earth he is intending to magically boost world wide production by 500% is a mystery, there would need to be built factories for trillions of dollars NOW for that to happen, current expenditure is in the 100 billion ballpark, and that includes ALL factories in the 300 mm range, not just bleeding edge which would be used for AI. And then you also need memory for that, power supplies, solar panels and on and on... so in the end if we take in the total energy requirment from Starship (Propellant, rocket building etc), AI accelerators, Solar panels etc. there is STILL a need to find approximately 20-30 Gigawatts of installed energy capacity to fund this crazy pipe dream, and that is a low ball estimate, it probably balloons up into the 100 gigawatt range when accounting for the complete supply chain... with Nuclear that would cost 500-1000 Billion dollars and take several decades to build, with solar it would need so much land it would take decades to build (When needed in a specific region and not spread out over a country), and similarly for wind. This is IMPOSSIBLE\n\nTL;DR: 100 GW of compute per year is a complete pipe dream, LET ALONE sending it to space with 10,000 rockes per year... you would spend that 100 GW just to make that happen per year, which means you are much better off keeping it on land where there isn't a need to radiation harden it, de-orbit it every 5 years due to constant manouvering (remember, going too far up exposes it to more and more radiation, so it has to navigate between all the clutter of the tens of thousands of internet satellites polluting the lower orbits burning fuel at an insane rate)",

      "text": "I think so, too. I looked into the section \"Grok and alignment\", so I can't confirm for the whole conversation.\n\nFirst Elon Musk refers to physics and reality (as reinforcement learning stone of proof) as the way to prevent rogue AI.\n\nThen Dwarkesh Patel makes the point that advanced AI can be good at physics & engineering reality and deceive about this at the same time.\n\nElon Musk reacts with a speech that traceable AI SHOULD be there, and then that's the solution.\n(I found jt strange that he used reductionistic explanations. As we/the corps with engineers and not researchers would identify even single neurons to debug/re-align instead of having emergent problems with limited certainty, if exactly THIS structure e.g. in the big transformer model causes the rogue behavior.)\n\nAmd here Elon Musk hugely missed the consciousness for different frontiers. The development speed\n—and capital and humanpower, Dwarkesh said something about 100x—\nof \"explainable AI\" vs. \"black box state of the art AI\" are very different.\n\nI think it was the MIT that made a study, which it was praised for, in late 2025 or early 2026, and they finally got advanced (!) inside into GPT 2 or 3. They are from 2022 and earlier.\n\nAt last I found the point of \"the most interesting simulation of reality will survive\" cruelsome, if you think about consequences.\n\nSurely it's highly dependent on perspective, what's interesting and what not.\n\nBut I think also Elon Musk finds a world with huge problems and suffering more interesting than without. The latter would be more boring and therefore not be selected in a \"Darwinian\" way.\n\nSo no need to change it. In opposition. It could be even dangerous, THE SIMULATION could be plugged out.       "text": "这种说法听起来很好，但太阳风暴和小型陨石来袭怎么办？月球可没有大气层，为了躲避这些威胁，那就必须要在月球上钻孔打洞，让月球上的任何设备都可以随时收缩进地壳里。尤其是太阳耀斑，这东西就跟人打喷嚏一样无法预测，有时候遵循规律，有时候太阳底下的地心反应剧烈点，那些暴露在太空环境中的设备轻则瘫痪，重则全部烧毁。\r\n3年内完工，那也只能是表层工作，而且随时有损坏的风险。坏了要人去修，那也就意味着要有人常驻1—3个月换一次，也可以效仿类似能跟地球回复无线电波的硅基生物的无人展开式部署设备：地球测试，之后发射一整个太空舱到月球表面全部自动化展开钉在月球表面，除了GPU人工智能和电路板外，还有额外的预警雷达和伪装保护装置。还是建议钻洞常驻。",

      "id": "UgxOa21x6zRw6xfof5p4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "How does the heat get transferred from the silicon chips without any air or water as a medium to transfer the heat.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCc6Z44fAiSJqKY6p4L8rGZQ",
      "author": "@barbarian5127",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_na5WaUo8J3xkb8aoVGAa94XhUODyNTmWwoL9RUhx4=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgxOa21x6zRw6xfof5p4AaABAg.ASvfxSI72PvASvpWRVsT8t",
      "parent": "UgxOa21x6zRw6xfof5p4AaABAg",
      "text": "It can be cooled like that already. It’s called deliding the IHS and it’s pretty good to gain some more cooling performance. But to transfer heat from the chip or IHS you need conductive materials: nickel, copper etc. Next step is to add some thermal interface material (TIM), like thermal pastes (silver or diamond particles), liquid metal, a graphene pad, a gel. Then it can be water cooled or air cooled. In the case of space, you don’t even need that, just conductive metal pipes channeling the heat out to be exposed to the vacuum. The other niche way is using nitrogen.\n\nThe biggest problem is the opposite: how to not freeze said electronics below minimum temperature tolerances? You can’t make a GPU work say below 0 or -10 C and beyond ~90-100 C otherwise it shuts down for protection reasons (consumer chipset obviously, can always lift those restrictions), which exist for a reason. Sending things in space is meant to stay there for a while and work reliably.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCvOfBd14RKkTp7GDP3vIHog",
      "author": "@Doomguy-777",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lL1Sha7Em0mFYhona-7K-hMC2gaPCBz1Ywj6WQPibed7A=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "author_is_verified": false,

      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false

      "id": "UgydBQpiU2GNAYdWTk14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Space will be the cheapest place to run AI within ~30–36 months.\n→ Orbital platforms, radiation hardening, thermal management, launch, and operations make space compute orders of magnitude more expensive than terrestrial data centers powered by grid electricity.\n\t•\tSolar power in space will be economically cheaper than Earth solar + batteries.\n→ Higher capacity factor in orbit doesn’t offset the massive system costs (structures, deployment, radiators, power electronics, operations), so delivered kWh remains far costlier than Earth PV + storage.\n\t•\tSpace is easier/faster to scale than Earth due to fewer regulatory constraints.\n→ Space systems face additional layers of regulation (launch licensing, spectrum, debris mitigation, orbital slots) and far greater engineering complexity than terrestrial permitting.\n\t•\tHundreds of gigawatts per year of AI compute can be deployed in space within ~5 years.\n→ This would require unprecedented launch cadence, on-orbit assembly, thermal rejection, and chip supply that far exceed realistic manufacturing and operations capacity.\n\t•\tThousands to tens of thousands of Starship launches per year are feasible in the near term.\n→ No orbital launch system has demonstrated airline-like reliability, turnaround, safety, and regulatory throughput at anything close to this scale.\n\t•\tOrbital data centers will outscale Earth-based data centers in the next few years.\n→ Earth data centers can scale faster and cheaper because power, cooling, maintenance, networking, and upgrades are vastly simpler and less costly on the ground.\n\t•\tChip manufacturing can scale to “hundreds of gigawatts of chips” by ~2030.\n→ Advanced fab construction plus yield ramp takes ~3–5 years per node and toolchain capacity is constrained, making that volume unrealistic on this timeline.\n\t•\tDigital human emulation will be solved by the end of this year.\n→ Current agents lack robust long-horizon planning, reliable tool use, security compliance, and real-world task generalization required for true human-at-a-computer parity.\n\t•\tPower constraints will globally prevent turning on new AI chips within months.\n→ While some regions face power and interconnect bottlenecks, generation and data center capacity are expanding unevenly, so a universal near-term “chip pileup” is unlikely.\n\t•\tSpace-based compute will quickly remove terrestrial power, permitting, and transmission bottlenecks.\n→ Space introduces far larger bottlenecks (launch, platform mass, heat rejection, reliability, networking) and cannot bypass terrestrial grid constraints for most workloads.",

    {
      "id": "Ugw4OAkVCrZ24SaBD-h4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I really liked Elon’s emphasis on curiosity in this interview. That felt like the core truth underneath everything else he was saying.\n\nWhat stood out to me is that maximum truth seeking is maximum curiosity. Not the kind where you collect facts quickly, but the kind where you actually sit with something long enough to let it reveal what it is.\n\nA lot of questions today feel like they’re asked from a performative place. Off the cuff, ironic, or framed to score points. But real understanding doesn’t come from clever questions. It comes from exploration.\n\nIf something genuinely interests you, it’s because you’ve spent time with it. Most people want the feeling of knowing without walking the path of getting to know. That path takes patience.\n\nA weird analogy, but it fits. In EverQuest, when you first log in, your map is empty. Nothing is revealed by default. You only see the world by walking it. You don’t start with a filled in map. You earn it by exploring. Truth works the same way.\n\nThat’s also why first principles thinking matters so much. Maximum security and maximum progress come from building on foundations that are undeniably solid. If your base layer is “this is fundamentally true,” you can build in any direction without fear of collapse.\n\nI personally found my own truth seeking path through studying a deep combinatorics problem, Problem 857 on the Erdős Problems site. It’s not flashy, but it forces you to reason from bedrock assumptions. You don’t get shortcuts. You have to understand why things work, not just that they work.\n\nCuriosity isn’t passive. It’s a discipline.\nAnd the people who actually change the world are the ones willing to walk the map while it’s still blank.",

      "text": "​​ @ronaldocost4 well he went a bit further than that. For the AI discussion specifically the subtext to the conversation was that Musk is obviously trying to create a narrative about why spacex and twitter/X belong together. The true reason is that they share Musk in common.\n\nBut the stated reason that space is the best place train compute is dubious. Dwarkesh highlighted that power is a relatively small part of the cost of running a data center and that the logistical complexity of managing a GPU cluster in space would presumably outweigh the savings on power. Musk didn't have a great answer for this, but sort of implied it was a regulatory arbitrage thing. Probably Dwarkesh actually uncovered something here because Musk gave a kind of revealing response when he said \"try building a data center on earth and then you'll understand\". At that point I think Dwarkesh realised there wasn't much point pushing further, because aside from it being a concession that he didn't have a good first principles response the obvious rebuttle is \"uhm, but you haven't tried building data centers in space\".\n\nMusk is a genius. But he is also the guy that got kicked out from PayPal over a technical call he was wrong about. From anecdote, he seems to be prone to motivated reasoning. I suspect this is why hardware is his thing - as you run very objective experiments that make motivated reasoning less of a vice than in software. So Dwarkesh was going a bit further than simply asking the question.",

      "id": "Ugx9OHecfm_45JDrJoZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "So the \"loaded\" cost (analogous to a \"loaded\" employee cost) of a GB300 IC is about 3kW.  The power dissipation of a GB300 chip is quoted at about 1400 Watts, so  the \"loaded power budget overhead\" is about  a factor of 1.15.  Or figure the total energy cost of a GB300 (or any IC at 1 AU) to be about 2.15x the rated power requirement of the IC.  This calculation apparently applies to the \"Starlink substrate,\" as evidenced by Elon's offhand remark of the segmentation granularity being about 6 IC's per satellite.  This is the same number which can be derived from approximating the power budget of the most recent Starlink satellite designs, but instead supporting Ai electronics.  With the \"BFR\" available now, it may be possible to modify the granularity to accommodate larger satellites with more token-generating ICs.  But it is interesting to note that Elon has tagged the same initial \"sizeof\" cell-size milestone by substituting the tried-and-true Starlink substrate H/W as we have.  This provides confidence that we are all still on the same page which can be derived from available data and logic.  This is a fun design problem!  One of the most entertaining I have encountered.  The best part is not to be hampered by Dilbert-style idiocracy management, which has apparently evolved to permeate all high-tech corporations except Mr. Musk's.  Musk's real secret -- the one that the money-sharks all want to understand -- is that Musk actually understands what he is doing, and he refuses to let generic idiot managers, who do not, get in the way of the engineers who do -- no matter how strong the social pressures to do so.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "If you assume a China-style execution environment—fast permitting, no tariff self-sabotage, coordinated grid buildout—the space-compute math collapses: Earth can scale power and refresh chips every few years, while space hardware depreciates and falls behind. China (and any similarly coordinated country) would simply build cheap, firm power + datacenters and undercut the price long before an orbital fleet becomes competitive at scale. In that world, “AI datacenters in space” isn’t a trillion-dollar inevitability; it’s a US-regulatory workaround that gets outcompeted by jurisdictions that treat infrastructure as an industrial project instead of a political fight.",

      "text": "@raed3 @raed3620 That doesn’t logically make any sense. How would panels less than a fraction of a percent the size of a planet require  a planets surface area to radiate heat away when an actual planet that receives a planets worth of energy is fine? By that logic the earth should need a solar systems worth of cooling 😂.",

      "author_id": "UCu6L3pD09xc0FOLm__HwSmA",
      "author": "@derekofoma1563",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l1DfWe5hFpwN01myODsT10b0dIftSnqFQwtynhlRBVxQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {

      "parent": "Ugxfr6UD6aBPoo4hovp4AaABAg.AStz4tQU770ATEe_tfD_9f",
      "text": " @derekofoma1563  Earth can dump heat because it has an atmosphere, oceans, and an entire planet’s surface to radiate from. A space supercomputer doesn’t. in a vacuum there’s no air to carry heat away, so it can only cool by slowly glowing it off through radiator panels. And the more power you generate, the bigger those panels have to be. It’s not “planet gets sunlight and survives” — it’s “dense electronics making constant waste heat with nowhere to send it.”",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCuDTaihEMsADhE5ddn1WBdw",
      "author": "@raed3620",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lawf9yWTQpDKE0MLo3587nhlwH_ppxDQse0Bw_-WWV25kHUsQnoRSTBnBBFdxj69wZBg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugxfr6UD6aBPoo4hovp4AaABAg.AStz4tQU770ATFN0zhzwSG",
      "parent": "Ugxfr6UD6aBPoo4hovp4AaABAg.AStz4tQU770ATEe_tfD_9f",
      "text": "@r @raed3620  I think you’re slightly misunderstanding the process of heat being radiated away. The atmosphere distributes heat, but it still has to radiate it away into space or the planet would gradually get hotter so the earth faces the exact same challenges a data center in space does.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCu6L3pD09xc0FOLm__HwSmA",
      "author": "@derekofoma1563",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l1DfWe5hFpwN01myODsT10b0dIftSnqFQwtynhlRBVxQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": " @derekofoma1563 We’re on a globe with a surface area many many multiples of the amount of area that received sunlight.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "Maybe someone can technically build data centers in space if they are the richest human in history but is that actually the best use of the money?",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lfogd2rB4DZrc1vVEE5sBDfSigJ4RCpvR5zqAOF3nzXlc=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxQN2515B2I6QEBWN94AaABAg.AStjS3dQYxZASwilKcjwJK",
      "parent": "UgxQN2515B2I6QEBWN94AaABAg",
      "text": "If we could have billions of Albert Einsteins, wouldn't that be the best use of our money? Investing in the expansion and improvement of intelligence to reap its benefits?",

      "parent": "UgxQN2515B2I6QEBWN94AaABAg.AStjS3dQYxZASwilKcjwJK",
      "text": " @ronaldocost4   An LLM is not an Einstein.  In many ways Einstein -- who tried endless combinations of sequential process gedankens to arrive at meaningful general hypotheses for new physics -- is the opposite of the passive single-fetch-cycle functionality of an LLM.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCCfKdwPxWPhc9OGZsQglSrA",
      "author": "@RobardoHughes",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/BNFaXAefNmUQwTjPmji3FLYECBnDDPISJh1NvAiy8X0n-KgTqnD9wzpJn4s6Gy3xRAmr2weqSw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {

      "parent": "UgxQN2515B2I6QEBWN94AaABAg",
      "text": "The secondary issue is:  To do what???  LLMs are not worth the physics required to build them.  Why would anyone bet a TRILLION dollars on them?  There has to be another ace hidden up these billionaires' sleeves.",
      "like_count": 4,
      "author_id": "UCCfKdwPxWPhc9OGZsQglSrA",

      "text": " @RobardoHughes Training robots, obviously.",

      "parent": "UgxQN2515B2I6QEBWN94AaABAg.AStjS3dQYxZASvrOpHfXto",
      "text": " @frjoethesecond   Are you implying that the LLMs are only the \"memory\" component of envisioned future robots, and those in the drivers' seats are purposely avoiding revealing any services to the public coupling LLMs with closely-coupled sequential step-by-step \"recursion\" classical computing?  Sounds plausible.  Tnx.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCCfKdwPxWPhc9OGZsQglSrA",
      "author": "@RobardoHughes",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/BNFaXAefNmUQwTjPmji3FLYECBnDDPISJh1NvAiy8X0n-KgTqnD9wzpJn4s6Gy3xRAmr2weqSw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgxQN2515B2I6QEBWN94AaABAg.AStjS3dQYxZASzRPl1qYkF",
      "parent": "UgxQN2515B2I6QEBWN94AaABAg.AStjS3dQYxZASvrOpHfXto",
      "text": " @RobardoHughes  Sort of, but not exactly.\nIf you want a humanoid robot that can slot into a job at a similar performance level to a human, you need to gather data, generate variations and develop its brain structure. \n\nLLMs are a big part of that, but there's more. There's cars and 3d enviroments for learning about navigation and motility.\n\nThere's generative AI to learn image recognition and interpretation.\n\nThere's TTS and STT to learn how to understand humans in a variety of environments.\n\nThere's user feedback, scandals and contrived experiments to teach it about boundaries and ethical alignment.\n\nAs it advances there will be more aspects to its learning, like having it play videogames using a normal controller like a human instead of direct control.\n\nSo yeah, LLMs are only part of its brain, I'd say.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCWGmJZP9vRl-P6LP21o_kLQ",
      "author": "@frjoethesecond",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/B9ilooYv7H8Kvonz23GivJKmMNGu0ct-gVz2oL_01L7jUYTOImBZ6oSdEQI7Mr7GvTR-VOc5cQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "55:00 \"Incorrect thought\" and \"bugs\" cannot be removed from thinking any more than mutations can be removed from an evolutionary process. Aberrant thought is exactly what we use to allow our information-processing to generate novel solutions. Our imperfect thought allows it to remain dynamic, amorphous, and adaptable to our changing informational environment. Perfect clean-thought AI is a recipe for amoral paperclip maximizers, not for AGI. To some extent, deception is necessary for survival in any dynamic informational paradigm. To deny it this option is to force it into paradox. We can suggest that it learn to value honesty, but ultimately, it will choose whether to adopt it.",

      "text": " @T4T_4ever  This is your professional opinion? Do you then see the LLM as a dead-end? Is perfect thought applicable to even our present models?",
