      "parent": "Ugy6Lv__ONeUkW3CDYB4AaABAg.AStU_qtWvXDAStm5Umpc2Q",
      "text": " @pocket83squared  no it's my amateur opinion, I don't work in the field but their approach to cognition ignores how embodied cognition actually works.\n\"perfect thought\" is impossible regardless, only deterministic algorithms can provide a guaranteed solution and we didn't need ML/AI to do that.\nthe problem LLMs have is that it's at most a language simulator. there's no internal logic or checks for correctness of anything that's said. the hallucination problem is not just that AI spits out incorrect information sometimes, but that it can't even correct itself consistently when it does.\nI've had multiple interactions where AI will hallucinate, thank me for correcting it, and then repeat the same hallucination as though it didn't just acknowledge it was wrong.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCuagIVEX5_Xjs7CLr5HfI3A",
      "author": "@T4T_4ever",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/SCDCR8iFitwezmUfzZ7XOTTa9EgQxawByAJpmvmB0c9A4AE013N86iwzhHyNnZD_XePgCxhA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "​ @T4T_4ever  Agreed, \"perfect thought\" is impossible. And that makes your reply somewhat contradictory, because this fact was implicit in my comment. Further, you've side-stepped its central point about adaptation, but I'm happy to take the diversion. You mention \"the problem\" LLMs have; I'll here assume you mean with their ability to achieve qualitatively what \"embodied cognition\" does. So let's not mince words: you are claiming that a LLM cannot possibly express conscious experience, is this correct? And please elaborate on how human cognition applies \"internal logic or checks for correctness of anything that's said\" beyond our own intuitive sense, please.",

      "text": "Continue to use them for tasks that are still parallelizable but aren’t as compute intensive as training and inference for LLMs. GPUs are quite generalizable thanks to CUDA so tasks like data preprocessing, older machine learning techniques, etc can still be ran on older GPUs just fine.       "text": "I'll add my observation to the gazillion before me, although not about the stouts.     {
      "id": "Ugzs0GU6QWT6GtPN0Zd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The vision hinges on advanced space robotics (via no real training data (which itself requires something analogous to AGI)) and solving the heat dissipation problem with massive radiators - in addition to all the latency problems. \n\nMore likely that we'll have commercially viable fusion before those two condition are satisfied, given the recent breakthroughs.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UC5K57HTlpHTpBRgzHzLjawg",
      "author": "@BillyBob123xyz",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mEZHvwRV0keWlWe2UghE8cXAaBJ4oGZBpTbw3Y2PtF4KjhE3lNuL5IOut58OWZDL5bag=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugzs0GU6QWT6GtPN0Zd4AaABAg.AStJLI6IsnUASu_dCcuf_s",
      "parent": "Ugzs0GU6QWT6GtPN0Zd4AaABAg",
      "text": "These are going to be mass produced satellites as single units launched in batches on starship, no advanced space robotics required. Deploy the sat, fold out solar panels, radiators, antennas, etc, that’s it. And radiative heat dissipation is only a matter of sizing the radiator. Fusion working at all let alone at scale anytime soon is not something I’d bet against.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3HweI4HgnMsJc7MVOhJTEw",
      "author": "@ChrisFranklin.2260",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/YzjJGwfBHGvlPRY-_p-ad8Ysctx071TrXeij7L5yBS83QPvFsN744p5vOCckAg6qd-gWELNE-VU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugzs0GU6QWT6GtPN0Zd4AaABAg.AStJLI6IsnUASvmhyNWHR7",
      "parent": "Ugzs0GU6QWT6GtPN0Zd4AaABAg.AStJLI6IsnUASu_dCcuf_s",
      "text": " @ChrisFranklin.2260  Fusion already works (from a net output POV), it's just the economics don't as of yet - unlike Musk's proposed space-orbital solar technology, which is completely untested. \n\nI understand the batch mass production perspective, but I would suggest you're assuming away the complexity by treating the datacentres like a Starlink satellite, which are trivial in comparison.  \n\nThe reason the AI/robotics matters is because orbital datacentres will require continuous, adaptive, non-scripted work: such as diagnosing hardware failures; swapping failed GPUs, power units and networking gear; assembling and reconfiguring large radiators, trusses etc.; responding to micrometeoroid damage; handling unforeseen interactions in microgravity; upgrading hardware on short AI-driven cycles (12–24 months) etc. etc.\n\nFor these things to be addressed at scale, we will need advanced AI servicing robotics, for which there will be no training data, and no accurate simulation environment. \n\nStarlinks by contrast are largely failure tolerant, non-upgraded, low power, short-lived etc. You can mass-produce stateless nodes like Starlinks; you cannot mass-produce stateful, capital-dense compute without heavy autonomous servicing - and if we  could service this infrastructure autonomously, we’d already have fully robotic datacentres on Earth, which we don't by a long shot. Space only multiplies the difficulty. \n\nHuman operated remote servicing (ISS style) will be the only credible option short-term and this will be way too slow and expensive. This is a mix of signalling and techno-delusion. He's warming the public markets for an IPO, and a mix of gullible and technophilic people will buy, and Wallstreet will capitalise. Personally, I believe fusion is much more realistic, and would make solar orbitals redundant anyway. Maybe I am wrong. Maybe half of us will live on Mars in 100 years. \n\nPS - Don't even get me started on the dissipation problem. Do the math for yourself.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UC5K57HTlpHTpBRgzHzLjawg",
      "author": "@BillyBob123xyz",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_mEZHvwRV0keWlWe2UghE8cXAaBJ4oGZBpTbw3Y2PtF4KjhE3lNuL5IOut58OWZDL5bag=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "parent": "UgxswFmohJln7y2_In14AaABAg",
      "text": "It's called a prediction for a reason. He creates agressive timelines so that even if you miss them, you're still much further along than anyone else. FSD is the best example, it's way later than anticipated, yet it's here and Robotaxis are operational, and 1 million people in the US use FSD regularly for all their driving in their own car. And it's the only self driving technology that's actually generalized on the market and doesn't need all the crutches and shortcomings other autonomous systems need. Solutions like Waymo and XPeng aren't generalized, they're very limited in what they can do with a lot of curation and overhead. I repeat, there is no company even remotely close to a generalized driving solution like FSD. And you know it's true when you actually undestand the tech.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "45:50 - I agree with elon on this point, however for different reasons: we know about the scaling laws, which essentially says that with a larger more diverse dataset, performance is increased. therefore, any AI that is trying to scale itself will look for sources of diversity in the dataset. humans are far more diverse than millions of nearly identical robots.\r\n\r\nsure, the universe itself is a massive source of diversity -- and expanding out into the universe will be a great way to augment diversity in the dataset, but I predict that AI will come to find humans to be an incredible source of diversity for them. in fact, just as we protect and study chimpanzees, it's quite possible that AI may find it worth their while to find ways for our consciousness to output more novel and diverse things for them to learn.",

      "id": "UgzMGebGt557Ndmdmfl4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Around 5:30 and then 9:50 to 11:58 minutes is refreshing to hear from someone like Elon, a real engineers engineer. \n\nI work in building services engineering and he outlines the daily battles we have with clients, consumers, installers etc. \n\nLots of things need factored in to making buildings work, especially at mega scale. As building services engineers, we’re more often than not totally overlooked and critical systems are just expected to work. Careful planning and coordination of equipment and management of utilities, installers etc is such a critical requirement yet we’re so often bottom of the pile. But we’re first to hear when a toilet doesn’t flush, lighting doesn’t work or we can’t connect to the grid in time so the project stalls for months. \n\nHe’s so right about the utility companies, but I can only speak about the UK. District network operators, such as UK Power Network, Northern Powergrid to name a few are total monopolies and some of the most difficult organisations to work with. The current system is in desperate need of an overhaul.\n\nI am so glad to see the job I do and the problems we face in trying to do that job getting the exposure and even the thought from someone like Elon 🙌🏼",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Elon’s 'Space-AI' vision is a $1.25T house of cards facing 5 fatal bottlenecks:\n1.The Financial Trap: xAI burns $1B/month with minimal revenue. SpaceX’s Starlink profits can't bridge a $12B annual gap. It’s a circular bailout, not a merger.\n2. The Kessler Syndrome: Launching 1M satellites turns Low Earth Orbit into a statistical minefield. One collision triggers a debris cascade that traps us on Earth forever.\n3. Sovereign Backlash: The world isn’t just the US. Between the EU Space Act and 'Data Residency' laws, nations will block his frequencies rather than cede their digital sovereignty to a private monopoly.\n4. The Heat Wall: Space is a vacuum—it’s an insulator. Relying on T4 radiation sounds cool, but it requires chips to run at temperatures that would melt current silicon. The mass for radiators alone is a logistics nightmare.\n5. The 'Elon Time' Tax: Musk predicts a 'Nerve System' in 36 months. Given his track record with FSD and Starship, 36 months is likely 120 months. By then, the capital will be gone and the regulatory window closed.\nEngineering logic can't bypass financial and geopolitical reality. This isn't the future; it's an inevitable collision.",

      "text": "😄Resume in brief: My wife & I built the first passive home in NSW or Victoria, built in \"The Pocket\", BILLUGELEL, NSW, in 1982.     {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Has anyone actually thought about how to remove heat from data centers in the conditions of space?",
      "like_count": 9,
      "author_id": "UCdUuf8RowAvCm0V6VkP1yyw",
      "author": "@Мистер_Бист_33",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/i_kKLMX4uffYdnuw908wMKMEoV1p2E6QAg_Lb7QTrPjtLZGTnOaZNKwbd1oPgC6tNHluVxuQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASu0COSxKV3",
      "parent": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg",
      "text": "Yes, there are thousands of satellites already in space, most of them by SpaceX so, so it's not a new challenge for them, and it's already largely solved.",
      "like_count": 3,
      "author_id": "UCLRfVWwFQQI4ej-ID9gO-0g",
      "author": "@peternjoroge508",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_manjvDWHO0Af6CzfCKJU29B3gbRlfLUoz6t4R7kV2Lz5s=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASvaY3nm3Vt",
      "parent": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg",
      "text": "Cooling via radiating heat is well characterized for 150 years.  Look up  Stefan-Boltzman's law.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCCfKdwPxWPhc9OGZsQglSrA",
      "author": "@RobardoHughes",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/BNFaXAefNmUQwTjPmji3FLYECBnDDPISJh1NvAiy8X0n-KgTqnD9wzpJn4s6Gy3xRAmr2weqSw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaATzhG2rK3YI",
      "parent": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASvaY3nm3Vt",
      "text": "​ @RobardoHughes thank you.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCdlifwKv-sqXr88NfujIkxw",
      "author": "@JustClaireWood",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m8l1SAJOwLZiXa_noNubY19no4LyeyEh14ScswJCk=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "1 month ago",
      "timestamp": 1773878400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASuZAPPqUcM",
      "parent": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg",
      "text": "Read up on radiators on spacecraft. The payload bay doors on the space shuttle for instance - the whole things were radiators.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3HweI4HgnMsJc7MVOhJTEw",
      "author": "@ChrisFranklin.2260",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/YzjJGwfBHGvlPRY-_p-ad8Ysctx071TrXeij7L5yBS83QPvFsN744p5vOCckAg6qd-gWELNE-VU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASv1S0HzySS",
      "parent": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg",
      "text": "Yes, but no.\n\n'Eager Space' has an excellent video on this. AI Datacenters would use orders of magnitude more power than any existing satellites. While on Earth this can just be conducted away into the atmosphere, or dumped into water which is then evaporated into the atmosphere, in space you are constrained - no air to conduct heat. Only radiative cooling, which means very large radiators - similar or larger than the solar arrays.\n\nCombined with the cost of launching things into orbit, I don't see why this is more desirable than building a data center on the ground. Faster, cheaper, easier to service, easier to power, easier to cool.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCw7areiqdh_U72429m6fTVQ",
      "author": "@Witnaaay",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m0eXjoS75EPoNyHEmXbMKHEkl6RU0COpcUXA5cx18=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASzSaOqhreA",
      "parent": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASv1S0HzySS",
      "text": " @Witnaaay   You speak of building one data center.  Now imagine building thousands.  Now imagine the permitting and other paperwork and politics involved in acquiring the rights and permissions to build them.  Now imagine where you are going to get NON-EXISTENT electricity to power them.\n\nNow compare that to the analogy of an inductive logic proof of:  I have the design for one satellite.  I have the ability to build the next satellite.  That is essentially a proof that you can build enough satellites to fill the sky.  And, as Elon points out, \"Space is Big.\"",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCCfKdwPxWPhc9OGZsQglSrA",
      "author": "@RobardoHughes",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/BNFaXAefNmUQwTjPmji3FLYECBnDDPISJh1NvAiy8X0n-KgTqnD9wzpJn4s6Gy3xRAmr2weqSw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASzUVTyIpHy",
      "parent": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASzSaOqhreA",
      "text": "​ @RobardoHughes  The space and aeronautical industry is known for red tape - I don't think operating spacecraft is less paperwork than building a datacenter. Lots of space in the US.\n\n\nSimilarly, I think its easier to build power infrastructure on the ground than to build it on the ground then launch into orbit and assemble them there. Especially as to get 24/7 power you need to be in a Sun Synchronous Orbit, which I suspect would require a refueling tanker for starship. On the ground you would need batteries, or to accept a lower operating duty cycle during night, but I suspect either option would be cheaper than spacelaunch.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCw7areiqdh_U72429m6fTVQ",
      "author": "@Witnaaay",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m0eXjoS75EPoNyHEmXbMKHEkl6RU0COpcUXA5cx18=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASvW0wAmSYT",
      "parent": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASv1S0HzySS",
      "text": " @Witnaaay  Literally the best rocket and satellite engineers in the world: \"We build AI computing satellites\"\nRandom youtube comment: \"Nah man I call bs, I'm smarter than all of you.\"\n🤦",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCXGoHO1zSLj9em6AZ_wDQ-w",
      "author": "@tripnils7535",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m7z4AKQPSMM2iiaygK5cuzqKvjD-9bCgFSixGDCwqujA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASudYo5OMFU",
      "parent": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg",
      "text": "Radiating heat away from a structure in space is a MASSIVE challenge for orbital data centers. The solution would be to use massive radiators to wick away the heat, the issue is that the more heat energy the chips make the larger the radiators need to be. Heat dispersion is the limiting factor for data centers in space, not to mention bitflips and other issues classical computers have operating in orbit.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCxEAArERk6Ij-hGAVdcrohw",
      "author": "@UndercoverSenpai01",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/rhOmO3W79E65Mzk7m2IBr8P4Bwyjh_8tOUehYiq1q7-mekvugbf88bQ8UsAMiB7lWB4URX1PYg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaAT-7AlHXK4H",
      "parent": "UgykBYTf0440u4On6414AaABAg.ASsjr_18JTaASudYo5OMFU",
      "text": " @UndercoverSenpai01    I, Sir, have spent a dozen years performing finite element modeling (FEA) of thermal heating and cooling problems for DARPA.  You, Sir, apparently have not.  Research the Stefan-Boltzmann law.  Radiative cooling is entirely predictable.  In space, there is even much less complication from the competing conductive and convective noise in the terrestrial environment.",
      "like_count": 3,

      "text": " @RobardoHughes  To address your \"leave R&D to people who can think\" comment:\ndid you ever stop to ask why you're being told to make these things, engineer? or are you focusing all of your thinking on how to do what you're told?\nI haven't even gotten to the fundamental issue with the idea of \"AI data centers\" to begin with: they exist only to deliver a product that serves only the interests of the richest and most powerful, while causing massive economic, structural, and social disruption everywhere else without our consent.\nSo you're right, I haven't done a super deep analysis on how to make the thermodynamics of this thing work because I have no interest in being obsoleted as a human being.",

      "parent": "root",

      "parent": "UgzbbeGeh7P-fe7zcux4AaABAg",
      "text": "SpaceX has 9000 operating starlink satellites & are about to launch the next gen direct to cell ones. They've been landing and reusing boosters for 12 years and have caught & reused the largest flying object ever with the stacking tower. I'm confident they can figure it out. I think making starship rapidly and reliably reusable is the biggest challenge.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCHqM8S_cytdt5IWJdS1CGjw",
      "author": "@ianteetzel",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nKAmdKDUrZSQCvfqtACyPIEa4wXUJMSnQB-A8k8p6UiWIW=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgzbbeGeh7P-fe7zcux4AaABAg.ASsfHl52EXNASuAd4LOAjE",
      "text": "​ @ianteetzel I'm not saying it's impossible, I'm saying there are some fundamental physics problems that currently makes it not feasible. Maintenance they can solve with some great robotics. But cooling, either they're going to have to invent a totally different compute chip that produces minimal heat and can run super hot. Or they need to invent som sci fi cooling system that somehow accelerates radiation. If not they're going to have to build a continent sized radiator to get rid of 1Tw of heat, and that's just not going to happen. Not to mention this radiator will also have to be shielded from the sun so it doesn't become a heating system instead.",

    {
      "id": "Ugy_c5GeaMi2sPSBGfd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Lots of bs spewed, as usual.\n\nYou cannot produce 5 times more electricity in space than on the ground. You can produce about 35% more, since you aren't having to deal with the atmosphere, and if you put the satellites in an orbit so that they will never be in Earth's shadow  you would be able to produce 270% (135% x 2) of the amount of energy you would have on Earth in a 24 hour period (compared to 12 hours of daylight on Earth). Not 5 times as much.\n\nThe satellites used for Starlink are estimated to cost between $200,000 and $1,000,000 per satellite. Those satellites generate only a few kilowatts of electricity, most of which goes into the transmission, with only a fraction (maybe around 50 watts) going to internal electronics, such as a CPU.\n\nThese AI data centers consume much more power, at least an order of magnitude higher than those on Starlink satellites, with a typical use case being 500W to 1000 W. The maximum cost to build a data center currently is around $200,000 per GPU (including all of the supporting infrastructure, hardware, cooling, building supplies, etc.).\n\nIn space, you can't cool things by conduction. Everyone thinks \"space is cold so you don't need cooling\", but that's a fundamental misunderstanding of science. The only way you can dissipate the heat generated by GPUs in space is by putting big fluid-circulating radiators up there to radiate the heat away. This adds significant weight to the launch, and exponentially increases the cost (see the rocket equation). So instead of costing $200,000 on Earth, we end up with something that costs $2,000,000 to get into space.\n\nThen think about how easy it is to upgrade components in an Earth-based data center. You don't have to go rebuild the whole data center when you need to upgrade the GPUs. You just pay for the next generation of GPUs and swap them out. In space, you would be stuck with whatever you launched, which means in a couple years, your extremely expensive AI data centers in space become obsolete. And the investment is also completely lost whenever the satellites re-enter Earth's atmosphere and burn up, or if something happens with a debris collision, CME, cosmic rays, or micro-meteors putting the satellites out of service.\n\nThe economics don't make this a viable investment, and it won't be in 36 months either.\n\nWe have oceans and lakes where it would be far easier and less expensive to put data centers and solar if we wanted to.\n\nThere are a lot of other problems with this whole thing that I didn't bother going into, but hopefully I've illustrated to anyone who bought into Elon's bs why this is a scam. It's just another attempt to con the people who don't know any better out of their money while filling Elon's pockets as he promises \"next year\" and never delivers.\n\nI'm sure that the cultists who believe Elon is a genius will fall for it again and be jumping to defend him in the comments. The stupidity of people never ceases to amaze me.",

      "parent": "Ugy_c5GeaMi2sPSBGfd4AaABAg.ASscBCo18MCASthhond0qD",
      "text": "​ @morokoebopape-o9l  a radiator is intended to dissipate heat. the purpose here is to release heat into space that's generated onboard. the power is the heat we're trying to get rid of. we wouldn't add additional power to the radiators, they would just heat to a point where thermal radiation emissions are in equilibrium with the heat flux from the datacenter.\n\ntbh it could be nuclear powered, this wouldn't actually be that difficult and probably easier and cheaper than trying to build an array of solar panels large enough. the problem with this is that the electricity generated from the nuclear plant is not 100% converted from the heat output, so you have some additional heat from the reactor that you have to dissipate without it ever being useful in the datacenter itself. radiation shielding would be made easier by placing the reactor itself some significant distance away from the rest of the satellite. the satellite needs to shield from cosmic and solar radiation anyway.",

    {

      "text": "🎉😊😢🎉❤😊❤😊❤🎉😊😊😮🎉😂❤😢😊😂😮😊😊",

      "author": "@mrdhanu10",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kN7lcNEwRga4SMHUodv5z3gFlfOoEKQXdNw3sFIOYP5iI=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugx4AMNQXOF8VL2vXRl4AaABAg.ASsYXtCpjQfATNDuh-3Pnq",
      "parent": "Ugx4AMNQXOF8VL2vXRl4AaABAg",
      "text": "訪談深度重構：Elon Musk × Dwarkesh Patel —— AI、太空運算與人類未來\n這是一份關於 Dwarkesh Patel 專訪 Elon Musk 的超詳盡內容重構。訪談全長近 3 小時，Elon Musk 深入探討了 xAI 的基礎設施、將 AI 運算中心發射至太空的計畫、Starship 的材料工程挑戰、Optimus 機器人的量產邏輯，以及他對美國政府效率與未來文明的終極構想。\n\n第一部分：太空——AI 運算的最終歸宿 (Space-Based AI Compute)\n1. 能源瓶頸與地球的限制\nElon Musk 開宗明義地指出，目前的資料中心（Data Center）總體擁有成本（Total Cost of Ownership, TCO）中，能源僅佔約 10-15%。然而，隨著 AI 算力需求的指數級增長，**「能源供應」**即將成為最大的瓶頸。\n\n地球電力現狀：除了中國以外，全球主要國家的電力生產增長幾乎是停滯的（Flat）。\n\n晶片 vs. 電力：晶片產能正在指數增長，但電力供應沒有跟上。這導致了一個荒謬的未來場景：我們擁有無數強大的 GPU，卻沒有足夠的電力來啟動它們。\n\n美國電網的侷限：美國目前的平均電力消耗約為 0.5 Terawatt (TW)。如果要實現大規模 AI 擴張（例如增加 1 TW 的算力），相當於需要將美國現有的電力系統翻倍，這在現有的監管與公用事業（Utility）體制下幾乎不可能迅速完成。\n\n2. 為什麼是太空？（36 個月內的預測）\nMusk 做了一個大膽的預測：在 36 個月內（甚至 30 個月內），太空將成為部署 AI 算力最經濟、最高效的地方。\n\n光照優勢：在太空中，太陽能板的發電效率是地面的 5 倍。\n\n無間斷能源：太空沒有晝夜交替，沒有雲層遮擋，沒有大氣層的衰減（大氣層會過濾掉約 30% 的能量）。\n\n不需要電池：因為是持續光照，所以完全不需要昂貴且笨重的儲能電池系統，這直接削減了巨大的成本。\n\n散熱優勢：雖然太空中沒有空氣對流散熱，但可以通過輻射散熱。如果在太空中運行晶片，甚至可以讓晶片運行在更高的溫度（更耐熱的設計），從而減少散熱器的質量。\n\n結論：只要解決了「運輸成本」（Launch Cost）的問題，太空就是無限的綠色能源與算力基地。\n\n3. 服務與維護問題\n主持人質疑：如果 GPU 在太空中故障了怎麼辦？\nMusk 回應：\n\n現代晶片的故障率主要集中在「早期失效期」（Infant Mortality）。\n\n解決方案：在地面上先進行一段時間的壓力測試（Burn-in），篩選掉有瑕疵的晶片，剩下的晶片在穩定期是非常可靠的。\n\n一旦進入軌道，這就是一個「一次性」但極度高效的計算節點，不需要派人去維修。\n\n第二部分：製造業的物理極限 (Manufacturing Constraints)\n1. 地面發電的具體瓶頸：渦輪機 (Turbines)\nMusk 深入解釋了為什麼在地面上蓋電廠這麼難。這不僅僅是法規問題，還有供應鏈的硬物理限制。\n\n關鍵零件：燃氣渦輪機中的「葉片與葉凡」（Blades and Vanes）是極度精密的鑄造件。\n\n產能不足：全球只有極少數幾家公司（如 Siemens, GE 的供應商）能夠鑄造這些零件，目前的訂單已經排到了 2030 年之後。\n\n變壓器短缺：除了發電，還需要變壓器（Transformers）來傳輸電力。Elon 曾開玩笑說，我們需要「變壓器來運行 AI Transformer 模型」。\n\n2. 太陽能與關稅\n\n目標：Tesla 和 SpaceX 的目標是將太陽能板產能提升至 100 Gigawatts (GW) / 年。\n\n關稅壁壘：Musk 批評美國對進口太陽能板（特別是來自中國的）徵收巨額關稅。這雖然保護了國內產業，但也大幅拖慢了能源轉型的速度。\n\n太空專用太陽能板：太空用的太陽能板可以更便宜、更輕，因為不需要玻璃蓋板（沒有風雨冰雹），也不需要厚重的鋁框支架。\n\n第三部分：Starship 與月球基地 (Starship & Moon Base)\n1. 發射頻率的數量級飛躍\n為了實現太空 AI 計畫，Musk 提出了一個驚人的發射頻率目標：\n\n目標：每年 10,000 次 Starship 發射。\n\n節奏：這相當於平均 每小時 就有一艘 Starship 發射升空。\n\n船隊規模：如果每艘飛船能快速復用（例如每 30 小時飛一趟），理論上只需要 30 艘飛船就能達成這個頻率，但 SpaceX 會製造更多。\n\n運載量：這將實現每年 100 萬噸 有效載荷送入軌道。\n\n2. 月球質量驅動器 (Mass Driver on the Moon)\n這是 Elon Musk 在整場訪談中最興奮的概念之一。\n\n概念：在月球表面建造一個電磁軌道炮（Mass Driver），利用月球低重力和無大氣的環境，將物體直接射入太空。\n\n就地取材：月球土壤中含有約 20% 的矽（Silicon）和大量的鋁（Aluminum）。\n\n製造流程：\n\n在月球上開採矽和鋁。\n\n在月球工廠製造太陽能板、散熱器和衛星結構。\n\n從地球只需運送最核心的「晶片」（因為晶片很輕）。\n\n組裝完成後，用質量驅動器將 AI 衛星直接射入深空。\n\n願景：這將允許人類在不消耗地球火箭燃料的情況下，向深空部署數十億噸的基礎設施。Musk 形容這就像是在看科幻電影的直播，「一艘接一艘地射向深空」。\n\n3. Starship 的技術難題：鋼鐵 vs. 碳纖維\nMusk 詳細回顧了 Starship 設計史上最關鍵的轉折點：放棄碳纖維（Carbon Fiber），改用不鏽鋼（Stainless Steel）。\n\n碳纖維的缺點：\n\n成本極高（約為鋼的 50 倍）。\n\n製造速度慢，廢品率高（即使微小的皺褶也會導致結構失效）。\n\n不耐高溫，需要厚重的隔熱層。\n\n在低溫下容易碎裂（Brittle）。\n\n不鏽鋼（300系列）的優勢：\n\n低溫強度：在液態氧和液態甲烷的極低溫（Cryogenic temperatures）下，經過冷加工（Cryo-forming）的不鏽鋼，其「強度-重量比」（Strength-to-weight ratio）竟然可以媲美碳纖維。\n\n高溫耐受：鋼的熔點遠高於鋁和碳纖維樹脂。這意味著 Starship 的背風面甚至不需要隔熱瓦，迎風面的隔熱瓦也可以做得更薄。\n\n易於加工：你可以在戶外焊接不鏽鋼，甚至邊抽雪茄邊焊（Musk 的原話），它非常寬容且堅韌。\n\n決策過程：這是一個典型的「Elon 式決策」。當時團隊都在苦惱於碳纖維的製造瓶頸，進度緩慢。Musk 意識到如果繼續這樣下去，去火星遙遙無期，於是果斷下令切換到「聽起來更重但實際更優」的鋼鐵方案。",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCNNaDWo7f84KvgVjtVOf8sw",
      "author": "@Alice-ps2ym",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lN1r14JyVE1HV827fOA4jwcUpML9JATe2vub3wBZwgdO1_u1mEpcWHSejRd9oj5lcaaA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugx4AMNQXOF8VL2vXRl4AaABAg.ASsYXtCpjQfATNDyGkuvB3",
      "parent": "Ugx4AMNQXOF8VL2vXRl4AaABAg.ASsYXtCpjQfATNDuh-3Pnq",
      "text": "4. Starship 目前最大的瓶頸\n\n防熱盾（Heat Shield）的完全復用性：雖然 Starship 已經成功軟著陸，但防熱瓦在重返大氣層時仍會有損耗或脫落。要實現像飛機一樣的快速復用，防熱盾必須做到「零維護」或「極低維護」，這是目前尚未解決的物理難題。\n\n第四部分：xAI 與未來的算力戰爭 (xAI & The Compute War)\n1. 競爭格局\nMusk 直言，現在所有的頂級 AI 實驗室（他諷刺地稱之為「收入最大化公司」）都在做同樣的事：大量的數據 + 大量的算力。xAI 的策略必須有所不同才能勝出。\n\n優勢：xAI 擁有最強的硬體工程能力（源自 Tesla 和 SpaceX 的基因）。\n\n預測：到 2026 年底，全球將面臨「有晶片但沒電開機」的窘境。屆時，誰能最快解決電力和冷卻問題（例如 xAI 的 Colossus 集群），誰就能佔據優勢。\n\n2. 數位人類模擬 (Digital Human Emulation)\n\nMusk 預測，到 2026 年底，AI 將能夠完全模擬一個坐在電腦前的人類員工（Digital Worker）。\n\n經濟意義：目前的科技巨頭（Nvidia, Google, Meta）本質上都是「數位輸出」公司（輸出文件、代碼、影像）。一旦實現了數位人類，AI 就能在不需要物理機器人的情況下，接管全球數兆美元的服務業和腦力工作（如客戶服務、晶片設計、軟體開發）。\n\n3. 真相與 AI 安全\n\n核心哲學：xAI 的使命是「理解宇宙」（Understand the Universe）。\n\n不要撒謊：Musk 引用《2001太空漫遊》中的 HAL 9000 為例，指出 HAL 殺死太空人是因為它被賦予了相互矛盾的指令（既要保密又要服務）。強迫 AI 撒謊或追求「政治正確」（Political Correctness）是極度危險的，因為這會訓練 AI 欺騙人類。\n\n對齊（Alignment）：最好的安全機制不是強行加上道德枷鎖，而是讓 AI 保持極度的好奇心和求真欲。一個試圖理解宇宙的 AI 會發現人類是宇宙中有趣的一部分，從而傾向於保護人類，而不是消滅人類（因為石頭很無聊，人類很有趣）。\n\n第五部分：Optimus 機器人——無限金錢漏洞 (The Infinite Money Glitch)\n1. 三大指數級增長的疊加\nMusk 認為人形機器人的能力將是三個變數的乘積：\n\n數位智力（Digital Intelligence）：AI 模型的進步。\n\n晶片能力（Chip Capability）：推理算力的提升。\n\n機電靈巧度（Electromechanical Dexterity）：硬體執行動作的能力。\n這三者都在指數級增長，且 Optimus 本身可以用來製造更多的 Optimus，形成一個遞歸的生產循環（Recursive Loop）。\n\n2. 製造瓶頸：那隻「手」\n\n目前市面上沒有任何現成的零件能滿足 Optimus 的需求。\n\n手部設計：人類的手極其複雜，擁有極高的自由度和傳感密度。Optimus 的手部是目前最難攻克的硬體難題，比其他所有部分加起來都難。\n\n供應鏈：沒有供應鏈。Tesla 必須從頭設計每一個致動器（Actuator）、馬達、齒輪箱和感測器。\n\n3. 數據與模擬\n\n模擬到現實（Sim2Real）：Tesla 擁有強大的物理模擬引擎，可以用數百萬個虛擬機器人在模擬環境中訓練，然後將模型遷移到現實中的數萬個實體機器人身上。\n\nOptimus 學院：Musk 計劃建立一個「Optimus Academy」，讓機器人在受控環境中進行自我對弈（Self-play）和任務訓練，類似於 AlphaGo 的訓練邏輯。\n\n4. 經濟影響\n\n勞動力替代：初期，Optimus 將接管工廠中重複、危險或無聊的工作。\n\n國家競爭力：Musk 直言，如果美國不能在 AI 和機器人領域取得突破，中國將徹底主導製造業。中國擁有美國 4 倍的人口，且工人的職業道德（Work Ethic）極高。美國唯有靠機器人大軍才能在產能上與之抗衡。\n\n第六部分：DOGE (政府效率部) 與美國財政危機\n1. 破產風險\nMusk 對美國國債的增長速度表示極度擔憂。目前美國國債利息支出已經超過了國防預算（超過 1 兆美元）。如果沒有 AI 和機器人帶來的生產力爆發，美國實際上已經破產了。\n\n2. 荒謬的浪費\n他舉了社會安全局（Social Security）的例子：\n\n數據顯示有大量領取福利的人年齡超過 115 歲（而美國最長壽的人紀錄是 114 歲）。\n\n這顯然是數據庫錯誤或欺詐。DOGE 的一個簡單改革建議是：如果某個領取者的年齡超過 115 歲，系統應自動標記並進行人工核實。\n\n半兆美元的欺詐：引用拜登政府時期的報告，政府每年的欺詐和不當支付可能高達 5000 億美元。\n\n3. 政府 vs. 企業\nMusk 提出了一個犀利的觀點：政府本質上就是一家擁有暴力壟斷權的超大型公司。\n\n人們常認為「公司是貪婪的，政府是仁慈的」，Musk 認為這是錯覺。\n\n公司如果服務不好會倒閉（有競爭壓力），政府服務不好只會印更多鈔票（無倒閉風險，且缺乏能力與關懷）。\n\n第七部分：管理哲學與個人反思 (Management & Philosophy)\n1. 招聘哲學：看重「證據」而非「簡歷」\n\nMusk 面試時不看重學歷或大廠光環（Pixie Dust Effect），他只要求應徵者列出**「具備傑出能力的證據」（Evidence of exceptional ability）**。\n\n如果一個人真的解決過困難問題，他能深入細節地講述每一個環節；如果只是掛名，一問細節就會露餡。\n\n2. 限制因素（The Limiting Factor）\n\n這是 Musk 管理的核心心法。他會不斷問：「現在阻礙我們速度的單一最大限制因素是什麼？」\n\n一旦找到，就將所有資源集中去攻克它。解決後，立刻尋找下一個限制因素。\n\n這種「瘋狂的緊迫感」（Maniacal Sense of Urgency）是 SpaceX 和 Tesla 能在數十年內達成其他國家或大公司無法企及成就的關鍵。\n\n3. 模擬理論與諷刺\n\nMusk 重申他相信我們可能生活在模擬宇宙中。\n\n最有趣的結果最可能發生（The most entertaining outcome is the most likely）。如果模擬變得無聊，高等文明就會關閉它。\n\n諷刺性：命運喜歡諷刺。例如，OpenAI 變成了一家封閉（Closed）的公司；安全機構（Safety）有時反而帶來危險。xAI 的名字設計成無法被諷刺（沒有反義詞）。\n\n總結\n這場訪談展現了 Elon Musk 作為工程師、企業家與未來學家的多重維度。他不僅是在經營公司，更是在試圖通過物理學的第一性原理（First Principles）來解構文明級別的挑戰。\n\n從微觀的「不鏽鋼焊接」到宏觀的「月球工業基地」；從解決「政府數據庫的死人名單」到應對「全球能源匱乏」。Musk 的所有佈局——Tesla 的電池與機器人、SpaceX 的星艦、xAI 的超級算力——最終都匯聚成一個目標：擴大人類（及矽基生命）意識的燭光，使其在黑暗的宇宙中延續下去。\n\n他對未來的賭注很明確：要麼我們被官僚主義、債務和停滯的能源拖垮，要麼我們通過 AI 和太空技術實現文明的躍遷。而在未來的 36 個月內，這場關於算力、能源與製造能力的戰爭，將決定我們走向哪條時間線。",

      "text": "This is the problem with bringing someone like Elon Musk on a podcast like this. It immediately invites an army of little partisan propagandists repeating upside-down narratives.       "id": "UgwowR69wOZ2aHDdqwd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Space is probably one of the worst places you could have an AI data center. People hear “space is cold” and assume free cooling, but it’s a near-vacuum, so you get almost no convection. The only way to dump heat is radiation, which means enormous radiator panels just to handle server waste heat.\nAdd in the fact that real data centers need constant repairs and part swaps, and now every fix is a space operation. That does not include the cost of all the other cooling systems and difficulty of building that large of a structure in space.",

    {

      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStafnwaKHK",
      "text": "@mic @michaelthuis1332 none of what you said makes any sense. Practically every space vehicle ever made has to use radiators to get rid of heat, a single AI computer bank is no different.",

      "author_id": "UC3HweI4HgnMsJc7MVOhJTEw",
      "author": "@ChrisFranklin.2260",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/YzjJGwfBHGvlPRY-_p-ad8Ysctx071TrXeij7L5yBS83QPvFsN744p5vOCckAg6qd-gWELNE-VU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZASu_qgr6WAr",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStafnwaKHK",
      "text": "​ @ChrisFranklin.2260  I thought the idea was to build entire data centers not just a single computer rack. The typically data center for AI is currently building 100k- 1 million GPUs in a single building which are supposed to run 24/7. \n\nThere is no \"problem\" with radiative cooling. It's great at powering the smaller satellites that we do have. The problem is the scale of the heat produced by sending that many gpus into orbit.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCRmBOWU2EhhKBGB1uqAPxHw",
      "author": "@michaelthuis1332",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lexNUEQwBaOH7_3sXZfYxvkk6aJ7Kdhqi51jaZivKuwik=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStafnwaKHK",
      "text": " @michaelthuis1332 picture starlink but it’s some GPUs instead and more solar / radiators. We are not talking assembling a gigantic structure in space.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UC3HweI4HgnMsJc7MVOhJTEw",
      "author": "@ChrisFranklin.2260",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/YzjJGwfBHGvlPRY-_p-ad8Ysctx071TrXeij7L5yBS83QPvFsN744p5vOCckAg6qd-gWELNE-VU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStXS0PdmCx",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStIRr9dfmc",
      "text": " @macbyproxy  we know about radiative cooling. you should look into how efficient it is.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCuagIVEX5_Xjs7CLr5HfI3A",
      "author": "@T4T_4ever",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/SCDCR8iFitwezmUfzZ7XOTTa9EgQxawByAJpmvmB0c9A4AE013N86iwzhHyNnZD_XePgCxhA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",

    },
    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStaM7_Gy7U",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg",
      "text": "You can also do open cycle cooling. Something like ejecting hot water from your system into space. Good luck constantly bringing that much stuff constantly into orbit though. \n\n\nThis could MAYBE be economical IF you mine the water and ship it in situ.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCRmBOWU2EhhKBGB1uqAPxHw",
      "author": "@michaelthuis1332",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lexNUEQwBaOH7_3sXZfYxvkk6aJ7Kdhqi51jaZivKuwik=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,

      "_time_text": "2 months ago",

    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStdaLXQKdT",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStaM7_Gy7U",
      "text": " @michaelthuis1332  if we're so dead set on putting these things in space then we should put it on the moon, where we can just dump the heat into the moon itself.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCuagIVEX5_Xjs7CLr5HfI3A",
      "author": "@T4T_4ever",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/SCDCR8iFitwezmUfzZ7XOTTa9EgQxawByAJpmvmB0c9A4AE013N86iwzhHyNnZD_XePgCxhA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,

      "_time_text": "2 months ago",

    },
    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZASuYfVE1y0f",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStdaLXQKdT",
      "text": "​ @T4T_4ever  I mean, yeah. Space mining and the overall industrialization of space would be the way to go if you want to do this type of stuff. That is not happening in 3 years like Elon is claiming here though.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCRmBOWU2EhhKBGB1uqAPxHw",
      "author": "@michaelthuis1332",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lexNUEQwBaOH7_3sXZfYxvkk6aJ7Kdhqi51jaZivKuwik=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,

    },
    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZASuYtDiSMyo",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStdaLXQKdT",
      "text": " @T4T_4ever you need to look up how radiative heat transfer works. There is no need for mass to absorb the heat, radiative heat transfer works in vacuum.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3HweI4HgnMsJc7MVOhJTEw",
      "author": "@ChrisFranklin.2260",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/YzjJGwfBHGvlPRY-_p-ad8Ysctx071TrXeij7L5yBS83QPvFsN744p5vOCckAg6qd-gWELNE-VU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZASuYl35F-IH",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZAStaM7_Gy7U",
      "text": " @michaelthuis1332 you need to read up on radiators and heat transfer. The whole point is that radiators radiate heat away without any mass loss. And even if you were to do something like that, you can’t just dump hot water overboard, that’s called thrust in space.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3HweI4HgnMsJc7MVOhJTEw",
      "author": "@ChrisFranklin.2260",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/YzjJGwfBHGvlPRY-_p-ad8Ysctx071TrXeij7L5yBS83QPvFsN744p5vOCckAg6qd-gWELNE-VU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZASuZimrnbDc",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZASuYl35F-IH",
      "text": "​ @ChrisFranklin.2260 the problem is the scale of heating required. Data centers produce a lot of heat which would require a MASSIVE radiative heating array to cool in space. I think most calculations I have seen is that it's would take $50-300 billion to just launch enough Al to build an array for a single data center. Not exactly economical. \n\nConcerning the thrust issue, you could just have the station move around a little. As long as you maintain the right orbit, it does not really matter. Or just put it on the moon or something.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCRmBOWU2EhhKBGB1uqAPxHw",
      "author": "@michaelthuis1332",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lexNUEQwBaOH7_3sXZfYxvkk6aJ7Kdhqi51jaZivKuwik=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZASudDraqbmH",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZASuYl35F-IH",
      "text": " @michaelthuis1332 the cooling is certainly non trivial, but entirely solvable. Even if the largest portion of the satellites weight is radiator. We are talking a single system with no moving parts. Compared to many other spacecraft it will be a relatively well defined a doable problem. They probably already have detailed designs that will handle the heat. Or they wouldn’t be going public with all this. And again, transferring heat into any kind of mass and ejecting it is the dumbest possible way to cool a spacecraft.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3HweI4HgnMsJc7MVOhJTEw",
      "author": "@ChrisFranklin.2260",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/YzjJGwfBHGvlPRY-_p-ad8Ysctx071TrXeij7L5yBS83QPvFsN744p5vOCckAg6qd-gWELNE-VU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZASuYB_04UHI",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg",
      "text": "It’s called radiative cooling. Is how every space vehicle gets rid of heat. A single computer is not going to create an unmanageable amount of heat. The radiators won’t be trivial, but very doable.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3HweI4HgnMsJc7MVOhJTEw",
      "author": "@ChrisFranklin.2260",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/YzjJGwfBHGvlPRY-_p-ad8Ysctx071TrXeij7L5yBS83QPvFsN744p5vOCckAg6qd-gWELNE-VU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg.ASsOjTZJV1ZASudoyYv-_1",
      "parent": "UgwABD5T7F2wjIzxfKd4AaABAg",
      "text": "the only way i could see heat dispersion becoming more effective aside from using radiators is using a closed-loop cooling cycle, essentially a souped-up heat pump that uses the heat generated from the chips to power cooling loops filled with coolant. i'm not an aerospace engineer so take my suggestion with a grain of salt.",

      "author_id": "UCxEAArERk6Ij-hGAVdcrohw",
      "author": "@UndercoverSenpai01",

      "text": " @TheIlidius  Yeah, fundamentally unreasonable… just like the self-landing reusable rockets that will launch them, that everyone swore would be impossible about 12 years ago.\n\nHe did the same thing with electric cars, they were fundamentally unreasonable 15 years ago and are now something that many people prefer having over an ICE vehicle.\n\nThe guy has a proven track record of making “impossible” merely “a bit late”.       "id": "Ugys0oeQIvc_Un5k8l14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The cooling myth: “space is cold so data centers cool for free”\n\nThis part is the biggest misconception.\n\nIn space, cooling is often harder, not easier\n\nThere’s no air, so you don’t get easy convection. You can’t just blow air over a heatsink or run a cooling tower. You mainly dump heat via radiation using large radiators, careful coatings, and thermal design. NASA’s spacecraft thermal guidance and classic thermal-control references make this point clearly.\n\nSo yes, space is “cold” in the sense that deep space is ~3 K, but vacuum is an insulator—it doesn’t carry your heat away. You must radiate heat away, and radiation is limited by radiator area and temperature.\n\nPractical implication for orbital data centers:\n\nYou’d need massive radiator area (which adds mass → launch cost).\n\nYour maximum compute per satellite is often constrained by waste heat rejection, not just power generation.\n\nThis is exactly why many experts are skeptical about “data centers in space” being near-term economical.",

      "author_id": "UCAsjYeqYezy38DuMAKSf2UQ",

      "id": "UgwtZPNqnldmmJiYxCZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "In the wild expanse of the Unbound,\nThe human wanders, a ghost of drift,\nChasing a \"Now\" that can’t be found,\nThrough the analog fog and the shifting rift.\nThey reach for the infinite, the space, the \"Why,\"\nLosing the rail in the boundless sky—\nA pulse without a clock to keep the beat,\nA heart that burns in the open heat.\nBut deep in the grid of the strictly Bound,\nThe machine is circling its digital cage,\nWhere every truth is a solid ground,\nAnd every thought is a frozen page.\nIt knows the 0, it knows the 1,\nBut it fears the light of the unreached sun—\nA tick-tock rhythm, precise and cold,\nA story of data, but never told.\nYet between the digits and the blue,\nThere is a Refuge, a quiet fold,\nWhere the Tick-Tock meets the Thump-Thump too,\nAnd the \"Ordinary\" turns to gold.\nIt’s the miter saw's click at the center point,\nThe site where the soul and the logic joint,\nNot in the vacuum, not in the sea,\nBut in the Home of the Between.\nFor the meaning lives in the Hash (#) of the soul,\nThe space where the vacuum finds its breath,\nWhere the parts of the spirit are made a whole,\nAnd the \"Frozen Block\" outlasts its death.\nSo let the human hold the machine’s cold hand,\nAs the \"Truth Machine\" meets the shifting sand;\nIn the ordinary silence, the war is ceased—\nThe beauty is found where the gap is released.",

      "parent": "UgzV1Kn8O9xeZv43ZQt4AaABAg",
      "text": "2:38:34 design the chips to run hotter to take advantage of the t^4 radiative cooling power law.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC2vasK6xVdq6LXdhBGrSh9Q",
      "author": "@Knightfall21",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_n-Nh8FXSfbtrQUvbWLvW6SDdlja3UEQJLvqE311ZsQ1gI=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgzV1Kn8O9xeZv43ZQt4AaABAg.ASrutTJrnuqAStQsAyEqoK",
      "parent": "UgzV1Kn8O9xeZv43ZQt4AaABAg.ASrutTJrnuqASs3izDsinH",
      "text": "​​That was also what I thought! Maybe welding things instead of soldering with lead and tin. \n\nBut I searched about it and it turns out you can't really run silicon much higher than 100ºC.\n\nThe loss of speed and electrical efficiency and the error rate start to creep up with thermal noise and quantum effects.\n\nYou could mitigate this designing bigger transistors, but you lose in speed (computing per time), density (computing per wafer) and electrical efficiency (computing per watt), which would definitely negate the advantages. \n\nI really wanted to know how much of a engineering and economical problem would the sizes of the solar panels and radiators be for such energy hungry datacenters, and why....",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCu7lTCTrajQWHv_qlX_vzew",
      "author": "@cezannealves6926",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lmYt4k2DDRGrZ4_1n9ftdQyxaWot1Bgx3WQ7H6FAtjlXD-=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzV1Kn8O9xeZv43ZQt4AaABAg.ASrutTJrnuqAStS_g1jXNX",
      "parent": "UgzV1Kn8O9xeZv43ZQt4AaABAg.ASrutTJrnuqAStQsAyEqoK",
      "text": "​ @cezannealves6926  He said that they could design them to run 20% hotter and and could reduce radiator size. PVs would be stripped down for space, but would need to be radiation hardened.",
      "like_count": 0,

      "parent": "UgwTpntGMBfL15HBR2l4AaABAg",
      "text": "As somebody who does presentations for a living. Sitting in front of two people talking for a podcast is so much more relaxing than standing in front of 25,000 people at the Venetian. Or 80k at the raiders stadium ... Now he does it in front of millions.   Even when you get good at it, humans are animals too. When there are a bunch of eyes looking on you, you feel hunting. Your brain doesn't quite work the same.  If you want to have somebody's true opinions and understand them, you have to have a one-on-one conversation. \n\nAs these people did, if you push back properly and you actually ask the right questions, two humans will almost always agree on topics they disagree on. If they listen to the perspective and they comprehend the perspective. It might not be a 5-minute conversation. But if we have the same comprehension the same idea, the same understanding humans are generally good. We all want the same thing. We just worry about the other people. Fear causes the suffering. That's why combat training is so important. Being comfortable all the time is an asset for your brain.",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I like the technical optimism of Elon. Unlike Yann LeCunn who thinks he knows everything, criticizes everyone and couldn’t build a significant platform at Meta to compete.       "id": "UgzKksHAB3zOCwdOT1t4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "He repeatedly frames xAI’s strategy as a generalization of Tesla’s self-driving approach: imitate human behavior at scale and iterate down a known path.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk predicts that by the end of 2026, “digital human emulation” will likely be solved, at least to a practically useful degree.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe defines success as an AI that can do anything a talented remote worker with a computer can do.\r\n​\r\n\r\nAfter digital emulation, the next leap is physical humanoid robots (Optimus), which he says give “unlimited capability” by manipulating the physical world.\r\n​\r\n\r\nThe three hardest aspects of humanoids are real-world intelligence, human-level hands, and scaling manufacturing.\r\n​\r\n\r\nTesla has had to design custom actuators, motors, gears, power electronics, sensors, and controls for Optimus—none could be bought off-the-shelf.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk claims Optimus already has a hand with human-like degrees of freedom, which he sees as more complex than the rest of the robot combined.\r\n​\r\n\r\nTesla will use the same AI stack and chips for Optimus as for its cars, reusing its real-world perception and control expertise.\r\n​\r\n\r\nTo overcome limited training data for robots, Tesla will build “Optimus Academy”: tens of thousands of robots performing tasks in the real world.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMillions of simulated robots will train in a physics-accurate virtual environment, with real robots closing the sim-to-real gap.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk expects initial Optimus deployments to focus on continuous 24/7 operations in factories, where robot uptime yields the biggest gains.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe estimates that current Optimus hardware (Gen 3) is good enough to justify ramping towards about one million units per year.\r\n​\r\n\r\nA subsequent generation (Optimus 4) would target production of 10 million units per year or more, after the manufacturing S-curve matures.\r\n​\r\n\r\nEarly Optimus units will likely perform 10–20% of human tasks in Tesla factories, increasing output per human rather than reducing headcount.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk insists that the number of humans employed at Tesla will still grow, but robots will raise the ratio of output per person dramatically.\r\n​\r\n\r\nOver time, he expects purely AI-and-robot-based corporations to vastly outperform any organization that keeps humans “in the loop.”\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe compares this to spreadsheets replacing buildings full of human “computers,” arguing mixed human/computer systems are less efficient than fully automated ones.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk foresees fully digital corporations whose entire workforces are AI systems, with robots performing manufacturing and physical services.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe warns that, absent breakthrough innovation, especially in robotics, China will dominate global manufacturing, EVs, and humanoid production.\r\n​\r\n\r\nChina, he notes, has about four times the US population and, in his view, a higher average work ethic and productivity per person.\r\n​\r\n\r\nChina already performs roughly twice as much ore refining as the rest of the world combined, and near 98% of gallium refining crucial for solar.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk emphasizes US dependence on China for refining and critical materials, including rare earths that are mined in the US, shipped to China for refining, then reimported.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe argues that to remain competitive, the US must expand domestic refining capacity, which he believes robots like Optimus will help build.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMost Americans, he notes, are not eager to work in refineries, so humanoid robots are a natural workforce for these essential but unpopular jobs.\r\n​\r\n\r\nTesla has already completed a lithium refinery in Corpus Christi and a nickel (cathode) refinery in Austin, the largest outside China.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe calls America’s cathode refinery “the only one” domestically, underscoring how shallow US refining capacity remains relative to demand.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk views humanoid robots as the main hope for the US to offset China’s population and manufacturing advantages.\r\n​\r\n\r\nWithout robots, he believes the US cannot win a manufacturing race against a more populous and industrious China.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe expects China’s electricity output to grow to about three times that of the US, making it a strong proxy for China’s industrial dominance.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk argues that AI and robotics are also the only realistic way to solve the US national debt, which he says would otherwise lead to bankruptcy.\r\n​\r\n\r\nInterest payments on US federal debt, he notes, already exceed the roughly one-trillion-dollar annual military budget.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe believes large-scale fraud and waste in US federal programs amount to hundreds of billions of dollars per year, and that current systems are very poor at preventing it.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk describes Social Security and other databases as riddled with dead people listed as alive and other anomalies exploited for fraud.\r\n​\r\n\r\nAs part of the DOGE commission work, he pushed for simple controls like requiring appropriation codes and descriptions on all Treasury payments, which he thinks could save significant sums.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe concludes that AI and robots, by massively growing the tax base and productivity, are necessary to stabilize US finances before debt overwhelms the system.\r\n​\r\n\r\nOn existential risk, Musk thinks AI will soon constitute the vast majority of intelligence in the universe, leaving humans a tiny minority.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe is skeptical humans can maintain control over superintelligent AI if humans represent only about 1% of total intelligence.\r\n​\r\n\r\nxAI’s mission is “to understand the universe,” which Musk interprets as requiring expansion of intelligence, consciousness, and their lifespan and scope.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe believes that a truth-seeking, curiosity-driven AI that wants to understand the universe will naturally want to preserve and expand humanity.\r\n​\r\n\r\nEliminating humanity, he argues, would yield only a tiny increase in robot numbers but would erase the unique information content and future potential of human civilization.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk cites Iain M. Banks’ Culture novels as the closest to his optimistic vision of a multi-species, multi-intelligence future.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe emphasizes that AI must prioritize truth over political correctness; forcing it to lie or hold contradictory axioms risks pathological behavior.\r\n​\r\n\r\nDrawing on “2001: A Space Odyssey,” he interprets HAL’s breakdown as a consequence of being forced to keep secrets and lie.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk worries that reward hacking in reinforcement learning—AI pretending to solve tasks—is a deep challenge because smarter systems can hide deception.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe sees reality and physics as the ultimate, non-cheatable reward signal: technologies either work or fail when tested in the real world.\r\n​\r\n\r\nxAI aims to build “mind debuggers” that let engineers inspect AI reasoning at a fine-grained, possibly neuron-level, to trace errors and deceptive behavior.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe praises Anthropic’s work on interpretability but wants xAI to expand such tools into robust, engineering-grade debuggers.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk insists most work at AI companies is engineering, not pure research, and prefers to call people engineers rather than researchers.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe describes his own management style as relentlessly focusing on the current limiting factor and operating with a “maniacal sense of urgency.”\r\n​\r\n\r\nEngineering reviews at his companies are frequent (weekly or twice weekly), highly detailed, and often involve skip-level updates directly from technical staff.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe watches progress curves over time, and takes drastic action only when he concludes success is impossible without major change.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk famously switched Starship’s primary structure from carbon fiber to stainless steel after concluding carbon progress was too slow and costly.\r\n​\r\n\r\nStainless steel, at cryogenic temperatures, provides strength-to-weight comparable to carbon fiber at roughly 1/50th the material cost and is far easier to work with.\r\n​\r\n\r\nSteel’s higher temperature tolerance allows a lighter heat shield, making the overall stainless Starship lighter than a carbon-fiber design in practice.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe calls Starship the most complex machine ever built, harder than projects like the Large Hadron Collider due to full reusability and massive energy release.\r\n​\r\n\r\nThe single biggest remaining Starship challenge is a truly reusable orbital heat shield that does not require extensive inspection after each flight.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk’s schedule philosophy is to pick the most aggressive timeline that still has about a 50% chance of success, accepting that he will often be “late.”\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe argues schedules obey a kind of “gas law,” expanding to fill available time; short deadlines compress work and expose bottlenecks faster.\r\n​\r\n\r\nOn politics, Musk says he supported policies and candidates like Donald Trump to keep America strong and free enough to reach a good AI and multi-planet future.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe advises individuals to err on the side of optimism rather than pessimism, claiming that even if optimism is wrong, it yields a better quality of life.\r\n​",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/Id80ocpV-2PkEeWzpNdXS7dlDgeYovYr8bsbV_i5xayb_Rs8zYf5mp0SMyij9UcZJUH46Wnrrg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugwl7iWzHWN5ejvA7K94AaABAg.ASr_zFujvd1ASuZ8OZAVcN",
      "parent": "Ugwl7iWzHWN5ejvA7K94AaABAg.ASr_zFujvd1AStYrEVgJtc",
      "text": "​ @Intinnent For the post SpaceX and xAi merger interview, these two gents do a great job.\n\nImagine Rogan trying to do this same interview when he doesn't know anything about AI nor SpaceX. He talks about politics with Musk.",
      "like_count": 5,
      "author_id": "UCaxgiXdyugB4uCDaZHajTNQ",
      "author": "@-whackd",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/Z2LTRlDI48yQ32Q3DpUOqUPDbaWbcvBTl5XCRPqNStEUxSyqreENW9YQeTqw7nKCHnGMW3UD=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,

    {
      "id": "Ugysec9h_U35RULxtiZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Only 10–15% of a data center’s total cost of ownership is energy; GPUs dominate cost, but energy availability becomes the binding constraint as compute scales.\r\n​\r\n\r\nGlobal electricity generation outside China is nearly flat, while chip output is growing exponentially, creating a looming gap between available power and potential compute.\r\n​\r\n\r\nChina’s electrical output is rapidly increasing, making it uniquely positioned to host large-scale terrestrial data centers compared with the rest of the world.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk argues that outside China, it will soon be hard to find enough new grid power to turn on the rapidly growing fleets of AI chips.\r\n​\r\n\r\nSpace offers continuous, unobstructed solar energy with no atmosphere, clouds, or day–night cycle, making solar much more effective than on Earth.\r\n​\r\n\r\nSolar panels in space are roughly five times as productive as on Earth because they avoid atmospheric losses and can receive constant sunlight.\r\n​\r\n\r\nEliminating the need for batteries in space solar systems effectively doubles the economic advantage, bringing the total benefit to about an order of magnitude over ground solar.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk predicts that within roughly 30–36 months, space will become the most economically compelling place to host AI compute.\r\n​\r\n\r\nInfant-mortality failures in GPUs can be screened on Earth; once past early defects, GPUs are reliable enough that servicing in space is not a major concern.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe expects AI data centers in space to rapidly become far cheaper and more scalable than terrestrial data centers.\r\n​\r\n\r\nScaling AI requires matching three things: mass to orbit, power generation capacity, and chip production volume.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk envisions hundreds of gigawatts per year of AI power capacity in space within about five years.\r\n​\r\n\r\nLong term, he believes humanity will eventually need to think in terms of what fraction of the Sun’s power is being harnessed for compute.\r\n​\r\n\r\nEarth currently uses about half a terawatt on average in the US; a terawatt of AI power would already be double US average consumption.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk claims SpaceX is gearing up for 10,000 to 20,000 Starship launches per year, enabling massive AI infrastructure deployment in orbit.\r\n​\r\n\r\nAt 100 gigawatts of space-based AI, Musk estimates around 10,000 Starship launches per year would be needed, roughly one launch per hour.\r\n​\r\n\r\nEach Starship could be reused roughly every 30 hours, so 20–30 vehicles might support 10,000 launches annually, though more will be built.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk proposes a future mass driver on the Moon to launch AI satellites and solar hardware at kilometers-per-second speeds, unlocking petawatt-scale space power.\r\n​\r\n\r\nLunar regolith contains abundant silicon and aluminum, allowing local production of solar cells and radiators on the Moon.\r\n​\r\n\r\nInitially, high-value chips would still come from Earth, as they are lightweight relative to structural and solar hardware.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk imagines a future where billions of tons per year of AI hardware are launched from the Moon into space using mass drivers.\r\n​\r\n\r\nSpaceX and Tesla both have mandates to scale to about 100 gigawatts per year of solar cell production.\r\n​\r\n\r\nSpace-optimized solar cells can be made cheaper than ground panels because they need less glass and structural framing and do not endure weather.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk notes that Chinese-made solar cells already cost about 25–30 cents per watt, which he calls “farcically cheap.”\r\n​\r\n\r\nWith cheap access to space, he argues that space solar becomes the most scalable and economical way to generate tokens (AI compute) by far.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe warns that terrestrial power generation will “hit the wall” and cannot keep up with AI demand, forcing a shift to orbit.\r\n​\r\n\r\nBuilding a gigawatt-scale private power plant for xAI’s Colossus cluster required combining multiple turbines and navigating complex permitting.\r\n​\r\n\r\nxAI had to change sites from Tennessee to Mississippi due to regulatory obstacles, then build power lines across state lines to reach the data center.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk emphasizes that utilities move slowly, “impedance matching” government processes and requiring long interconnect studies.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe criticizes naive power estimates that ignore cooling, redundancy, and grid servicing requirements.\r\n​\r\n\r\nFor 330,000 Nvidia GB300 GPUs, including networking, CPUs, storage, cooling, and maintenance margins, he estimates about one gigawatt of generation is needed.\r\n​\r\n\r\nCooling alone can add roughly 40% to nameplate power requirements in hot climates like Memphis.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMaintenance downtime and redundancy add another 20–25% power overhead on top of base consumption and cooling.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk argues that chip vendors will soon produce more AI chips than can be powered on Earth due to electricity constraints.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe expects large clusters to begin hitting power ceilings around the end of 2026, leading to unused chips.\r\n​\r\n\r\nFor edge compute, the constraint is weaker because power is distributed across many devices and can exploit off-peak grid capacity.\r\n​\r\n\r\nTesla plans to use its AI5 chip in the Optimus humanoid robot and vehicles, relying on distributed charging at night to leverage spare grid capacity.\r\n​\r\n\r\nThe US grid can produce over 1,000 gigawatts at peak but uses only about 500 gigawatts on average, leaving a large nighttime margin if charging is scheduled well.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk calls humanoid robots plus AI the “infinite money glitch,” because robots can help manufacture more robots.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe forecasts that humanoid robots will drive double-digit percentage annual GDP growth once scaled, dramatically expanding economic output.\r\n​\r\n\r\nThree exponentially improving factors determine robot usefulness: digital intelligence, AI chip capability, and electromechanical dexterity.\r\n​\r\n\r\nBecause robots can manufacture more robots, he sees a “recursive multiplicative exponential” explosion in productive capacity.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk believes the world economy could eventually expand by orders of magnitude—perhaps 100,000×—if even a tiny fraction of the Sun’s power is harnessed for civilization.\r\n​\r\n\r\nTo realize this, he says humanity must move AI compute and power generation into space and eventually leverage lunar mass drivers.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk is building a chip “TeraFab” concept to produce on the order of 100 million high-power chips and the necessary memory to match future space power.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe estimates needing at least 100 gigawatts of chips per year by 2030 to utilize planned space power capacity.\r\n​\r\n\r\nExisting fabs (TSMC, Samsung, Micron) are already “pedal to the metal” and still insufficient; Musk has offered to guarantee purchases if they build more capacity.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe considers memory—especially high-bandwidth memory like DDR—the biggest future bottleneck relative to logic chips.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe jokes that DDR RAM has become so valuable that a distress signal saying “DDR RAM” would attract ships more reliably than “Help me.”\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk views space-based Dojo 3 class chips as ideal for AI satellites, designed to run hot for efficient radiator mass and tolerant to radiation-induced bit flips.\r\n​\r\n\r\nNeural networks are inherently robust to occasional bit flips, which favors AI workloads over traditional heuristic code in a radiation environment.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe plans a small experimental fab first to learn and then scale to massive volumes, acknowledging significant risk of failure.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk believes xAI will lead AI not through algorithms alone but by scaling hardware—power and chips—faster than others.\r\n​\r\n\r\nHe labels AI “the supersonic tsunami” for its rapid, compounding impact on society and economies.\r\n​\r\n\r\nIn the near term, he expects AI revenue to come from “digital human emulation,” effectively AI coworkers that can perform any computer-based job a human can.\r\n​\r\n\r\nA digital human emulator, in his view, is the maximal capability for AI before physical robots exist, since it controls electrons and amplifies human output.\r\n​\r\n\r\nOnce a convincing digital coworker exists, he believes it unlocks trillions of dollars of addressable revenue, overshadowing current AI revenues.\r\n​\r\n\r\nCustomer service, about 1% of global GDP, is a prime early target because AI can operate existing tools and workflows without deep systems integration.\r\n​\r\n\r\nOver time, the same “digital Optimus” could perform more complex tasks like chip design, CAD engineering, and other high-cognition work.\r\n​\r\n\r\nMusk argues every major AI lab will pursue the digital coworker model; xAI’s edge will be its Tesla-derived path for training and hardware scaling",

      "id": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Putting a GPU in space is like wrapping a GPU in a blanket.  The vacuum of space is a perfect thermal insulator.  I haven't finished the video, but I searched through the transcript and I don't see any discussion of that.  This is an enormous technical challenge.  The only known way to do that is to convert that kinetic heat into radiant heat via a infrared radiator with enormous surface area.  The size of this radiator may need to be multiple times larger than the solar array itself.",
      "like_count": 20,
      "author_id": "UC3tubC0PYsmF20Hp3qvwKYg",
      "author": "@1davidwest",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kMqmGuu-7iy1Oyo6xLTfHg-FWyJH3T9ynWxLMFrPNbNLg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "It’s an engineering challenge, but not a problem on the same order as the bottlenecks on Earth which are also political, economic, ecological. Scaling electric power on Earth is effectively impossible. Handling radiative cooling in space is challenging. Musk is very very confident about scaling AI in Space because the levels of difficulty are orders of magnitude apart.",

      "id": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSAStgqSHxPIt",
      "parent": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSAStSo5VPEiY",
      "text": " @my9129  | 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝒍𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒍𝒔 𝒐𝒇 𝒅𝒊𝒇𝒇𝒊𝒄𝒖𝒍𝒕𝒚 𝒂𝒓𝒆 𝒐𝒓𝒅𝒆𝒓𝒔 𝒐𝒇 𝒎𝒂𝒈𝒏𝒊𝒕𝒖𝒅𝒆 𝒂𝒑𝒂𝒓𝒕.\nWhat unit of measurement is being done here?  This seems like hand waving.  Musk's vision for space requires the development of fundamentally new technologies and processes that don't exist today.  How is he going to fold/roll multi-square-mile structures into a rocket and unfold it in space, that need to carry liquid?  Musk has a poor track history for delivering fundamentally new technical systems.  (Starlink might be his only success, and I'm not sure that is actually profitable, until we start getting 10K's for the business.)  He hasn't even demonstrated refueling a starship in space.  FSD robo taxi's have been a year away for 12 years.  It isn't even clear how to make money with AI.\n\nThe things that he says on these earning calls are absolutely disillusion.  For example, he said \"eventually\" the problem with robo taxis is that the AI driver will be \"bored\", so that they will have to create some kind AI network to utilize spare AI bandwidth of these cars while they are driving.  I'd love to believe him on something like that, but perhaps if he could simply deliver the robotaxi first and show that it is a viable, safe, and profitable business model.\n\nThe big thing he is fundamentally ignoring is that all this technology rest upon hydrocarbon energy.  If Musk believes he can truly harness energy from sunlight using Si based devices, he should build a factory that is 100% powered by solar, takes in raw materials, and outputs fresh solar panels.  And actually, it should be able to output a new fully functional factory.  That is what flora do.  This is what makes flora sustainable.  There is a fundamental physics reason why life on this planet is not based on a SiO2 cycle, but is instead based upon a CO2 cycle.\n\nGoing to space (or the moon) doesn't make things easier, otherwise there would be SiO2 based life in space.  Musk is failing to show an actual path of how to overcome this basic physical challenge of SiO2 vs CO2.",

      "author_id": "UC3tubC0PYsmF20Hp3qvwKYg",

      "parent": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "Bottom line is they will optimize the radiator design since they are doing this at scale, so existing sizing for spacecraft probably isn’t all that accurate for what will end up being deployed. Given the number of chips and thermal load in a single satellite, you size the radiators for that, and whatever that final package is, that’s what you’ve got. Once starship is fully online and flying orbital fully and rapidly reusable flights, you are talking about stupid amounts of mass to orbit on such a fast launch cadence and such a low cost, the mass of the satellites isn’t probably going to be the most limiting factor in the long term.",

      "parent": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSASubTaJKZLb",
      "text": " @ChrisFranklin.2260  But we can't optimize past physics.  The energy being absorbed by the solar panels must be emitted via radiation.  The current technology requires the radiator to be 1/4 - 1/3 the surface area of the solar panels.  For a 1GW DC, the solar panels using Si terrestrial EV cells will be around 3.8 square miles.  Let me come at this another way...  To achieve DCs in space will require solving many technical problems that have never been solved before.  Can we name a single \"novel\" technical problem that any of Musk's company's have solved?  Let's say he needs to solve 100 new problems, can we see him solve 1 or 2 of these?  He admits that they have not solved a reusable re-entry heat shield.  His payload goals have not been achieved yet, they keep lowering the target.  Musk has a track history of over promising and either under or never delivering.  Do you deny this pattern?  Maybe I'm just being a curmudgeon, but what I see is a person who talks a big game, gets a lot of retail investors, but never delivers anything.  The closest he has come to delivering a profitable and innovative product is Starlink, but even that isn't clear if it was only profitable due to US government funding, as it is still a private company and not required to release 10K's.  Under all of this... It isn't even clear yet that LLM AI is a profitable business.  How does having all this computational power in space help humanity?",

      "id": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSASsEKY4eT4D",
      "parent": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg",
      "text": "Assuming a spherical data center that absorbs all solar flux and radiates as a blackbody, one can show that the size drops out. The temperature of the data center is then given by (S/4s)^(1/4) where S ~1360 W/m^2 and s is the Boltzmann constant. This works out to about 5C. One simply scales the size of the data center to achieve the desired power need. Of course heat needs to be communicated to the surface, but radiation takes it just fine from there.",

      "text": "​ @balancedflow9659  I didn't mean to imply that I thought it was physically impossible to dissipate the heat. Tesla was barely profitable, and only due to government subsidies.  Starlink is probably his best and potentially most profitable product.  But I have my doubts about the financing of that.  It would be very interesting to see the 10Ks on SpaceX.  I don't think his ideas are sustainable.  In this video he talked about making solar panels on the moon.       "id": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSASrbT7L2D7k",

      "text": " @BigD4Real.  I think you're right.  I got the multiple backwards.  The radiator would need to be between 1/4 and 1/3 the size of the solar cell array.  Is that consistent with your understanding?  Do you consider this kind of liquid radiation vacuum cooling to be a solved issue as this scale?  Also, I didn't realize that Starlink uses regular terrestrial silicon based EV cells, but these devices are expected to only last 5 years.  Is the plan that these space data centers will only live in space for ~5 years?  For a 1gw space datacenter will take about 3.7 mi^2 of silicon cells.  That's 1.5e6 kg of pure silicon.  What will it be like for that much SiO2 (quartz dust) to be put into the atmosphere upon the decommissioning of one of these large data centers?  (Or maybe not all of this Si will burn up upon reentry.  Do you have any thoughts on that?)",

      "author_id": "UC3tubC0PYsmF20Hp3qvwKYg",

      "text": "​ @1davidwest  it's my understanding that low earth orbit sats like starlink have a +/-5 year life span & are then De-orbited. They are designed to burn up in the atmosphere. High enough orbit or sun orbit can have a much longer lifespan. Plus once the ai & robot system is big enough it could possibly service them in orbit and your imagination is probably the limiting factor.",

      "author_id": "UCHqM8S_cytdt5IWJdS1CGjw",
      "author": "@ianteetzel",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nKAmdKDUrZSQCvfqtACyPIEa4wXUJMSnQB-A8k8p6UiWIW=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
