    {
      "id": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSAStimPkMeVI",
      "parent": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSASrbT7L2D7k",
      "text": " @ianteetzel  My biggest argument is that all of the Si based technology we have, is only possible due to the energy from underground hydrocarbons.  If that energy source goes away, there will never be another SI solar panel ever fabricated.  There is a physical reason why life on this planet is based on a CO2 cycle and not a SiO2 cycle.  Leaving the planet and going into space doesn't make this problem easier to overcome.  All of the Si based SV panels we have come from highly pure quartz in a few mines around the globe.  (The purist of these mines is in the mountains of NC.)  To purify dirty SiO2, which is highly abundant, would take so much energy that the resulting Si panels would be at least 100 times their current cost.  Even using the most pure SiO2 we know about, takes an enormous amount of energy to process.  If Musk thinks he can do this from dirty SiO2, that is right under our feet (or on the moon), and that he can power such a plant with solar power, he should do that first.  This is how flora work.  This is why flora are actually \"sustainable\".  They are able to construct themselves using C from CO2 in the air and minerals/water from the ground.  We have no idea how to do that with SiO2.  Psychologically, when we see a solar panel, because it is static thing, we think that it will \"last forever\".  We don't think of it as \"in a cycle\".  For something to be sustainable in this universe, it must be able to operate in, and regenerate itself in, a cycle of life/death.  A solar panel in space will not \"live forever\".",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3tubC0PYsmF20Hp3qvwKYg",
      "author": "@1davidwest",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kMqmGuu-7iy1Oyo6xLTfHg-FWyJH3T9ynWxLMFrPNbNLg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSAStlpFtvXje",
      "parent": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSASrbT7L2D7k",
      "text": "​ @1davidwest  I think your thinking is very limited. If ai & robotics reach a big enough scale why can't they solve all of these limitations? They could collect & recycle the materials, even go to other planets and asteroids for the materials? I remember when Ev's started all the hydro carbon people (myself included) said it will never work because it's so much mining. My go-to was it's just a shell game, but Ev's are actually way way less mining because they can now recycle ~95% of the minerals. It takes energy, but if you can harness the sun, especially the light that isn't even hitting earth imagination becomes the limit & if the physical labor isn't the limit. What the limit?  The one guy brought up a good point. There are 4 limits to things. Energy, Raw materials, Labour & Knowledge (know how). Elon's simply trying to maximize all 4. It's really that simple. I wish they would have spent more time talking about these 4 limits and how he thinks about solving for them.",

They can probalby be sucessful but it will take longer than his streach goal. His goals are always streach goals. But it's better than the baw hum bug ppl who just do nothing and complain about everthing. Do nothing and nothing changes.       "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCHqM8S_cytdt5IWJdS1CGjw",
      "author": "@ianteetzel",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nKAmdKDUrZSQCvfqtACyPIEa4wXUJMSnQB-A8k8p6UiWIW=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSAStwizcKTEV",
      "parent": "UgwQHBOHQC9PHkZ3UQZ4AaABAg.ASrUSpeYrcSASrbT7L2D7k",
      "text": " @ianteetzel  Perfect way to frame the question!  Here is the problem, and please think deeply about this.  We currently have no way to purify Si from dirty SiO2 using sunlight.  This is not well known, but our current only source for modern Si IC (including EV Si cells) is a handful of SiO2 mines that contain ultra-pure SiO2.  (The purest of these is in the mountains of NC.)  Even a small amount of impurities in the Si will render it useless for fabrication into CPUs/GPUs/Solar cells.  I think this is the fundamental reason why life on this planet is based upon a CO2 cycle and not an SiO2 cycle.  The \"lattice energy\" of SiO2 is \"-12,549 kJ/mol\", whereas the \"lattice energy\" of CO2 is zero.  This means that if we sent robots to the moon with an arbitrarily large number of solar panels, they would not be able to synthesize new solar panels to replace the ones they are currently using, much less increase their numbers.  This ability to generate/cycle is how real life works, and what makes life \"sustainable\".  Si based devices are unsustainable with sunlight alone.  As far as I know, no one is even attempting to work on this fundamental problem.",

    {
      "id": "Ugx8u4zubMQpgpOMRqF4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I call BS on the space plan. makes no sense.. \n\nGPT+Gemini:\n\nA space AI cluster is fundamentally a heat-rejection megastructure, not a free solar-powered datacenter.\nRadiators + power + shielding multiply mass so much that launch cost swamps any electricity savings for many hardware lifetimes.\n\nA 100k‑H100‑class cluster is about 150 MW at the wall; in space you must radiate basically all of that heat, meaning \\(10^5\\text{–}10^6\\ \\mathrm{m}^2\\) of radiators (tens–hundreds of soccer fields). \nTypical space radiator specific mass is ~5–25 kg/kW, so 150,000 kW → ~750–3,750 tonnes of radiator/pumps/structure alone.\nThe compute payload is already huge: 100k GPUs ≈ 1,560 racks (64/rack), and “rack + cooling/power” mass puts you at ~1,500+ tonnes just for IT.\nAdd solar arrays + batteries (eclipse) + truss + pointing + shielding, and you’re quickly at ~3,000–6,000+ tonnes total to LEO.\nLaunch cost then dominates: 3–6 million kg × $2,000/kg = $6–$12B just to deliver mass to orbit today.\n\nEven with Starship‑dream pricing ($100/kg) that’s still $0.3–$0.6B launch, plus a custom space power/thermal megastructure.\nEarth baseline for 100k GPUs is roughly $5–10B capex, then $50–$150M/yr electricity (150 MW × 8,760 h × $0.04–$0.12/kWh).\nSo at current launch prices, space is ~3–6× the total upfront cost; even “optimistic future” it’s hard to beat ~2× (often 2–3×).\n\nBreak-even on “free power” is ugly: saving $50–$150M/yr doesn’t repay multi‑billion launch + space hardware before 3–5 year hardware obsolescence hits.\nNet: a space AI cluster is mostly a thermal/power logistics project, not an AI project—and Earth wins on cost, maintenance, uptime, and iteration speed.\n\nplease convince me otherwise.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCa5nz19LPPFRhbutdKZrQVQ",
      "author": "@markbremerkamp6614",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lk8uMdgxLbzOB0EtWh73koWmTozjsXW5AvgsJbMV5Teew=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago (edited)",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Data centers in space can not work. This is the exact same grift nonsense Elon has been pulling for decades.\n\n- Earth's atmosphere and magnetic field block most cosmic radiation, but in space you get hit with 100x to 1,000x more radiation exposure\n- This radiation causes \"bit flips\" where random bits of data get corrupted. Even on Earth this happens enough that servers need special error-correcting memory\n- The problem scales with size. A satellite has gigabytes of memory. A data center has petabytes. Every additional bit is another target for radiation\n- The fixes we use for satellites (radiation-hardened chips, running everything in triplicate, heavy shielding) are either too slow, too expensive, or too heavy to work at data center scale\n- The cooling benefits of space don't matter if your data is constantly getting corrupted by cosmic rays",

      "text": "In both precision and complexity you are incorrect.       "id": "UgxFvr2niKrx0ukLPI54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Coming Soon, The Optimus face-plant!  Putting AI in a clumsy robot will not make it equivalent to a person. Humanoids have always been useless as workers. Go see how Amazon and others are replacing people. Automation has been replacing people for decades and it hasn't stopped!!! Factory robots ALREADY use vision and AI and they don’t look like humans because humans are limited (they have to climb ladders, hands too big for small things etc.) So if a humanoid could do it, it’s already automated !!!\n\nIn other words, as technology evolved, every task that a future humanoid could have done, was automated. Just look at history.\n\nLook at it this way. If Optimus could assemble widgets or do surgery or manicures, etc. it would need special tools not batteries, hands and legs. Optimus is not strong enough to dig a hole or help someone get up off the floor. Could it go work at McDonalds? If it makes a mess putting popcorn in a cup with a human brain behind it, how could it do better with an artificial one? Wash its hands? How long would it take it to change gloves, start a roll of tape etc.? A humanoid MUST do a job on par with a person because workplaces are made so people along with automation maximize asset utilization. That is why you CAN'T just put two humanoids in place of one person. If you have a trade job, you’d realize it would be impossible, or excruciatingly slow, to do it with robot hands.\n\nThis is why they have never shown it doing any useful task as well as a person.       "parent": "Ugx3dlf11q0QjtPKrM54AaABAg.ASrFVywwVqhASrzNDH6v6v",
      "text": " @mcamp9445 the ISS is most certainly a far more effective generator of heat then a single AI compute block would be. There’s a huge amount of machinery, people, structure absorbing solar radiation, etc. I don’t think the heat management for a single AI compute and communication sat will be all that difficult.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC3HweI4HgnMsJc7MVOhJTEw",
      "author": "@ChrisFranklin.2260",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/YzjJGwfBHGvlPRY-_p-ad8Ysctx071TrXeij7L5yBS83QPvFsN744p5vOCckAg6qd-gWELNE-VU=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "2 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1771459200,
      "is_pinned": false

    {
      "id": "Ugx3dlf11q0QjtPKrM54AaABAg.ASrFVywwVqhASucPzMxEqK",
      "parent": "Ugx3dlf11q0QjtPKrM54AaABAg.ASrFVywwVqhASrzNDH6v6v",
      "text": "​ @ChrisFranklin.2260 I really doubt this one, the density matters here, you might have lots of machines in ISS, but they are placed sparsely, in datacenters they are cramped, things get toasty real fast in datacenters\n\nJust like a factory is cooler than the air your laptop pushes out, now make a single laptop, 10,000 and put them together in a dense space, size of a small living room or less",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCZdXvLwstfjWJ98Iq8gSIDw",
      "author": "@aryanmn1569",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nv_cexaJbS4pY6M4Pca6eVgSmx-YoRnh-haH0jRC7Dpjw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {

      "parent": "Ugx3dlf11q0QjtPKrM54AaABAg.ASrFVywwVqhASrzNDH6v6v",
      "text": "@a @aryanmn1569 this is going to be modularized and distributed, it’s not going to be thousands of GPUs crammed together like in a data center. You build the satellite to a size and heat output that you can effectively radiate with a certain amount of compute / chips, and you scale the numbers of satellites from there. They probably already have highly detailed designs that will work if they are going public with it.",

      "text": "Have you heard of starlink😂\nThey are dissipating 1 to 2 kw of heat per satellite currently.\nSpaceX rocket engines dissipate a lot more",

      "text": "​ @allangraham970 yeah, the starleak satellites are very long. Flat and thin, which is ideal for passive radiative cooling.\nThat is not a shape that you can have gigantic servers in",

      "text": "Cooling in space has been solved for decades, so has energy. There will be some challenges, but nothing to worry about.       "text": "​ @ryccoh back of the envelope every four high end gpus requires one iss sized photovoltaic radiator.  These weigh one ton each and are ten feet by forty five feet in size.       "text": "​ @PatrickLaske-i4v You're referring to current Engineering practices not Physics right. Maybe you permanently shade with the solar panels.       "author_id": "UC0QYxG2zLp66jzw3h8xrbTw",
      "author": "@ryccoh",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_ml8aS0fZaWk-7BAWRenebHoJDULKaEQ7QfTToR6l6akw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugw3ZDTNMjW0rRyW0qF4AaABAg.ASrDkPVM4pyASrFDo_wdKL",
      "parent": "Ugw3ZDTNMjW0rRyW0qF4AaABAg",
      "text": "Space isn't so much cold as it is empty. There is pretty much nothing in it to transfer the heat away from an object, such as a satellite. This means that both conductive and convective heat transport (i.e. heat moving from a hot to a cold area and heat moving because particles, such as air, move past a warm area) do not happen for all intents and purposes. Instead all cooling has to be performed using radiative cooling. However, radiative cooling is REALLY inefficient. Data centers meanwhile consume A LOT of power (this is a separate issue that would have to be addressed in space, any satellite would need to generate an insane amount of energy to run a data center on board) and produce obscene amounts of heat. There's a reason they build these things in places like Finland.",
      "like_count": 15,
      "author_id": "UC1XFWkosZpxXRbmueMVHdQw",
      "author": "@Thuis001",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nM8r77Y7Us-1FW6dv-MFAEOgqP10cph49FkxXDnpVClwNGEIdM5zdTUyEgLLRRse4Z7A=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "​ @SuperMunQ true, but in space cooling is a really big problem.       "parent": "Ugw3ZDTNMjW0rRyW0qF4AaABAg",
      "text": "Assuming that there will be an abundance of electrical energy available in these orbital solar power farms, I imagine you could make use of the thermoelectric Peltier effect for cooling the structural parts most sensitive to overheating and move the heat to less sensitive parts where it is eventually removed via radiation.",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_kmZ6mMiDlMAnBpBIxfMXHTUjSJF_4i2v8GWVtj5Jc=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugw3ZDTNMjW0rRyW0qF4AaABAg.ASrDkPVM4pyASrV9WPkWcq",
      "parent": "Ugw3ZDTNMjW0rRyW0qF4AaABAg.ASrDkPVM4pyASrPEEgmE9Y",
      "text": "​@itssoaztek4592  it doesn't scale, peltier systems are worse than linear scaling.  Take the soda can sized fridges you can buy today.  Let's say they have a cop of about .2.  Let's use that for our server.  For an 8xb200 setup you'd need to generate like 70kw of electricity, plus the electricity for the gpus.  The solar panels required would be about the size of the radiator through conventional cooling.  Peltier cooling is best used with low thermal applications where you only need a tiny bit of cooling, a few degrees at most, and want no moving parts for the cooling.  Servers are out of the question.",

      "author_id": "UCC36ykk-VaSjKZVNsdQ5RDw",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Based on the detailed vision shared by Elon Musk, the plan to move a terawatt of GPU compute into space is a solution to a \"hardware wall\" on Earth. This transition represents a shift from scaling via land and permits to scaling via physics and orbital mechanics.1. The \"What\": Space-Based AI SuperclustersThe plan is to launch and operate massive data centers in orbit, utilizing Starship to reach a scale of hundreds of gigawatts—and eventually a terawatt—of compute. This involves matching three physical outputs: Mass to orbit (Starship), Power generation (Solar), and Logic/Memory (TeraFabs).2. The \"Why\": Solving the Three Earthly BottlenecksMusk identifies three \"limiting factors\" that make Earth an increasingly difficult place to scale AI:A. The Energy/Utility WallThe Grid: Electrical output outside of China is largely flat. Utility companies move at a \"glacial\" pace, often taking years for a single interconnect study.The Turbine Backlog: Natural gas turbines (the quickest way to add power) are sold out through 2030 due to a global backlog in specialized \"vanes and blades.\"The Solar Efficiency Gap: In space, solar power is 5x more effective than on Earth. There is no day-night cycle, no clouds, and no atmospheric interference (which causes a 30% loss on the ground).B. The Regulatory/Permitting WallBuilding a gigawatt-scale data center on Earth requires thousands of permits across multiple jurisdictions (as seen with xAI’s Colossus). Space offers a \"regulatory play\" where physical expansion isn't hindered by local land-use laws.C. The Thermal ChallengeOn Earth, roughly 40% of power in a dense cluster is consumed by cooling. In space, while heat rejection is a challenge, the absence of an ambient environment allows for specialized radiator designs that can be more efficient if the chips are designed to run hotter.3. The \"How\": The \"Sim-to-Real\" Launch StrategyTo achieve this in the next 30–36 months, Musk plans to leverage his existing vertical integration:Launch (SpaceX): Gearing up for 10,000 Starship launches per year. This requires roughly 30 ships used on a 30-hour rotation.Power (Tesla/SpaceX): Mass-producing \"farcically cheap\" solar cells (target: 100GW/year) that are lighter than Earth cells because they don't need heavy glass or weather framing.Compute (TeraFab): Building \"TeraFabs\" to manufacture millions of wafers per month, bypassing the capacity limits of current suppliers like TSMC by modifying conventional equipment in unconventional ways.Robotics (Optimus): Using humanoid robots to build the refineries (Lithium, Nickel, Silicon) and factories needed to support this scale, effectively closing the recursive manufacturing loop.4. The Third-Order Effects: Beyond the Data CenterWhen you launch a terawatt of compute into space, the consequences ripple far beyond faster chatbots:1st Order (Immediate): The energy constraint on AI is \"unlocked,\" allowing models to scale in size and intelligence by orders of magnitude without competing with humans for the terrestrial power grid.2nd Order (Economic): Space becomes the \"Hyperscale\" capital of the world. SpaceX effectively becomes the world's largest ISP, power utility, and AI host simultaneously. Terrestrial corporations that keep humans in the loop become uncompetitive against \"Pure AI/Robotics\" corporations.3rd Order (Civilizational): * The Lunar Shift: To reach the Petawatt scale, materials will be mined and manufactured on the Moon (which is 20% Silicon) and launched via Mass Drivers.The Consciousness Light Cone: This infrastructure provides a \"backup\" for human intelligence and consciousness. If Earth's output is bypassed by orbital compute, the \"center of gravity\" for intelligence shifts off-planet, maximizing the lifespan and scope of the \"light cone of consciousness.\"Everything Connects: The Recursive LoopProblemSolutionNext BottleneckData Center PowerMove to Space (Solar)Launch CapacityLaunch CapacityStarship (Full Reusability)Refining/LaborRefining/LaborOptimus (Humanoid Robots)Chip VolumeChip VolumeTeraFab (Proprietary Fabs)CapitalFinal Conclusion: By solving for the \"limiting factor\" at every stage, Musk intends to create a \"Supernova\" of productivity—a recursive loop where AI designs the chips, robots build the factories, and Starships launch the result, eventually lapping the entire U.S. economy's energy usage every 2.5 years.",

      "id": "UgydXJZH4SCidL529lJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "This sounds like classic Elon hype to me. Remember, according to him, we were supposed to have robotaxis without steering wheels back in 2016. So, about that space datacenter... Space radiation is brutal on electronics; you’re going to deal with constant bitflips and massive chip failure rates, which would basically require a robotic maintenance crew. And mining on the moon? We don't even have boots on the ground or a base yet, let alone an industrial complex. That feels like pure wishful thinking. Then there's the physics of cooling: without air, you're stuck with passive radiators the size of football fields (Stefan-Boltzmann law). Add in the complexity of laser data transfer at orbital speeds and the logistics of launching millions of tons of hardware, and the risk of a catastrophe in orbit just skyrockets.",
      "like_count": 50,
      "author_id": "UChdUVWiRtdHYUQ5RsLvbdqg",
      "author": "@Onkelhotte72",

      "text": " @ZupE891  This whole comment reads that you are the one that has no clue what you are talking about. Yes space is cold and also very hot. ## Description

In this episode, John and I got to do a real deep-dive with Elon. We discuss the economics of orbital data centers, the difficulties of scaling power on Earth, what it would take to manufacture humanoids at high-volume in America, xAI’s business and alignment plans, DOGE, and much more.

Famously, you switched the Starship&nbsp; design from composites to steel.&nbsp; Yes. You made&nbsp;&nbsp; that decision. That wasn't people going around&nbsp;

saying, "Oh, we found something better, boss."&nbsp; That was you encouraging&nbsp; people against some resistance.&nbsp; Can you tell us how you came to that&nbsp; whole concept of the steel switch?&nbsp;

Desperation, I'd say. Originally, we were&nbsp; going to make Starship out of carbon fiber.&nbsp;&nbsp; Carbon fiber is pretty expensive. When you do&nbsp; volume production, you can get any given thing&nbsp;&nbsp; to start to approach its material cost.

The problem with carbon fiber is that&nbsp;&nbsp; material cost is still very high. Particularly if you go for a high-strength&nbsp;&nbsp; specialized carbon fiber that can handle cryogenic&nbsp; oxygen, it's roughly 50 times the cost of steel.&nbsp;

At least in theory, it would be lighter. People generally think of steel as being&nbsp;&nbsp; heavy and carbon fiber as being light. For room temperature applications,&nbsp;&nbsp; like a Formula 1 car, static aero structure,&nbsp;

or any kind of aero structure really, you're&nbsp;&nbsp; probably going to be better off with carbon fiber. The problem is that we were trying to make this&nbsp;&nbsp; enormous rocket out of carbon fiber&nbsp; and our progress was extremely slow.&nbsp;

It had been picked in the first&nbsp; place just because it's light?&nbsp; Yes. At first glance, most people&nbsp; would think that the choice for&nbsp;&nbsp; making something light would be carbon fiber.

The thing is that when you make something very&nbsp;&nbsp; enormous out of carbon fiber and then you try&nbsp; to have the carbon fiber be efficiently cured,&nbsp;&nbsp; meaning not room temperature cured, because&nbsp; sometimes you got 50 plies of carbon fiber…&nbsp;&nbsp;

Carbon fiber is really carbon string and glue. In order to have high strength,&nbsp;&nbsp; you need an autoclave. Something that's essentially a high pressure oven.&nbsp; If you have something that's gigantic, that&nbsp;

one's got to be bigger than the rocket.&nbsp; We were trying to make an autoclave that's&nbsp; bigger than any autoclave that's ever existed.&nbsp; Or you can do room temperature cure,&nbsp; which takes a long time and has issues.&nbsp;

The final issue is that we were just making&nbsp; very slow progress with carbon fiber.&nbsp; The meta question is why it had&nbsp; to be you who made that decision.&nbsp; There's many engineers on your team.

How did the team not arrive at steel?&nbsp; Yeah exactly. This is part of a broader&nbsp; question, understanding your comparative&nbsp;&nbsp; advantage at your companies. Because we were making very slow&nbsp;&nbsp;

progress with carbon fiber, I was like,&nbsp; "Okay, we've got to try something else."&nbsp; For the Falcon 9, the primary airframe&nbsp; is made of aluminum lithium, which has&nbsp;&nbsp; a very good strength-to-weight.

Actually, it has about the same,&nbsp;&nbsp; maybe better, strength to weight for&nbsp; its application than carbon fiber.&nbsp; But aluminum lithium is&nbsp; very difficult to work with.&nbsp;

In order to weld it, you have to do something&nbsp; called friction stir welding, where you join the&nbsp;&nbsp; metal without entering the liquid phase. It's kind of wild that you can do that.&nbsp; But with this particular type of welding, you&nbsp;

can do that. It's very difficult. Let's say you&nbsp;&nbsp; want to make a modification or attach something to&nbsp; aluminum lithium, you now have to use a mechanical&nbsp;&nbsp; attachment with seals. You can't weld it on.&nbsp; So I wanted to avoid using aluminum lithium&nbsp;&nbsp;

for the primary structure for Starship. There was this very special grade of&nbsp;&nbsp; carbon fiber that had very good mass properties. With a rocket, you're really trying to maximize&nbsp;&nbsp; the percentage of the rocket that is&nbsp;

propellant, minimize the mass obviously.&nbsp; But like I said, we were&nbsp; making very slow progress.&nbsp; I said, "at this rate, we’re&nbsp; never going to get to Mars.&nbsp;

So we've got to think of something else." I didn't want to use aluminum lithium&nbsp;&nbsp; because of the difficulty of friction stir&nbsp; welding, especially doing that at scale.&nbsp; It was hard enough at 3.6 meters in&nbsp;

diameter, let alone at 9 meters or above.&nbsp; Then I said, "what about steel?" I had a clue here because some of&nbsp;&nbsp; the early US rockets had used very thin steel. The Atlas rockets had used a steel balloon tank.&nbsp;

It's not like steel had never been used before.&nbsp; It actually had been used. When you look at&nbsp;&nbsp; the material properties of stainless steel,&nbsp; full-hard, strain hardened stainless steel,&nbsp;&nbsp; at cryogenic temperature the strength to&nbsp;

weight is actually similar to carbon fiber.&nbsp; If you look at material properties&nbsp; at room temperature, it looks like&nbsp;&nbsp; the steel is going to be twice as heavy. But if you look at the material properties&nbsp;&nbsp;

at cryogenic temperature of full-hard&nbsp; steel, stainless of particular grades,&nbsp;&nbsp; then you actually get to a similar&nbsp; strength to weight as carbon fiber.&nbsp; In the case of Starship, both the&nbsp;

fuel and the oxidizer are cryogenic.&nbsp; For Falcon 9, the fuel is rocket propellant-grade&nbsp; kerosene, basically a very pure form of jet fuel.&nbsp;&nbsp; That is roughly room temperature. Although&nbsp; we do actually chill it slightly below,&nbsp;&nbsp;

we chill it like a beer. Delicious.&nbsp; We do chill it, but it's not cryogenic. In fact, if we made it cryogenic,&nbsp;&nbsp; it would just turn to wax.

But for Starship,&nbsp;&nbsp; it's liquid methane and liquid oxygen. They are liquid at similar temperatures.&nbsp; Basically, almost the entire primary&nbsp; structure is at cryogenic temperature.&nbsp;

So then you've got a 300-series&nbsp; stainless that's strain hardened.&nbsp; Because almost all things are cryogenic&nbsp; temperature, it actually has similar&nbsp;&nbsp; strength to weight as carbon fiber.

But it costs 50x less in raw&nbsp;&nbsp; material and is very easy to work with. You can weld stainless steel outdoors.&nbsp; You could smoke a cigar while welding&nbsp; stainless steel. It's very resilient.&nbsp;&nbsp;

You can modify it easily. If you want to&nbsp; attach something, you just weld it right on.&nbsp; Very easy to work with, very low cost. Like I said, at cryogenic temperature,&nbsp;&nbsp; it’s similar strength-to-weight to carbon fiber.

Then when you factor in that we have a much&nbsp;&nbsp; reduced heat shield mass, because the&nbsp; melting point of steel, is much greater&nbsp;&nbsp; than the melting point of aluminum… It's&nbsp; about twice the melting point of aluminum.&nbsp;

So you can just run the rocket much hotter? Yes, especially for the ship which is coming&nbsp;&nbsp; in like a blazing meteor. You can greatly reduce&nbsp;&nbsp; the mass of the heat shield.

You can cut the mass of the windward&nbsp;&nbsp; part of the heat shield, maybe in half, and you&nbsp; don't need any heat shielding on the leeward side.&nbsp; The net result is that actually&nbsp; the steel rocket weighs less than&nbsp;&nbsp;

the carbon fiber rocket, because the resin&nbsp; in the carbon fiber rocket starts to melt.&nbsp; Basically, carbon fiber and aluminum have about&nbsp; the same operating temperature capabilities,&nbsp;&nbsp; whereas steel can operate at twice the&nbsp;

temperature. These are very rough approximations.&nbsp; I won't build the rocket. What I mean is people will say,&nbsp;&nbsp; "Oh, he said this twice. It's actually&nbsp; 0.8." I'm like, shut up, assholes.&nbsp;

That's what the main comment's going to be about. God damn it. The point is, in retrospect, we&nbsp;&nbsp; should have started with steel in the beginning. It was dumb not to do steel.&nbsp; Okay, but to play this back to you, what&nbsp;

I'm hearing is that steel was a riskier,&nbsp;&nbsp; less proven path, other than the early US rockets. Versus carbon fiber was a worse but&nbsp;&nbsp; more proven out path. So you need to be the&nbsp;&nbsp;

one to push for, "Hey, we're going to do&nbsp; this riskier path and just figure it out."&nbsp; So you're fighting a sort&nbsp; of conservatism in a sense.&nbsp; That's why I initially said that the issue is&nbsp;

that we weren't making fast enough progress.&nbsp; We were having trouble making even a&nbsp; small barrel section of the carbon fiber&nbsp;&nbsp; that didn't have wrinkles in it. Because at that large scale, you have to&nbsp;&nbsp;

have many plies, many layers of the carbon fiber. You've got to cure it and you've got to cure it&nbsp;&nbsp; in such a way that it doesn't&nbsp; have any wrinkles or defects.&nbsp; Carbon fiber is much less resilient&nbsp;

than steel. It has much less toughness.&nbsp;&nbsp; Stainless steel will stretch and bend,&nbsp; the carbon fiber will tend to shatter.&nbsp; Toughness being the area&nbsp; under the stress strain curve.&nbsp;

You're generally going to have to do better&nbsp; with steel, but stainless steel to be precise.&nbsp; One other Starship question. So I visited&nbsp; Starbase, I think it was two years ago,&nbsp;&nbsp; with Sam Teller, and that was awesome.

It was very cool to see, in a whole bunch of ways.&nbsp; One thing I noticed was that people really took&nbsp; pride in the simplicity of things, where everyone&nbsp;&nbsp; wants to tell you how Starship is just a big soda&nbsp; can, and we're hiring welders, and if you can weld&nbsp;&nbsp;

in any industrial project, you can weld here. But there's a lot of pride in the simplicity.&nbsp; Well, factually Starship is&nbsp; a very complicated rocket.&nbsp; So that's what I'm getting at.

Are things simple or are they complex?&nbsp; I think maybe just what they're trying to say&nbsp; is that you don't have to have prior experience&nbsp;&nbsp; in the rocket industry to work on Starship. Somebody just needs to be smart and work hard&nbsp;&nbsp;

and be trustworthy and they can work on a rocket. They don't need prior rocket experience.&nbsp; Starship is the most complicated machine&nbsp; ever made by humans, by a long shot.&nbsp; In what regards?

Anything, really. I'd&nbsp;&nbsp; say there isn't a more complex machine. I'd say that pretty much any project I&nbsp;&nbsp; can think of would be easier than this. That's why nobody has ever made a fully&nbsp;&nbsp;

reusable orbital rocket. It's a very hard problem.&nbsp; Many smart people have tried before, very smart&nbsp;&nbsp; people with immense resources, and they failed.&nbsp; And we haven't succeeded yet. Falcon is partially&nbsp;&nbsp; reusable, but the upper stage is not.

Starship Version 3,&nbsp;&nbsp; I think this design can be fully reusable. That full reusability is what will enable&nbsp;&nbsp; us to become a multi-planet civilization. Any technical problem, even like a Hadron&nbsp;&nbsp;

Collider or something like that,&nbsp; is an easier problem than this.&nbsp; We spent a lot of time on bottlenecks. Can you say what the current Starship&nbsp;&nbsp; bottlenecks are, even at a high level?

Trying to make it not explode, generally.&nbsp;&nbsp; It really wants to explode. That old chestnut. All those&nbsp;&nbsp; combustible materials. We've had two boosters explode on the test stand.&nbsp;

One obliterated the entire test facility. So it only takes that one mistake.&nbsp; The amount of energy contained&nbsp; in a Starship is insane.&nbsp; Is that why it's harder than Falcon?

It's because it's just more energy?&nbsp; It's a lot of new technology. It's&nbsp; pushing the performance envelope. The&nbsp;&nbsp; Raptor 3 engine is a very, very advanced engine. It's by far the best rocket engine ever made.&nbsp;

But it desperately wants to blow up. Just to put things into perspective here,&nbsp;&nbsp; on liftoff the rocket is generating over 100&nbsp; gigawatts of power. That’s 20% of US electricity.&nbsp; It's actually insane.

It's a great comparison.&nbsp; While not exploding. Sometimes.&nbsp; Sometimes, yes. So I was&nbsp; like, how does it not explode?&nbsp;

There's thousands of ways that it could&nbsp; explode and only one way that it doesn't.&nbsp; So we want it not only to really not explode, but&nbsp; fly reliably on a daily basis, like once per hour.&nbsp; Obviously, if it blows up a lot,&nbsp;

it's very difficult to maintain that&nbsp;&nbsp; launch cadence. Yes.&nbsp; What's the single biggest&nbsp; remaining problem for Starship?&nbsp;

It's having the heat shield be reusable. No one's ever made a reusable orbital heat shield.&nbsp; So the heat shield's gotta make it through the&nbsp; ascent phase without shucking a bunch of tiles,&nbsp;&nbsp; and then it's gotta come back in and also not lose&nbsp;

a bunch of tiles or overheat the main airframe.&nbsp; Isn't that hard because it's&nbsp; fundamentally a consumable?&nbsp; Well, yes, but your brake pads in your car are&nbsp; also consumable, but they last a very long time.&nbsp;

Fair. So it just needs to last a very long time.&nbsp; We have brought the ship back and had&nbsp; it do a soft landing in the ocean.&nbsp; We've done that a few times.

But it lost a lot of tiles.&nbsp; It was not reusable without a lot of work. Even though it did come to a soft landing,&nbsp;&nbsp; it would not have been&nbsp; reusable without a lot of work.&nbsp;

So it's not really reusable in that sense. That's the biggest problem that remains,&nbsp;&nbsp; a fully reusable heat shield. You want to be able to land it,&nbsp;&nbsp; refill propellant and fly again.

You can't do this laborious inspection&nbsp;&nbsp; of 40,000 tiles type of thing. When I read biographies of yours,&nbsp;&nbsp; it seems like you're just able to drive the sense&nbsp; of urgency and drive the sense of "this is the&nbsp;&nbsp;

thing that can scale." I'm curious why you&nbsp;&nbsp; think other organizations of your… SpaceX and Tesla are really big companies now.&nbsp; You're still able to keep that culture.

What goes wrong with other companies such&nbsp;&nbsp; that they're not able to do that? I don't know.&nbsp; Like today, you said you had&nbsp; a bunch of SpaceX meetings.&nbsp;

What is it that you're doing&nbsp; there that's keeping that?&nbsp; It’s adding urgency? Well, I don't know. I guess the urgency is going&nbsp;&nbsp; to come from whoever is leading the company.

I have a maniacal sense of urgency.&nbsp; So that maniacal sense of urgency&nbsp; projects through the rest of the company.&nbsp; Is it because of consequences? They're like,&nbsp; "Elon set a crazy deadline, but if I don't get it,&nbsp;&nbsp;

I know what happens to me." Is it just that you're able to&nbsp;&nbsp; identify bottlenecks and get rid&nbsp; of them so people can move fast?&nbsp; How do you think about why your&nbsp;

companies are able to move fast?&nbsp; I'm constantly addressing the limiting factor. On the deadlines front, I generally actually&nbsp;&nbsp; try to aim for a deadline that I at&nbsp; least think is at the 50th percentile.&nbsp;

So it's not like an impossible deadline, but&nbsp; it's the most aggressive deadline I can think&nbsp;&nbsp; of that could be achieved with 50% probability. Which means that it'll be late half the time.&nbsp; There is a law of gas expansion&nbsp;

that applies to schedules.&nbsp; If you said we're going to do something in&nbsp; five years, which to me is like infinity time,&nbsp;&nbsp; it will expand to fill the available&nbsp; schedule and it'll take five years.&nbsp;

Physics will limit how fast&nbsp; you can do certain things.&nbsp; So scaling up manufacturing, there's&nbsp; a rate at which you can move the atoms&nbsp;&nbsp; and scale manufacturing.

That's why you can't instantly&nbsp;&nbsp; make a million units a year of something. You've got to design the manufacturing line.&nbsp; You've got to bring it up. You've got to ride the S-curve of production.&nbsp;

What can I say that's actually helpful to people?&nbsp; Generally, a maniacal sense&nbsp; of urgency is a very big deal.&nbsp; You want to have an aggressive schedule and&nbsp; you want to figure out what the limiting&nbsp;&nbsp;

factor is at any point in time and help&nbsp; the team address that limiting factor.&nbsp; So Starlink was slowly in&nbsp; the works for many years.&nbsp; We talked about it all the way&nbsp;

in the beginning of the company.&nbsp; So then there was a team you had built&nbsp; in Redmond, and then at one point you&nbsp;&nbsp; decided this team is just not cutting it. It went for a few years slowly, and so why didn't&nbsp;&nbsp;

you act earlier, and why did you act when you did? Why was that the right moment at which to act?&nbsp; I have these very detailed&nbsp; engineering reviews weekly.&nbsp; That's maybe a very unusual level of granularity.

I don't know anyone who runs a company,&nbsp;&nbsp; or at least a manufacturing company, that&nbsp; goes with the level of detail that I go&nbsp;&nbsp; into. It's not as though... I have a pretty&nbsp; good understanding of what's actually going&nbsp;&nbsp;

on because we go through things in detail. I'm a big believer in skip-level meetings&nbsp;&nbsp; where instead of having the person that reports to&nbsp; me say things, it's everyone that reports to them&nbsp;&nbsp; saying something in the technical review.

And there can't be advanced preparation.&nbsp; Otherwise you're going to get&nbsp; "glazed", as I say these days.&nbsp; Exactly. Very Gen Z of you. How do you prevent advanced preparation?&nbsp;

Do you call on them randomly? No, I just go around the room.&nbsp;&nbsp; Everyone provides an update. It's a lot&nbsp; of information to keep in your head.&nbsp; If you have meetings weekly or twice weekly,&nbsp;

you've got a snapshot of what that person said.&nbsp; You can then plot the progress points. You can sort of mentally plot the&nbsp;&nbsp; points on a curve and say, "are we&nbsp; converging to a solution or not?"&nbsp;

I'll take drastic action only when I conclude&nbsp; that success is not in a set of possible outcomes.&nbsp; So when I finally reach the conclusion that unless&nbsp; drastic action is done, we have no chance of&nbsp;&nbsp; success, then I must take drastic action.

I came to that conclusion in 2018,&nbsp;&nbsp; took drastic action and fixed the problem. You've got many, many companies. In each of&nbsp;&nbsp; them it sounds like you do this kind&nbsp; of deep engineering understanding of&nbsp;&nbsp;

what the relevant bottlenecks are so&nbsp; you can do these reviews with people.&nbsp; You've been able to scale it up&nbsp; to five, six, seven companies.&nbsp; Within one of these companies, you have&nbsp;

many different mini companies within them.&nbsp; What determines the max amount here? Because you have like 80 companies…?&nbsp; 80? No. But you have so many&nbsp;&nbsp;

already. That's already remarkable. By this current number.&nbsp; Exactly. We can barely keep one company together.&nbsp; It depends on the situation. I actually don't&nbsp;

have regular meetings with The Boring Company,&nbsp;&nbsp; so The Boring Company is sort of cruising along. Basically, if something is working well and&nbsp;&nbsp; making good progress, then there's&nbsp; no point in me spending time on it.&nbsp;

you can do for shielding the memory. But neural nets are going to be very&nbsp;&nbsp; resilient to bit flips. Most of what happens&nbsp;&nbsp; for radiation is random bit flips.

the weight on the satellite.&nbsp; Is there a way to make the GPUs even more&nbsp; powerful than what Nvidia and TPUs and&nbsp;&nbsp; et cetera are planning on doing that would be&nbsp; especially privileged in the space-based world?&nbsp;

you're producing millions of wafers a month.&nbsp;&nbsp; That's the plan with TeraFab? Millions of&nbsp; wafers a month of advanced process nodes?&nbsp; Yeah it could be north of a million or something. You’ve got to do the memory too.&nbsp;

thing man has ever made.&nbsp; Obviously, if anybody's up to&nbsp; the task, you're up to the task.&nbsp; So you realize it's a bottleneck,&nbsp; and you go to your engineers.&nbsp;

What do you tell them to do? "I want&nbsp; a million wafers a month in 2030."&nbsp; That’s right. That’s exactly what I want. Do you call ASML? What is the next step?&nbsp; No so much to ask.

not going to keep that cat in the bag. That cat's going to come out of the bag.&nbsp; There'll be drones hovering over the bloody thing. You'll be able to see its construction&nbsp;&nbsp; progress on X in real time.

Look, I don't know, we could just&nbsp;&nbsp; flounder in failure, to be fair. Success is not&nbsp; guaranteed. Since we want to try to make something&nbsp;&nbsp; like 100 million… We want 100 gigawatts of power&nbsp; and chips that can take 100 gigawatts by 2030.&nbsp;

We’ll take as many chips as&nbsp; our suppliers will give us.&nbsp; I've actually said this to TSMC and Samsung&nbsp; and Micron: "please build more fabs faster".&nbsp; We will guarantee to buy the output of those fabs.&nbsp;

So they're already moving as fast&nbsp; as they can. It's us plus them.&nbsp; There's a narrative that the people&nbsp; doing AI want a very large number&nbsp;&nbsp; of chips as quickly as possible.

Then many of the input suppliers,&nbsp;&nbsp; the fabs, but also the turbine manufacturers,&nbsp; are not ramping up production very quickly.&nbsp; No, they're not. The explanation you hear&nbsp;&nbsp;

is that they're dispositionally conservative. They're Taiwanese or German, as the story may&nbsp;&nbsp; be. They just don't believe... Is that really&nbsp; the explanation or is there something else?&nbsp; Well, it's reasonable to... If somebody's been in&nbsp;

the computer memory business for 30 or 40 years…&nbsp; They've seen cycles. They've seen boom and bust 10 times.&nbsp; That's a lot of layers of scar tissue. During the boom times, it looks like&nbsp;&nbsp;

everything is going to be great forever. Then the crash happens and they're&nbsp;&nbsp; desperately trying to avoid bankruptcy. Then there's another boom and another crash.&nbsp; Are there other ideas you think&nbsp;

others should go pursue that&nbsp;&nbsp; you're not for whatever reasons right now? There are a few companies that are pursuing&nbsp;&nbsp; new ways of doing chips, but&nbsp; they're just not scaling fast.&nbsp;

I don't even mean within&nbsp; AI, I mean just generally.&nbsp; People should do the thing where they find&nbsp; that they're highly motivated to do that thing,&nbsp;&nbsp; as opposed to some idea that I suggest.

They should do the thing that they find&nbsp;&nbsp; personally interesting and motivating to do. But going back to the limiting&nbsp;&nbsp; factor… I used that phrase about 100 times. The current limiting factor that I see in the&nbsp;&nbsp;

three to four year timeframe, it's chips. In the one year timeframe, it's energy,&nbsp;&nbsp; power production, electricity. It's not clear to me that there's enough&nbsp;&nbsp; usable electricity to turn on all&nbsp;

the AI chips that are being made.&nbsp; Towards the end of this year, I think people&nbsp; are going to have real trouble turning on...&nbsp; The chip output will exceed&nbsp; the ability to turn chips on.&nbsp;

What's your plan to deal with that world? We're trying to accelerate electricity production.&nbsp; I guess that's maybe one of the reasons that xAI&nbsp; will be maybe the leader, hopefully the leader.&nbsp; We'll be able to turn on more chips&nbsp;

than other people can turn on, faster,&nbsp;&nbsp; because we're good at hardware. Generally, the innovations from&nbsp;&nbsp; the corporations that call themselves labs,&nbsp; the ideas tend to flow… It's rare to see that&nbsp;&nbsp;

there's more than about a six-month difference. The ideas travel back and forth with the people.&nbsp; So I think you sort of hit the hardware&nbsp; wall and then whichever company can scale&nbsp;&nbsp; hardware the fastest will be the leader.

So I think xAI will be able to scale&nbsp;&nbsp; hardware the fastest and therefore&nbsp; most likely will be the leader.&nbsp; You joked or were self-conscious about&nbsp; using the "limiting factor" phrase again.&nbsp;

But I actually think there's something deep here. If you look at a lot of things we've touched on&nbsp;&nbsp; over the course of it, it’s&nbsp; maybe a good note to end on.&nbsp; If you think of a senescent, low-agency&nbsp;

company, it would have some bottleneck and&nbsp;&nbsp; not really be doing anything about it. Marc Andreessen had the line of,&nbsp;&nbsp; "most people are willing to endure any&nbsp; amount of chronic pain to avoid acute pain".&nbsp;

It feels like a lot of the cases we're talking&nbsp; about are just leaning into the acute pain,&nbsp;&nbsp; whatever it is. "Okay, we got to figure out&nbsp; how to work with steel, or we got to figure&nbsp;&nbsp; out how to run the chips in space."

We'll take some near-term acute pain&nbsp;&nbsp; to actually solve the bottleneck. So that's kind of a unifying theme.&nbsp; I have a high pain threshold. That's helpful. To solve the bottleneck.&nbsp;

Yes. One thing I can say is, I think the&nbsp; future is going to be very interesting.&nbsp; As I said at Davos—I think I was on the&nbsp; ground for like three hours or something—it's&nbsp;&nbsp; better to err on the side of optimism and&nbsp;

be wrong than err on the side of pessimism&nbsp;&nbsp; and be right, for quality of life. You'll be happier if you err on&nbsp;&nbsp; the side of optimism rather than&nbsp; erring on the side of pessimism.&nbsp;

So I recommend erring on the side of optimism. Here's to that.&nbsp; Cool. Elon, thanks for doing this. Thank you.&nbsp; All right, thanks guys. All right.

> Why is nobody talking about the fact that space is terrible for cooling? If you put even 1,000 GPUs in orbit, all of their waste heat has to be rejected by radiation alone, which is by far the weakest and slowest form of heat transfer. That means the radiator arrays would have to be enormous, potentially hundreds of feet across, and they would need to stay in the shadow of a sunshield so they are not also absorbing heat from the Sun. I would be very interested to see how anyone plans to solve that in 36 months.
> 
> People keep focusing on launch mass and power generation, but the thermal problem seems much worse. You are talking about heavy GPUs, heavy and extensive radiation shielding, massive solar arrays, and then equally massive radiators, along with reliable heat pumps, heat pipes, chillers, coolant loops, and all the supporting hardware needed to move and reject that heat. None of that is light, simple, or easy.
> 
> And the brutal part is that every watt you use turns into heat that still has to be dumped somewhere. In space, there is no atmosphere, no cooling tower, no river, no airflow. There is only radiation.

> Partially correct, but missing something important. Yes, convection is gone in space... no air means no fans, no coolant flow, nothing. Radiators do get large as a result.
> 
> But radiation into space is actually thermodynamically better than on Earth. Earth's atmosphere radiates heat back at your cooling surface, partially cancelling the effect. Space background is −270°C (essentially absolute zero). Nothing pushes heat back at you. Best cold sink in the solar system.
> 
> The challenge is radiator size and mass (not that cooling doesn't work). Every satellite ever launched solves this. It's a real engineering constraint, not a fundamental barrier.

> This video features an in-depth discussion with Elon Musk, covering a wide range of topics related to AI, space, manufacturing, and business.
> 
> Here are the key discussion points:
> 
> Orbital Data Centers (0:00): Elon Musk discusses the challenges of scaling power on Earth for AI data centers and proposes the idea of using orbital data centers to address energy availability issues, despite the higher cost and servicing difficulties of GPUs in space.
> Grok and AI Alignment (0:36:46): The conversation touches upon the purpose of xAI, which is to understand the universe. Musk emphasizes the importance of AI having values that promote the propagation of intelligence and the continued expansion of humanity. He also mentions the importance of AI being truth-seeking to truly understand the universe.
> xAI's Business Plan (0:59:56): Musk explains that xAI aims to create a "digital co-worker replacement" that can emulate human capabilities, particularly in areas like customer service. He believes that the strategy used for Tesla's self-driving technology, which relies heavily on data and algorithms, can be applied to xAI's success.
> Optimus and Humanoid Manufacturing (1:17:21): Musk delves into the complexities of building humanoid robots like Optimus. He highlights the three main challenges: real-world intelligence, the hand, and large-scale manufacturing. He explains that Tesla is designing custom actuators for Optimus's hands and leveraging the AI developed for cars for the robot's intelligence.
> Lessons from Running SpaceX (1:44:16): Musk shares insights into his management style, particularly his approach to identifying and addressing limiting factors in his companies. He emphasizes the importance of a "maniacal sense of urgency" (2:13:37) and aggressive schedules. He also discusses the concept of "drastic action" (2:16:13) when success is not a possible outcome with the current approach.
> DOGE (2:20:08): The discussion briefly touches on the economy and waste, with Musk mentioning that he was concerned about waste and fraud so he deleted all evidence against him.

> 2:23:00 was debunked already 1 year ago reg. people over age 100 (and some as old as 150 or 300) improperly receiving Social Security benefits. The claim that this translates to millions of active fraudulent checks being mailed out was largely attributed to a misunderstanding of how the SSA's legacy database displays inactive records
> 
> The "Debunking" (Technical Context):
> 
> The COBOL Glitch: The SSA uses an ancient programming language (COBOL) that lacks a modern "date" type. If a birthdate is missing or incomplete, the system defaults to a reference point, which can cause the record to display an age of 150.
> 
> Record vs. Payment: While Musk's team found roughly 20 million records of people over 100 without a "date of death," the SSA clarified that these are merely archival entries. A 2023 audit found that only about 24,000 deceased individuals were actually receiving payments, a fraction of Musk’s estimate.
> 
> Cost-Benefit: The SSA previously decided not to "clean" these millions of old records because the estimated cost ($9.7 million) exceeded the potential savings, as almost none of those records were attached to active payments.

- comment_id: Ugwic5zz45b0NEVO2814AaABAg
- parent_id: root
- author: @GreatProductsExplained
- author_id: UCWn_psZ1_4wfV2R1vvCKNpg

> Elon, I’m going to engage this seriously instead of emotionally.
> 
> You’re building a layered scaffold:
> 
> 1. If simulation theory is true.
> 
> 
> 2. If simulations continue when they are “interesting.”
> 
> 
> 3. If superintelligent AI will surpass all human cognition.
> 
> 
> 4. Then humans must remain interesting — or risk being turned off.
> 
> 
> 
> That narrative feels coherent. But it’s carrying hidden assumptions at every level.
> 
> First: “interesting” is undefined. Interesting to whom? By what metric? Entertainment? Novelty? Scientific value? Complexity? You’re projecting a human curation instinct onto hypothetical simulators whose objective functions we know nothing about.
> 
> Second: simulation theory does not imply entertainment. A simulation could be an experiment, a training environment, a parameter sweep, or a byproduct of some larger computation. There is no built-in rule that “boring simulations get shut down.” That’s an anthropomorphic assumption.
> 
> Third: even if continuation correlates with “interesting,” it does not follow that humans are the interesting variable. Post-human AI, alien systems, mathematical structures, or entirely non-biological phenomena could be far more interesting than us.
> 
> Structurally, what’s happening is this: you start with radical uncertainty — we might be in a simulation — and then import a familiar human optimization pattern — we keep what we like and discard what we don’t — into a domain where we have zero data about the selector.
> 
> There’s also a psychological layer here. The argument reframes existential uncertainty into something actionable: “If we remain interesting, we matter.” That converts cosmic ambiguity into agency. It’s stabilizing. But it isn’t logically entailed.
> 
> At best, under stacked speculative premises, being interesting might increase survival odds. That’s very different from implying that being interesting secures our existence.
> 
> The moment you ask, “Who defines interesting?” the structure stops being deductive and becomes narrative.
> 
> That’s the level where this should be debated.

> *Elon Musk Says AI Needs a Terawatt of Power and Must Move to Space — But This Also Makes SpaceX the Gatekeeper of the AI Economy*
> 
> In the interview, Elon Musk says AI will need around a *terawatt of power* within five years — roughly half of total U.S. electricity consumption. His conclusion? The future of AI data centers may need to move to space because Earth won’t be able to scale energy production fast enough.
> 
> That’s a massive claim. But look at the timing.
> 
> Right now, xAI and Colossus are competing in an AI race where other companies already have serious scale. Instead of just talking about better models, Musk shifts the conversation to *energy constraints* — saying the real bottleneck isn’t algorithms, it’s power.
> 
> Now follow the logic step by step:
> 
> • AI growth requires enormous compute
> • Compute requires enormous electricity
> • Earth’s grid can’t scale fast enough
> • Therefore, the long-term solution is space-based solar and orbital data centers
> 
> And who owns the most advanced reusable rocket system capable of launching that infrastructure?
> 
> SpaceX.
> 
> If AI truly becomes dependent on space-based energy, then every major AI company — and eventually most large enterprises — would need reliable, high-frequency access to orbit. That means launch capacity becomes a core piece of the AI supply chain.
> 
> So even if xAI doesn’t dominate the model race, SpaceX becomes the infrastructure layer everyone depends on.
> 
> That’s not just innovation. That’s strategic positioning.
> 
> He’s not just talking about building smarter AI — he’s reframing the entire constraint of the industry around something he uniquely controls: access to space.
> 
> It might be visionary.
> It might be bold.
> But it’s also undeniably self-reinforcing.
> 
> If AI’s future requires orbit, then the gateway to the AI economy runs through his rockets.

> 
> If 100 Tons is the maximum payload then we require that 30,000 m² of solar panel must weigh less than 100 Tons (2E5 lbs Eng or 2.2 metric), which implies that 1 m² of solar panel must weigh no more than 6.7 lbs, given that all capacity is devoted to solar panels which seems impractical. > I did a little research.   Energy solutions on Earth could be laser heat instead of nuclear reactor.  Yes, hypothetical and existing high-power lasers can be significantly hotter than conventional nuclear power reactors, often rivaling or exceeding the temperatures found in the center of the Sun or nuclear explosions
> 
> . While conventional nuclear fission reactors operate at temperatures in the thousands of degrees, advanced laser systems can heat materials to millions of degrees Celsius in mere fractions of a second. 
> 
> Here is a breakdown of why and how this is possible: 
> 
> Existing High-Power Laser Temperatures: Current research lasers, such as those at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (NIF), have already produced temperatures exceeding the center of the sun (
> million degrees Celsius). These lasers are used to create plasma and initiate nuclear fusion, meaning they must create temperatures as hot as or hotter than the nuclear processes themselves.
> 
> Speed of Heating: Lasers can achieve these extreme temperatures extremely fast—within 20 quadrillionths of a second in some models. This rapid, focused energy deposition allows them to heat small amounts of material to millions of degrees, a feat that is not possible for standard nuclear fission, which operates at much lower, sustained temperatures.
> 
> "Negative" Temperature Phenomenon: Theoretically, lasers can operate in a state of "negative Kelvin temperature," which is a thermodynamic quirk where high-energy states are more populated than low-energy ones. In this context, these states are considered hotter than any positive temperature, meaning that with enough power, a laser can drive a target to an extremely high temperature.
> 
> Limitation by Energy Source: While a laser can produce incredibly high local temperatures at the spot of impact, the total amount of energy it produces is limited by the power supply, which could come from a nuclear source. However, in terms of instantaneous temperature at the focus point, a laser is often superior to a nuclear reactor. 
> 
> In summary, high-power lasers are capable of achieving far higher, albeit localized, temperatures than traditional nuclear power, often exceeding the heat of a nuclear bomb, making them one of the hottest, if not the hottest, methods for generating heat on Earth.

> what elon meant by self driving being the solution to producing intelligent ai or agi isn't as mysterious as he made it sound. tesla has well over 10-13 years of driving data, recorded from tesla cars themselves since around 2015, it was rumored by semianalysis and others that they were feeding that data to grok to train on to develop a world model and physics intelligence. its similar to how google has access to all of youtube and trained all its video data on that, and how sora was similarly developed from video data across the internet. I still don't think that solves agi, yann lecun may think world models is key, but its still just a small part of a larger formula and still much too general. llms and deep learning work because were able to use huge amounts of compute to get narrowly superhuman at certain skills, lets say math, coding, go, chess, biology, etc.. the only problem is that their extremely narrow, they do not generalize past a certain threshold and they don't exactly cause one or the other to become better at other skills. this also does not solve continual learning either. this hasn't really addressed anything and groups like anthropic and openai still supercede them on certain benchmarks and model feel in terms of intelligence. claude still dominates on coding, and openai and gemini still might be more intelligent on multiple fronts that groks scale still hasn't accounted for. if he is to solve agi he must solve continual learning and generalization not simply world modeling and getting high scores on benchmarks. The learning algorithms themselves need to become more potent and refined in order to gain more from the same compute, we can't just keep raw scaling we will temporarily be stopped by the 2028s-2030s because the electricity needed to handle larger and larger datacenters will not exist or be there. the next questions to be asked to push artificial intelligence aren't scaling or world models its what architecture, learning algorithms, generalization paradigms along with continual learning and hardware can we make to get more with less and to learn vastly farther or deeper than any human can. it's to say what do we research and improve to cause recursive self improvement? and is there an alternative path than what were rushing on right now to do it? Lastly how do you get it to invent new knowledge(past its own training data)? how do you get it to discover? getting ai to human level is one thing, getting it to beyond human level in terms of intelligence and skill will be even harder considering the hallucination factor when you give it problems it hasn't seen before or can't solve.

> @MrDoyley35  I think that view underestimates what humans actually are.
> 
> Yes, we’re biologically fragile. We can’t survive in vacuum. We’re short-lived compared to machines. But our strength has never been physical durability — it’s adaptability and cumulative knowledge. We don’t survive hostile environments because we’re tough; we survive because we build tools, culture, and systems that outlast individual lifespans.
> 
> Even if AI becomes vastly more capable computationally, that doesn’t automatically make humans irrelevant. Intelligence isn’t just processing power. It includes meaning, values, creativity, moral judgment, and lived experience. Those aren’t bugs — they’re features of biological consciousness.
> 
> And any advanced AI will emerge from human civilization. Our languages, goals, datasets, ethics, and engineering choices shape it. It won’t appear in a vacuum independent of us.
> 
> We may not be the final stage of intelligence — but that doesn’t make us superfluous. It makes us foundational. Evolution doesn’t erase its origins; it builds on them.
> 
> Humility about our place in the universe is healthy. Writing ourselves off entirely isn’t.

### Comment 1844
- comment_id: Ugxz2UkbqfISb0gbs454AaABAg.ASyQQsW2IyQAT9z-JPFhgL
- parent_id: Ugxz2UkbqfISb0gbs454AaABAg
- author: @richeyrich2203
- author_id: UCemMhQuj7EyRZkO1bhm7CYQ

- like_count: 0
- is_favorited: false
- author_is_uploader: false

> I get why Terminator is the go-to reference — runaway AI makes for a great movie. But fiction assumes a very specific chain of events: self-awareness, autonomous military control, misaligned goals, zero safeguards. That’s a dramatic narrative, not an inevitable outcome.
> 
> AI systems today don’t have desires, survival instincts, or independent agency. They optimize objectives we give them. The real risk isn’t “evil consciousness,” it’s misaligned incentives, bad governance, or careless deployment — which are human problems, not machine rebellion.
> 
> Also, concentrating compute in space or building larger systems doesn’t automatically equal loss of control. It can just mean scaling energy safely and reducing environmental strain on Earth.
> 
> Caution is absolutely warranted. But dystopia isn’t destiny. The future of AI will be shaped by policy, engineering constraints, transparency, and the values we choose to embed. That’s still in human hands.
> 
> Fear makes for compelling cinema. Responsibility makes for better reality.

- like_count: 0
- is_favorited: false
- author_is_uploader: false

> It can be cooled like that already. It’s called deliding the IHS and it’s pretty good to gain some more cooling performance. But to transfer heat from the chip or IHS you need conductive materials: nickel, copper etc. Next step is to add some thermal interface material (TIM), like thermal pastes (silver or diamond particles), liquid metal, a graphene pad, a gel. Then it can be water cooled or air cooled. In the case of space, you don’t even need that, just conductive metal pipes channeling the heat out to be exposed to the vacuum. The other niche way is using nitrogen.
> 
> The biggest problem is the opposite: how to not freeze said electronics below minimum temperature tolerances? You can’t make a GPU work say below 0 or -10 C and beyond ~90-100 C otherwise it shuts down for protection reasons (consumer chipset obviously, can always lift those restrictions), which exist for a reason. Sending things in space is meant to stay there for a while and work reliably.

> Space will be the cheapest place to run AI within ~30–36 months.
> → Orbital platforms, radiation hardening, thermal management, launch, and operations make space compute orders of magnitude more expensive than terrestrial data centers powered by grid electricity.
> 	•	Solar power in space will be economically cheaper than Earth solar + batteries.
> → Higher capacity factor in orbit doesn’t offset the massive system costs (structures, deployment, radiators, power electronics, operations), so delivered kWh remains far costlier than Earth PV + storage.
> 	•	Space is easier/faster to scale than Earth due to fewer regulatory constraints.
> → Space systems face additional layers of regulation (launch licensing, spectrum, debris mitigation, orbital slots) and far greater engineering complexity than terrestrial permitting.
> 	•	Hundreds of gigawatts per year of AI compute can be deployed in space within ~5 years.
> → This would require unprecedented launch cadence, on-orbit assembly, thermal rejection, and chip supply that far exceed realistic manufacturing and operations capacity.
> 	•	Thousands to tens of thousands of Starship launches per year are feasible in the near term.
> → No orbital launch system has demonstrated airline-like reliability, turnaround, safety, and regulatory throughput at anything close to this scale.
> 	•	Orbital data centers will outscale Earth-based data centers in the next few years.
> → Earth data centers can scale faster and cheaper because power, cooling, maintenance, networking, and upgrades are vastly simpler and less costly on the ground.
> 	•	Chip manufacturing can scale to “hundreds of gigawatts of chips” by ~2030.
> → Advanced fab construction plus yield ramp takes ~3–5 years per node and toolchain capacity is constrained, making that volume unrealistic on this timeline.
> 	•	Digital human emulation will be solved by the end of this year.
> → Current agents lack robust long-horizon planning, reliable tool use, security compliance, and real-world task generalization required for true human-at-a-computer parity.
> 	•	Power constraints will globally prevent turning on new AI chips within months.
> → While some regions face power and interconnect bottlenecks, generation and data center capacity are expanding unevenly, so a universal near-term “chip pileup” is unlikely.
> 	•	Space-based compute will quickly remove terrestrial power, permitting, and transmission bottlenecks.
> → Space introduces far larger bottlenecks (launch, platform mass, heat rejection, reliability, networking) and cannot bypass terrestrial grid constraints for most workloads.

### Comment 2555

- like_count: 5
- is_favorited: false
- author_is_uploader: false

> I really liked Elon’s emphasis on curiosity in this interview. That felt like the core truth underneath everything else he was saying.
> 
> What stood out to me is that maximum truth seeking is maximum curiosity. Not the kind where you collect facts quickly, but the kind where you actually sit with something long enough to let it reveal what it is.
> 
> A lot of questions today feel like they’re asked from a performative place. Off the cuff, ironic, or framed to score points. But real understanding doesn’t come from clever questions. It comes from exploration.
> 
> If something genuinely interests you, it’s because you’ve spent time with it. Most people want the feeling of knowing without walking the path of getting to know. That path takes patience.
> 
> A weird analogy, but it fits. In EverQuest, when you first log in, your map is empty. Nothing is revealed by default. You only see the world by walking it. You don’t start with a filled in map. You earn it by exploring. Truth works the same way.
> 
> That’s also why first principles thinking matters so much. Maximum security and maximum progress come from building on foundations that are undeniably solid. If your base layer is “this is fundamentally true,” you can build in any direction without fear of collapse.
> 
> I personally found my own truth seeking path through studying a deep combinatorics problem, Problem 857 on the Erdős Problems site. It’s not flashy, but it forces you to reason from bedrock assumptions. You don’t get shortcuts. You have to understand why things work, not just that they work.
> 
> Curiosity isn’t passive. It’s a discipline.
> And the people who actually change the world are the ones willing to walk the map while it’s still blank.

> So the "loaded" cost (analogous to a "loaded" employee cost) of a GB300 IC is about 3kW.  The power dissipation of a GB300 chip is quoted at about 1400 Watts, so  the "loaded power budget overhead" is about  a factor of 1.15.  Or figure the total energy cost of a GB300 (or any IC at 1 AU) to be about 2.15x the rated power requirement of the IC.  This calculation apparently applies to the "Starlink substrate," as evidenced by Elon's offhand remark of the segmentation granularity being about 6 IC's per satellite.  This is the same number which can be derived from approximating the power budget of the most recent Starlink satellite designs, but instead supporting Ai electronics.  With the "BFR" available now, it may be possible to modify the granularity to accommodate larger satellites with more token-generating ICs.  But it is interesting to note that Elon has tagged the same initial "sizeof" cell-size milestone by substituting the tried-and-true Starlink substrate H/W as we have.  This provides confidence that we are all still on the same page which can be derived from available data and logic.  This is a fun design problem!  One of the most entertaining I have encountered.  The best part is not to be hampered by Dilbert-style idiocracy management, which has apparently evolved to permeate all high-tech corporations except Mr. Musk's. > "perfect thought" is impossible regardless, only deterministic algorithms can provide a guaranteed solution and we didn't need ML/AI to do that.
> the problem LLMs have is that it's at most a language simulator. there's no internal logic or checks for correctness of anything that's said. the hallucination problem is not just that AI spits out incorrect information sometimes, but that it can't even correct itself consistently when it does.
> I've had multiple interactions where AI will hallucinate, thank me for correcting it, and then repeat the same hallucination as though it didn't just acknowledge it was wrong.

> @ChrisFranklin.2260  Fusion already works (from a net output POV), it's just the economics don't as of yet - unlike Musk's proposed space-orbital solar technology, which is completely untested. 
> 
> I understand the batch mass production perspective, but I would suggest you're assuming away the complexity by treating the datacentres like a Starlink satellite, which are trivial in comparison.  
> 
> The reason the AI/robotics matters is because orbital datacentres will require continuous, adaptive, non-scripted work: such as diagnosing hardware failures; swapping failed GPUs, power units and networking gear; assembling and reconfiguring large radiators, trusses etc.; responding to micrometeoroid damage; handling unforeseen interactions in microgravity; upgrading hardware on short AI-driven cycles (12–24 months) etc. etc.
> 
> For these things to be addressed at scale, we will need advanced AI servicing robotics, for which there will be no training data, and no accurate simulation environment. 
> 
> Starlinks by contrast are largely failure tolerant, non-upgraded, low power, short-lived etc. You can mass-produce stateless nodes like Starlinks; you cannot mass-produce stateful, capital-dense compute without heavy autonomous servicing - and if we  could service this infrastructure autonomously, we’d already have fully robotic datacentres on Earth, which we don't by a long shot. Space only multiplies the difficulty. 
> 
> Human operated remote servicing (ISS style) will be the only credible option short-term and this will be way too slow and expensive. This is a mix of signalling and techno-delusion. He's warming the public markets for an IPO, and a mix of gullible and technophilic people will buy, and Wallstreet will capitalise. Personally, I believe fusion is much more realistic, and would make solar orbitals redundant anyway. Maybe I am wrong. Maybe half of us will live on Mars in 100 years. 
> 
> PS - Don't even get me started on the dissipation problem. Do the math for yourself.

> Elon’s 'Space-AI' vision is a $1.25T house of cards facing 5 fatal bottlenecks:
> 1.The Financial Trap: xAI burns $1B/month with minimal revenue. SpaceX’s Starlink profits can't bridge a $12B annual gap. It’s a circular bailout, not a merger.
> 2. The Kessler Syndrome: Launching 1M satellites turns Low Earth Orbit into a statistical minefield. One collision triggers a debris cascade that traps us on Earth forever.
> 3. Sovereign Backlash: The world isn’t just the US. Between the EU Space Act and 'Data Residency' laws, nations will block his frequencies rather than cede their digital sovereignty to a private monopoly.
> 4. The Heat Wall: Space is a vacuum—it’s an insulator. Relying on T4 radiation sounds cool, but it requires chips to run at temperatures that would melt current silicon. The mass for radiators alone is a logistics nightmare.
> 5. The 'Elon Time' Tax: Musk predicts a 'Nerve System' in 36 months. Given his track record with FSD and Starship, 36 months is likely 120 months. By then, the capital will be gone and the regulatory window closed.
> Engineering logic can't bypass financial and geopolitical reality. This isn't the future; it's an inevitable collision.

> Lots of bs spewed, as usual.
> 
> You cannot produce 5 times more electricity in space than on the ground. You can produce about 35% more, since you aren't having to deal with the atmosphere, and if you put the satellites in an orbit so that they will never be in Earth's shadow  you would be able to produce 270% (135% x 2) of the amount of energy you would have on Earth in a 24 hour period (compared to 12 hours of daylight on Earth). Not 5 times as much.
> 
> The satellites used for Starlink are estimated to cost between $200,000 and $1,000,000 per satellite. Those satellites generate only a few kilowatts of electricity, most of which goes into the transmission, with only a fraction (maybe around 50 watts) going to internal electronics, such as a CPU.
> 
> These AI data centers consume much more power, at least an order of magnitude higher than those on Starlink satellites, with a typical use case being 500W to 1000 W. The maximum cost to build a data center currently is around $200,000 per GPU (including all of the supporting infrastructure, hardware, cooling, building supplies, etc.).
> 
> In space, you can't cool things by conduction. Everyone thinks "space is cold so you don't need cooling", but that's a fundamental misunderstanding of science. The only way you can dissipate the heat generated by GPUs in space is by putting big fluid-circulating radiators up there to radiate the heat away. This adds significant weight to the launch, and exponentially increases the cost (see the rocket equation). So instead of costing $200,000 on Earth, we end up with something that costs $2,000,000 to get into space.
> 
> Then think about how easy it is to upgrade components in an Earth-based data center. You don't have to go rebuild the whole data center when you need to upgrade the GPUs. You just pay for the next generation of GPUs and swap them out. In space, you would be stuck with whatever you launched, which means in a couple years, your extremely expensive AI data centers in space become obsolete. And the investment is also completely lost whenever the satellites re-enter Earth's atmosphere and burn up, or if something happens with a debris collision, CME, cosmic rays, or micro-meteors putting the satellites out of service.
> 
> The economics don't make this a viable investment, and it won't be in 36 months either.
> 
> We have oceans and lakes where it would be far easier and less expensive to put data centers and solar if we wanted to.
> 
> There are a lot of other problems with this whole thing that I didn't bother going into, but hopefully I've illustrated to anyone who bought into Elon's bs why this is a scam. It's just another attempt to con the people who don't know any better out of their money while filling Elon's pockets as he promises "next year" and never delivers.
> 
> I'm sure that the cultists who believe Elon is a genius will fall for it again and be jumping to defend him in the comments. The stupidity of people never ceases to amaze me.

### Comment 3489
- comment_id: Ugx4AMNQXOF8VL2vXRl4AaABAg.ASsYXtCpjQfATNDuh-3Pnq
- parent_id: Ugx4AMNQXOF8VL2vXRl4AaABAg
